The teacher and students were gathered around a table with the entire class, engaged in a discussion about the form and content of the play Fences. The teacher explained that students would be working in groups to analyze the play through various thematic lenses. Identified themes included masculinity, racism, injustice, and trauma. Each group was assigned two themes to guide their discussion, and this information was also displayed visually on the classroom TV.

Students then moved to their designated group tables and immediately began their discussions. They used a spiderweb discussion rubric that outlined expectations for participation and engagement. When asked, students shared that they had previously annotated the text as part of their summer work.

Throughout the visit, all students were actively engaged in conversations centered on their assigned themes. The teacher circulated among the groups, observing and interacting with students. When asked about his note-taking, he explained that he was documenting students use of specific examples from the play during their discussions.

As a next step, students mentioned they would participate in a fishbowl activity to share insights from their group discussions. The teacher noted that the groups were formed using a strength-based approach and that he would be mapping the student dialogue and taking notes on individual contributions during the activity.

We began our first week by sharing family photos and exploring our cultural backgrounds. The students were especially curious about the variety of languages spoken in our classroom, sparking engaging discussions.

This unit offers meaningful opportunities for students to share their celebrations, and personal stories. One highlight will be our "Name Stories", where students will discover the connections between their names and their cultural heritage, helping them take pride in their roots.

We will also create "Language Profiles" together, allowing each student to share the languages they speak or hear at home, along with special words or phrases from their culture. I am also having daily read aloud that focuses on diversity and how we are 'same same but different'. 

The aim is to foster empathy, celebrate diversity, and strengthen bonds as students learn about each others identities.

They used a framework to respond to eight statements, indicating whether they agreed or disagreed and providing explanations for their opinions. The teacher instructed the students to finish their thoughts, mentioning it was fine if they weren't fully complete. She then introduced a "Compass Points" activity, sharing it visually on the TV and explaining it verbally. In this activity, the teacher presented a statement, and students moved to one of four sides of the room to show if they strongly agreed, agreed, strongly disagreed, or disagreed. There were visuals labeling the room and the students were asked to physically choose a side.

The teacher emphasized the importance of hearing from all voices during this activity. As she read a statement, students positioned themselves accordingly and shared their reasoning for their choices. The discussions were characterized by students exchanging thoughts, acknowledging each other's contributions, and using each other's names to build on ideas. They communicated using positive and supportive language.

This activity was repeated three times, allowing all students the opportunity to share with the group. During their discussions, the teacher made connections to the upcoming novel they would be studying in class.

Thank you for coming in Lori. We're at the very beginning stage for Grade 10 Math Core and the fundamental concept is function. Some hooks and scaffoldings are still in place so unsurprisingly no one knew why we are learning this. In my humble opinions, I think sometimes it works better when someone knows how before knowing why, just like human beings in the old days figured out that shaking off clothes can let off the dust, before we discovered the Newton's Law of Inertia. Math is applied to many different fields in the real world and in this course we will be exposing students to many different applications including earthquake magnitude, pH scales, tidal patterns, loudness of sound, etc. At this stage, we focus on building the basic understanding, and sometimes I think it is also a great idea where we just enjoy the beauty of patterns in math, which is what the Criterion B in MYP is focusing as well. When being asked "why are we learning so many unless math?" by students, I always use yoga as an analogy. We learn all the yoga moves that we rarely have chance to perform in everyday life, yet those moves implicitly help our coordination and mental health. Some aspects of math are for the same purpose too. The logical reasoning and problem solving can help us see things in different perspectives, which can implicitly help us in observation and decision making in our everyday life. Math includes real-life applications and logic, where both of them are extremely helpful to how we see our world. 

I also noticed that this class contains fast and slow learners, so at times we do have people finishing faster and people finishing slower. Therefore, I choose to help weaker students first, and once the class roster is fixed, I will start creating seating plans to pair students with different levels so they can help each other.

Students observed a model for Pattern One, checked their notes for reference, and prepared to share later with peers.

Students were challenged to create three examples, each using a different verb. Many began writing quickly, while some asked clarifying questions as the teacher circulated. Using the dry-erase table-tops, students wrote large-scale examples in varied colors and styles, underlining the pattern. As they worked, some monitored their pace in response to the teachers time cues.

First, I was thrilled that the observation happened right as we were doing something exciting in class! Its always a dynamic lesson when students get to see photos being taken live on the front screen.

For example, I asked them, Show me how you control aperture or Show me how you control shutter speed, then let them take over. If they werent sure what to do, they could "phone a friend" and ask a group member for help. It worked okay, but it might be a little early in the unit to put students on the spot. Next year, I think Ill wait until the 4th or 5th class before having them use the camera in front of everyone. By then, theyll have a stronger foundation to build on.

These first few lessons are a bit chaotic since the students are still learning the basics of cameras and photography. I dedicate three full days to shooting photos, which we then upload to Teams for class critiques. This isnt graded beyond participation, and I emphasize that critique is an essential part of learning photography. They should get comfortable with not getting things right the first time.

When we make movies, there are constant reshoots, and the same mindset applies. They shouldnt fall in love with their first take; theyre only graded on the final product. The key is to keep going until they get it right!

Hi Virginia,

Thank you so much for taking the time to observe my lesson today.
My intention for the warmup activity was to maintain a fast-paced environment to keep students engaged, active, and focused. I've found that starting the lesson this way helps them practice using their eyes and ears to follow instructions from the very beginning.

The cones serve as a visual and spatial guide for two main purposes. 1, to help students understand personal spacing and 2, to ensure their safety as they moved. I also structure the warmup with multiple, tiered challenges. This allows students to experience moments of success while also encountering tasks that require continued effort, which I believe helps build their resilience and motivation.
To answer your question about how I would handle a student still intentionally bumping, first I would say that I likely will find this will discontinue to happen. Routines will be reinforced each class to help them understand it is not appropriate. If a few students continue with this after a lesson or two, I will begin to make sure that I am in proximity and help give more personal cues to the student.  Sometimes I will pause and reset the class and have a brief conversation about the importance of spacial awareness and safety. Another method I have used in the past is greet the student before class or before the activity and give them the personal challenge of not bumping. These methods should work and within a few classes it becomes habit for them. 

Thanks again for coming and hope to see you back in the gym again soon!

When the weather forced us indoors, I was initially concerned about maintaining engagement with a completely different lesson. However, I decided to involve students in the problem-solving process rather than simply directing them through a backup plan.
Student Collaboration:
I was impressed by how quickly students brainstormed indoor alternatives and helped determine our activity sequence. Their input genuinely shaped the lesson structure, and I found this collaborative approach actually enhanced rather than hindered our time management.
Student Leadership:
Allowing students to lead the warm-up activity felt natural and kept them invested in the lesson. It also freed me to observe and support individual needs, like the student experiencing back pain.
Inclusive Modifications:
The students' suggestion to adapt basketball into line basketball was brilliant - it maintained the connection to our planned one-touch fitness game while ensuring everyone could participate meaningfully. These student-initiated modifications often work better than my original plans.
Learning Outcome:
What could have been a disruptive lesson change became an opportunity for authentic student agency. The fitness activities still served their curricular purpose as preview/review, but students gained valuable experience in collaborative problem-solving and adaptability - skills that extend well beyond PHE class.
This experience reinforced my belief that students can be trusted partners in their learning, even when circumstances require quick pivots.

Your wondering is a pretty big question! We are working to foster a culture of caring and support in our KG classes. With a safe space where students feel safe to take risks and try new things, students will be able to take the risks (emotional and social, not physical) and push themselves farther. In my experience, that is the moment when a student will surprise themselves and discover that they are, in fact, musicians. Another part of this is in setting them up for success, carefully tailoring the activities to give them the greatest chance of getting that sense of accomplishment. 

Additionally, we are looking at another facet of this, reflection. We encourage self-reflection and self-motivated growth. (e.g. "how did that song/game go? What went well? What could have gone better? What can you change next time?") As the semester progresses and we gear up for the concert preparation cycle, this will shift more to the forefront.

At this time of the year, we are getting to know our spaces and our boundaries, what is possible and what activities are available. To do so we focus a lot on the different things we can do in Tiger Class.

In the first month of school, I try to model lots of different activities so students can see some of the options. We sometimes look at photos or videos of the students engaging in different activities during reflection time. We put these videos on the screen and the featured student can choose to share what they were working on or thinking about during that play. Other students can ask questions and perhaps they will be encouraged to try out those activities next time. 

Another way we can talk about what we are thinking sometimes occurs after our morning meeting or after story time in the afternoon. I ask the students to think about all the things they can do in Tiger Class (we can make say them out loud) and to choose something they would like to play with. Then, students share their choices about what they will do after leaving our circle time. This might give some other students some fresh ideas. 

In addition, we encourage our families to look at Seesaw photos together. We provide them with some prompts for questions to ask their children. This helps parents to get better answers when they ask their child the question, "What did you do at school?".

The dots were colored to indicate which day the students worked at which station. Sonia used the MATHS format, introduced by Tonya Gilchrist during PD last year.

The students walked around the room saying mingle, mingle until Sonia called out create groups of 6. Students quickly created groups of 6. Sonia counted the number at each group and celebrated each complete group. In the second round, Sonia told the students they would make a group of 2+3. Students shouted 5 and went to make groups. The students were excited and the room got a bit noisy. Sonia called them back together and then had the students count the groups by 5s. Students played one more round of the game. 

When the game was over, Sonia asked the students to put their hands down and put eyes on her. She asked the students if they remembered their stations and sent them off to work.

As the students began working in their different centers, the noise level in the room grew. Most of the conversation in the groups was happening in Chinese. Sonia rang a chime and reminded the students at the H station to keep their voices at a quieter level. 

Sonia worked with a small group of students while the other students engaged in their stations.

Thanks for the visit and for the thoughtful feedback.
Although students worked from the same template (the units must-know characters), the task was personalized. Using their iPads, students consulted online dictionaries to look up and add self-selected new words. This allowed each child to choose vocabulary aligned to their level and interests; stronger writers could add multiple words, and early finishers transitioned to a character flashcard game that reinforced recall and stroke accuracy. As the unit progresses, I will layer in tiered choices using a Must/Should/Could structureMust: write target characters accurately in sentences; Should: add at least one self-selected word and use it in context; Could (extension):build a short paragraph or incorporate an idiom/collocation. I will also provide scaffolds (e.g., sentence frames, optional Pinyin-to-characters revision, stroke-order animations) and quick checks for understanding to form flexible groups. In this way, we maintain common learning goals while honoring diverse readiness levels, ensuring every student is supported, challenged, and engaged.
For the second wondering, we do not assign routine written homework and our standing expectation is reading only. If a class task extends beyond the allotted timeeven with in-class supportstudents may complete it at home. No new content is introduced as homework, and any at-home work should take no more than 1015 minutes. I will communicate this to parents. Students who cannot complete work at home will be given class time during the next session without penalty.

In my lessons, I can guide students in practicing empathy by embedding structured opportunities for perspective-taking. For example, when we explore Rammy Makes a Choice, I can extend scenarios by asking students to consider not only what they would do, but also how another student in the situation might feel. Students could turn to a partner and finish prompts such as, If I were in their shoes, I might feel
 or What might my friend need from me in this situation?

I also plan to model empathetic responses by verbalizing my own thought process (e.g., I notice that if someones crayon broke, they might feel disappointed, and I could help by sharing mine). Building on the movement activity, I could adapt the pairing routine so that after students identify whether a situation is a big or small problem, they also practice responding with an empathetic statement or action. For example, in the scenario where someone is left out of a game, an empathetic statement might be, I would feel sad if I couldnt join. Do you want to play with us? and an empathetic action could be making space in the group and inviting them in.

These opportunities keep empathy rooted in real-life classroom and peer situations, aligning with our school goals of fostering social-emotional growth, strengthening relationships, and supporting student well-being.

The documentation allows us to develop a deeper understanding of each child and their growth. Many of our students use their native language when engaged in play, and by listening carefully to these conversations (as Ms. Yvonne did in both Chinese and English), we gain valuable insight into their thinking, understanding of the world, and knowledge base. We see that they are fluent and confident in expressing complex ideas in their home language, which helps us recognize their true capabilities.

This information enables us to be more intentional in our planning, creating meaningful provocations that build on what we learn from the documentation. It supports us in personalizing learning experiences, ensuring we are responding to the whole child and not just what we observe in English. For example, based on Ms. Yvonnes notes, students were collaboratively building a zoo, using blue Magna-Tiles for aquatic animals and green ones for land animals. With this knowledge, we can extend their learning by offering opportunities to investigate animals and their habitats, providing additional building materials, or even planning a field trip to the zoo.

Equally important, having dated records of observations, photographs, and notes allows us to look back and clearly see each childs growth. Sometimes these changes are visible in just a matter of weeks, while other times they unfold gradually over months. This documentation helps us track developmental progress, celebrate milestones, and plan the next steps with greater accuracy and intention.

Upon entering, students were observed sitting with notebooks and laptops open, following along with the teachers PowerPoint presentation. Most students were writing key points from the slides into their notes. During questioning, however, only one student regularly responded aloud. The teacher posed questions on buoyancy using examples such as a duck, a person floating, ice, and fish. While several students looked up or nodded slightly, almost all verbal answers came from a single student seated near the front.

Students had limited opportunities to share their own ideas before information was provided directly. For example, the teacher explained details about fish bladders and their relationship to depth, with students primarily copying notes rather than engaging in extended discussion. At one point, two other students responded tentatively with single-word answers, which were affirmed briefly without names being used.

When the topic shifted to viscosity, the teacher asked if students had heard of the term. After silence, the definition was read aloud, and again the same student provided most responses, with one additional student contributing an example (honey). While students were attentive and compliant in note-taking, their engagement in dialogue was minimal and opportunities to process or check for understanding together were very limited.

column10: Students were aware, if not fully attentive, to the presentation and diligently recorded key points from the slides into their notebooks, demonstrating focus and a willingness to capture core information.

column13: A few students tentatively attempted to contribute answers beyond the dominant voice in the room (e.g., mass and honey), reflecting some willingness to participate even when not consistently invited by name.
column14:
How might students be supported to engage in more frequent, distributed participationsharing ideas, clarifying thinking, and responding to one anotherso that understanding can be checked and built collectively rather than primarily through note-taking?

Additional Direct Feedback

Currently, questioning patterns direct nearly all interactions to a single student. Calling on students by name and distributing participation more equitably would give all learners space to contribute and demonstrate their thinking.

Avoid moving on immediately after asking Ok? or Clear? Instead, pause and require students to articulate their understanding before advancing to the next slide.

Eye contact and body orientation signal inclusivity. Turning questions only toward one student unintentionally narrows engagement; scan the room and invite multiple voices into the dialogue.

Consider restructuring pacing: allow time for students to converse or think aloud before recording notes. This would shift the balance from teacher-provided answers toward student processing and peer learning.

Build in wait time after posing questions. Silence can be productive if students know they are expected to respond.

column18: Thank you for taking the time to observe my class and share your feedback. I appreciate your suggestions about distributing participation more equitably and allowing more wait time for responses. For context, when you entered, I was introducing key biological terms and definitions to prepare students for the upcoming activity. Since many students are still developing confidence with scientific vocabulary, this segment was intentionally teacher-led to ensure they had the language to engage in the work that followed. After your observation, students rotated through seven hands-on water property stations. At each, they explored the property demonstrated, discussed its importance to living organisms, and later completed a Kahoot review. These activities provided opportunities for collaboration, processing information, and applying concepts beyond note-taking. Partner discussions were embedded in tasks, though not always in the elbow partner format you suggested. Stations included: Molecular model kits, Floating a paper clip on water, Dropping water on a penny, Testing if ice sinks or floats, Dissolving salt in water, Observing the heating curve of water & Watching capillary action in a tube. I recognize that, within the 8 minutes you observed, student responses may have seemed limited. However, judging overall engagement based on this snapshot may not fully reflect the lesson design or student participation across the period. I also want to share encouraging feedback. Joe observed my class and said, I am so happy to see fun activities in your lessons every day. I need to include more in mine. He later messaged me, It was amazing to see your kids laughing, engaged, and learning. Finally, I am still learning student names and using strategies to address them equitably. I avoid cold-calling while they are developing confidence with terminology, as some have shared they understand concepts but struggle to articulate answers. I value your feedback & will continue working on suggested strategies.

They demonstrated awareness that accuracy in this lab was critical for preparing for an upcoming summative. When retrieving and handling dry ice, the teacher actively monitored stations to ensure safety, rotated between groups, and reminded students of time constraints. Teacher prompts (Why do you not want it to touch the side?) and encouragement (Its okay, try. Just do your best.) supported students in refining their methods and achieving more accurate results.

column18: For call and response activities, I start with responses that are fixed, such as the line from a story or song that does not change. I am also watching and listening to the students as they sing to notice if some of them are singing all the words with me, then I can gradually release responsibility for the entire song to them, usually by asking them to "teach" me the song or story. For other opportunities to co-create learning experiences, I am moving around the classroom during the day being invited by students to play with them or see what they are doing. I can also start playing with toys by myself which will draw the attention of students who will want to join. During the play we are giving suggestions for what to do next, suggesting complications (oh no! The dinosaur is sneezing. It has a cold. What can we do?).

What I could have done : 
Students would write / say sentences using both the verbs and the vocabulary. (Students could have written on their table).
Students could have said / written more specifically what they have for their breakfast (which is different than what French people have. For that activity, students might not have had enough vocabulary and I was afraid to not have enough time to help everybody. (It is very much culturally specific!)

Upon entering, students were observed working quietly at tables on their laptops to finish design briefs in a PowerPoint. Several students explained that this was preparation for a summative and that they appreciated having class time to work on it. Students expressed having some choice in the piece of furniture they designedsuch as chairs that were more comfortable, relaxing, or adaptable in heightbut all were working toward the same purpose: creating a more comfortable and relaxing piece of furniture. The target audience was appropriately set as peers in their own age group, allowing them to connect the project to their lived experiences with classroom furniture.

Students used the teacher-provided template to guide their work and were encourage to use data from measurements they had previously taken to inform their designs. While most could describe the assignment clearly, a few gave incomplete or inconsistent answers about their designs purpose, intended audience, or making the connection to the earlier data activity.

The teacher checked in individually with students, encouraging them with tips on how to do their best and reminding them to use past learning and research (e.g., measurements) to strengthen their work. Students were supported in translanguaging, with the teacher allowing them to draft in Chinese and use a dictionary tool to clarify meaning in English. The class was orderly and productive, and students remained highly focused throughout. As I exited, the teacher had begun closing the lesson by reviewing expectations and affirming effort with enthusiastic phrases that motivated students to continue.

Upon entering, students were observed in the idea-generating stage of a design cycle, working on bridge concepts for Criterion B. They explained that they had completed research on the functions and some design elements of bridges and were now creating multiple rough drafts to consider. "These are our raw ideas," stated one.  Students anticipated giving feedback to peers and then narrowing down their designs.

Students were directed to read their feedback, reflect quietly on 23 ideas to develop further, and record their narrowed choices on sticky notes for submission. While some students reflected thoughtfully, others struggled to remain quiet during this independent stage, and chatting continued to build across the large group of 26. It was challenging to ascertain to what degree of success they had reflected, but it did seem that all completed the task at least superficially.  The teacher gave further instructions for storing and labeling their work.  All students appeared attentive and complied with directions.

In conversation, students described incorporating elements of Chinese design and local culture into their ideas, indicating the authenticity and variety of approaches encouraged. They appreciated the freedom to create multiple drafts before deciding which concepts to pursue more fully.

During this lesson, students were in the idea-generation stage of Criterion B, drawing multiple bridge concepts in the first half of class before providing peer feedback and reflecting in the second half. They then narrowed their ideas to two or three designs to develop further. With a class of 26, maintaining quiet focus during independent reflection was sometimes challenging, and many students needed occasional redirection to stay on task. However, all students completed the activity and responded positively once expectations were reinforced.
 
This unit was inherited and restructured at the start of the year to make it more authentic and locally relevant. Students are designing a bridge that could serve as a landmark in Guangzhou, drawing inspiration from Chinese cultural and architectural elements. Moving forward, I plan to experiment with different attention and transition strategies such as the Adaptive Schools hand-up signal or a short countdown to support smoother, more age appropriate focus shifts. This will help students strengthen self-regulation skills and understand that effective communication requires shared protocols, creating a more inclusive and purposeful classroom environment.

column7:
At the beginning of the lesson, students were introduced to the concepts of objectives, obstacles, and tactics, displayed on the screen. The teacher explained these ideas by reading directly from the slides and connecting them to Romeo and Juliet, which she noted students had read or would soon read in English depending upon their grade level. This attempt to create a clear connection across subjects seemed appropriate, but the students who had read the play weren't asked to share their ideas, making it a more teacher-directed connection.

Students listened attentively during the introduction.  When asked if they were clear, there were no objections, so the teacher proceeded to the day's task. 

Despite the absence of two classmates and the small size of the class (5 students), students adapted to a modified group structure. They participated enthusiastically in multiple rounds of improvisation, creatively applying tactics and obstacles to meet the given objectives. At one point, students were so engaged that they requested additional time to keep working.

The teacher used a timer to manage pacing, which helped students sustain focus and energy across the activity.
column9: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column10: Students engaged with creativity and enthusiasm in their improvisations, taking the given objectives and obstacles and transforming them into playful, meaningful performances. Their request for extra time reflected both enjoyment and ownership of the activity.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: Students demonstrated adaptability by fully committing to the modified activity structure despite classmates being absent. Their willingness to dive in and contribute reflected a sense of trust in the learning environment.
column14:
How might students be invited to articulate objectives, obstacles, and tactics in their own words before beginning the activity, so that their understanding is checked and their voices help shape the framing of the activity?

Additional Direct Feedback:

The opening of the lesson was highly teacher-directed. Consider shifting more responsibility to students at this stagesuch as having them read the slide, paraphrase a concept, or connect the idea to Romeo and Juliet themselves. This would allow students to take greater ownership of the learning and demonstrate comprehension.

Pausing for a deliberate check for understanding before launching into activities would help ensure that all students are ready to apply the concepts meaningfully in their improvisations and fully understood the directions.

Both of the above suggestions could be easy tweaks which would completely shift the lesson from teacher-driven (controlled) to more student-centered and agentic.

column18:
Thank you for the observation and feedback. 

I was encouraged to see that students creativity and collaboration were acknowledged, especially their enthusiasm for extending the activity and their adaptability in a smaller group setting.

The feedback regarding the opening of the lesson was very useful. I agree that the introduction was more teacher-directed, and I recognize the importance of creating more space for students to take responsibility at this stage. Based on this feedback, in the following lesson I applied this suggestion by asking students to explain and demonstrate the concepts of objectives, obstacles, and tactics to classmates who had been absent. This allowed students to articulate their understanding, reinforce/review key ideas, and establish a stronger sense of ownership in the activity. They did so successfully and the absent student was able to catch up. 

Moving forward, I will continue to build in further opportunities for students to paraphrase definitions, check understanding, and connect concepts themselves before beginning the main task. This will ensure that comprehension is visible and will support a shift toward more student-centered learning earlier on in the process.

column7:
Students were seated in their table groups, some at standard desks and chairs, others at lower sitting tableswhile the teacher stood at the front of the room introducing an auditory letter recognition activity. Each student had an individual erasable writing template and a marker at their workspace. As the teacher observed the class, she identified which students appeared prepared and discussed what readiness looked like before beginning.

The activity started with the teacher instructing students to write the letter or letters that corresponded to a specific sound she pronounced aloud. After giving them time to record their responses, both the teacher and the educational assistant circulated around the room to monitor progress and provide support. Students identified they wanted to share raised their hands, while others were called on directly. When responses were shared, students erased their boards and prepared for the next auditory prompt.

Once the letter recognition portion was complete, the teacher extended the challenge to focus on whole words. She wrote beginning, middle, and end on the board, prompting students to identify which sound in a given word had changed and to determine whether a sound was added, deleted, or replaced. During this phase, the teacher checked in with each student individually.

Before concluding, she asked the class to participate in one more activity before giving them an opportunity for a movement activity. Students dispersed to find open space in the room, and together they transitioned into a kinesthetic exercise spelling out words using the shapes of their bodies. The combination of auditory, visual, and physical elements encouraged full participation, with all students contributing to the learning experience.
column10: During the activity, students were given the opportunity to engage by indicating their willingness to contribute through raising their hands. The teacher then selected individual students to share their responses or ideas with the class. This approach encouraged inclusivity while allowing for a variety of perspectives to be heard. As a result, a significant number of students took part, demonstrating enthusiasm and active participation throughout the session.

column13: Recognizing the need for physical movement, the teacher incorporated a kinesthetic element into the lesson. Students transitioned from sitting to standing, engaging their whole bodies to form the shapes of letters and collectively spell out words. Throughout the activity, they demonstrated their understanding in multiple ways by writing their responses on their boards, verbalizing their answers to the class, and physically representing their ideas through movement. This multimodal approach kept energy levels high, supported diverse learning styles, and maintained active engagement from all students.

Students are currently leveled into three main groups to ensure their needs are met at an appropriate pace and level. One group is pulled out by Jonathan to extend learning for students working beyond the 60% group, while Ms. Felix and Ms. Ickey pull out another group to support emerging learners. The students who remain in my classroom during that time receive lessons aligned with the 2nd grade pacing and needs identified through the BOY benchmark assessments.

After the lesson, all students return to the classroom and have opportunities to practice the skill independently, with a partner, or with myself or Ms. Elizabeth, depending on the day. The five station groups are also scaffolded to address individual needs more specifically than the UFLI lessons alone, allowing us to target learning even more effectively.

When I checked in with students during the activity, most corrections were related to learning how to use the phonics whiteboards since they are new materials. Academically, the majority of students demonstrated understanding and were able to complete the task independently. A few students benefited from hearing words pronounced more dramatically to distinguish commonly confused vowel sounds (such as short a and short e) or from receiving extra support in segmenting sounds within a word.

Students were observed to be ready with their music and enthusiastic to perform a new piece, which they described as really beautiful. This was their first time working through the score, one that a student indicated would likely be performed at a future concert.
The teacher mentioned that he would change his conducting style before they began, and a few students noticed the difference and commented after when prompted.  The teacher affirmed their responses and explained his intention. 

As the teacher fetched sheet music for one student, others intuitively set up for the next activity and began warming up independently, stopping attentively when signaled to regroup. Students followed along with their parts, adjusted to tempo corrections, and responded to sectional focus (e.g., percussion, saxophones, 3rd clarinets). They remained attentive to quick verbal and visual cues and demonstrated strong self-discipline as members of the ensemble.

When prompted to self-assess their second attempt at this new piece of music, students raised their hands to indicate improvement, showing awareness of their collective progress. One student explained to me that he found the piece particularly challenging as a less experienced musician in the group and because it was his first time reading in ¾ time, which he pointed to on the music while speaking with me.  The clarinet players indicated that they found it helpful when the teacher played his instrument with them to model.

Kyle is faciltiating the G4  community time and has the screen and space set up in the G4 RamSpace.

He explains that we will be finding out more about their secret friend through letter writing. 
Students have questions and raise their hands - Kyle asks them to hold their questions and promises "all will be revealed" 
Kyle explains that the letters they will be writing will be Anonomous and explains what this means and so asks students not to sign their names or tell their secret friend too much about their school or grade level. 
Kyle provides students with some time to think - "what questions might you ask your secret friend if you are trying to find out more about them so you can make them a gift?" 
Kyle invites students to turn and talk.. and repeats the question.. 
The other G4 teachers and EAs join the students for the conversations and support in the prompts. 
Kyle gives FA countdown. 
Kyle asks for three students to share examples of the type of question they might ask their secret friend. 
Student responses include: "What do you like to do?" , "What is your favourite hobby?", 
Kyle praises George for waiting patiently with his hand up. 
Students continue to share ideas with whole group. "Are you a boy or a girl?" , "Do you wear glasses?" 
Kyle reminds students we are looking for information so we know what to make them as a gift? - So would that be an important question?  
Kyle then redirects attention to the screen and the next slide.. and introduces some of the ideas he had - the screen is divided in half (Split screen) 
Basic facts about the secret friend, and refers to the language profile students have previously created - giving us information about our secret friend. 
The other side of the screen is more "Open, or deeper questions"

Kyle again makes reference to some of the connection games students have been playing in class to get to know each other.

Clarifying question from students " Can everyone we are writing to read / understand English? " - Kyle assures them that they can.

column7: This observation summary reflects the recent Caregiver Coffee session, DEI Education Series: Overview of Student Support Services and Service Provisions. As part of this presentation, Delissa collaborated with the Upper Elementary Learning Support Teacher to deliver a short workshop for parents. Their objective was to foster empathy among parents for students with additional learning needs. To illustrate these challenges, task instructions were presented in a hard-to-read font, background noise was played, and some tasks were written in deliberately complicated language to make them nearly indecipherable. As parents struggled to complete the tasks, Delissa explained that this mirrors the daily learning experiences of some students. Afterward, various tools were introduced to help parents access the tasks more effectively and focus their attention  for example, magnifying glasses, noise-cancelling headphones, and other supportive aids. The key takeaway was that learning support teachers work to identify the right tools and strategies to help students access learning equitably and achieve success.

Thank you for the thoughtful question! I noticed moments when students required different levels of scaffolding, which is why I incorporated differentiation throughout the lesson. For example, when asking students to predict what the little snake would eat, some students responded quickly, while others hesitated. I provided additional support through visuals, gestures, and repetition for those who needed it, while extending learning for more confident students by asking them to justify their answers or use the vocabulary in a sentence.

In a mixed-ability group, I look for cues such as facial expressions, response time, and language choice to determine the level of scaffolding required. I aim to maintain an inquiry-based approach by asking questions and encouraging students to explore meaning at their own level of understanding. Storytelling at the Kindergarten level is an excellent way to foster inquiry while also developing language and vocabulary. When comprehension gaps appeared, I provided support without taking away their agency, ensuring all students could engage meaningfully with the story and vocabulary. I am still exploring ways to differentiate effectively to support diverse needs and learning styles.

Thank you again for this question?it really helped me reflect on my practice and think more deeply about how to balance scaffolding and inquiry in a mixed-ability classroom.

Amelie began the lesson with the guidance song to help the students calm down. She brought out a picture of a pie and invited the students to smell the pie and blow it out. She told the students this is what she does when she needs to focus and feel calm.
Next, Amelie showed the students a bag that she brought. She reminded the class eyes are watching, easrs are listening. Using a very quiet voice, she told the students that she wouas going to pull out items from her bad one at a time and asked them to think, if they were going to put them into to groups, how would they do that. One by one, Amelie pulled them out and had the students name the items. Once all the items were out, she reminded the students that they are going to think about how to group these items. She modeled naming groups such as young and old, boy and girl.
One student shared her thinking - Amelie noted that the items are not boys or girls. She then put the items in big and small. She noted that we also can have big or small problems. She pulled out a bar with pictures to note big and small problems. Amelie asked the students to share what a problem is. Then she told the students that a big problem is when there is an emergency, when someone is or might get hurt or if we cant solve it on our own.
Amelie asked the students to think what are some small problems that we have. She shared pictures on the Seewo to help the students think about different problems. She put the problem scale in front for the students to refer to and she asked the students to think about different scenarios. When the students thought about the problems, Amelie asked different students to use a visual ring on the scale to show if they decided it was a big or small problem. She reminded the students that when they have a small problem, they dont have to cry, but they can say I can solve it. Students noted that they could use Rammys Choices to help them solve the problem. Amelie also asked the students to share ideas about how they could solve the problem in the scenario.

column18:
Thank you for your thoughtful and encouraging feedback. I'm glad the opening ritual was effective - I just started doing it with the students this year. I also appreciate you noting the use of visual aids, which is also one of things I want to work more on. The students' ability to connect this new learning to existing tools like "Rammy's Choices" was a fantastic moment that showed their growing agency.

The biggest challenge will be that a child's emotional reaction (e.g., feeling very sad or angry) does not always correlate with the actual size of the problem. A seemingly small problem like a broken crayon can feel like a "big" problem to a frustrated child. Students may initially classify any problem that upsets them as "big. A child's background and temperament will influence their perception. A student who has never experienced a scraped knee might see it as a huge emergency, while another might see it as a minor inconvenience.

I would explicitly teach that we can have big feelings about small problems, and that's okay. The next step is to help them calibrate their reaction to match the size of the problem. We could use a visual like a thermometer, where the problem size is on one side and the expected reaction size is on the other.

This cannot be a one-time lesson. I plan to embed it in everyday life - When a problem arises in class, we can gently reference the scale. ("I see there's a problem. Let's think about the size of this problem. Is it a 'we need a teacher right now' problem or an 'I can use my words' problem?) Create a classroom anchor chart with clear, picture-based examples of big and small problems that we co-create and refer to often would be a good idea too. I will work with teachers to gauge their preferences.

With only five students, use tight, joyful routines that make peer learning feel natural and safe. The strategies below nurture collaboration and peer-to-peer learning.
 Set up three stations. Teacher Table (tones/formation), Word Lab (manipulatives and write-and-wipe), and a Practice Corner for paired speaking/readingrotating every 68 minutes; the Rotating Buddy fills any odd group and offers quick support, keeping practice balanced and focused on full sentences. 
	Use Fishbowl and Coach. Two students hold a short target-language exchange while three coaches with a mini checklist (clear voice, accurate tones, full sentences), give a quick two stars and a wish, then rotate so everyone both practices and coaches.
	2 pairs and 1 buddy. Group five learners into Pair A, Pair B, and one Rotating Buddy who switches after each activity. This boosts talk time and lets the buddy act as a mini knowledge messenger, carrying ideas and strategies between pairs. Assign simple rotating rolesspeaker, coach, writer, checker. In this way, every student practices language, supports peers, and stays accountable.

I am glad you noticed students felt free to ask questionsthat is what I aim for. It is a pity I missed one student when turning back to the board; the more questions, the richer the discussion. This is a large group, and managing time and attention can be challenging.

Some of my own reflections:

- One students intervention was less about content and more about frustration from feeling overwhelmed. I reminded them that this is THE topic in Math Applications where they face a completely new concept with different language and approaches, so it is normal to feel overwhelmed and important to practice patience.

- That student wanted to move quickly to how to calculate. I suspect that many prefer formulas to avoid critical thinking. A key focus of mine is to push beyond formulas and encourage deeper reasoning.

Interestingly, that same student later shifted into abstract thinking and suggested approximating the curve like a line of best fitan original idea not in my plan. I immediately adapted the explanation around it, which motivated him, reduced his anxiety, and seemed to help the class connect better. These are the moments I value, when student input reshapes the flow of the lesson.

Often such shifts mean the remainder of the class diverges from the original plan, and that happened here. But adapting based on student ideas has worked well for me many times.

- Regarding broader participation: yes, this was a teacher-led session. This was an introduction to a new topic, I chose this time to establish a foundation first. Other times I begin with explorations or investigations, which allow more peer interaction and one-on-one discussions. That order changes, this year the next class we will use this approach.

- On stopping the video: students enjoy the videos, but with demanding material they disengage after a few minutes. The videos also contain many ideas worth pausing to clarify, stopping the video helps to keep the students engaged.

Although the students were easily distractible, they remained engaged and attempted to complete the work.

Are you sure? and recorded their data collaboratively. The teacher monitored pace and provided steady encouragement, reinforcing the importance of accuracy without taking over the work.

The teacher maintained patience and positivity throughout the observed interactions.

When I entered, students were working quietly on laptops, spread around the room, some at table and others in more comfortable seating. The teacher was at a table in the front, also working on her laptop, and did not immediately notice my arrival.

Students explained that they were researching "old people from a long time ago"/historical figures (e.g., Gandhi, Mandela...) to learn what they thought about rights and freedoms, though they expressed some uncertainty about the ultimate purpose of the work or what they would do with the information once gathered. Students shared that they had not chosen whom to research; rather, the teacher had assigned a list of people and provided the resources.

Several students appeared disengaged or unclear. One student at the back had math homework open and only switched to the class assignment when approached.  Another was observed watching a video unrelated to class and when asked, told me he planned to finish the classword at home. Four students in the corner, seated on beanbags, explained that they were reviewing prior Lesson 10 work while others were working on Lesson 11, research. They clarified that the independent, silent format was in place because of MAP testing, so students had something to do as they finished at different times.

As additional students re-entered from testing, the teacher instructed the class to finish watching the videos as homework and check their answers in Teams. This was delivered as students were packing and preparing to leave, and students began to walk out as soon as the teacher has finished speaking. Of particular concern, I learned at the end of class that MAP testers had been sent across the hall to work in the study box unsupervised.  The teacher and I discussed the need for active monitoring, and the better choice might have been to allow the finished students to work independently in the open areas outside the classroom while she monitored the testers.  Her choice to do the opposite was based on a desire to keep them on-task in the classroom, not realizing that the MAP testing students might use the lack of supervision to their advantage while taking the language test.

While there were a couple of students observed to be off-task, the majority appeared to be taking advantage of the time given to stay current on their assignment.
column14:
I wondered how might students be given more clarity and engagement around the why of the research task and more opportunities to share their findings, so they see purpose in their work and connect it to larger concepts of rights and freedoms?

Additional Direct Feedback:

Students did not demonstrate clear understanding of the purpose of the research or how it connected to subsequent learning. Stronger framing of objectives and explicit checks for understanding are needed so students know the why and what next of their tasks.  Even bringing students together in those last few minutes of class and getting some of them to share their big "discoveries" of the day might have allowed you to know if the work they were doing was on track to meet expectations.  Directions at the end of class were unclear and delivered without closure. Consider using an attention-getter, summarizing key points, and providing a clear sense of next steps.

Monitoring of student engagement was inconsistent. While some students worked as intended, others were off-task (e.g., doing unrelated homework) without teacher redirection. Proactive movement around the room is necessary to maintain accountability.

The decision to send MAP testers to an unsupervised location across the hall was a serious lapse in judgment. Test conditions must be secure, and this incident may require results of several students (6?) to be invalidated. As discussed, please self-report this to the coordinator.

The students were seated on the floor at the front of the room as Patti led a discussion about a passage they had just read. She encouraged them to think about the characteristics of the two boys in the story, repeatedly rephrasing her question to draw out more ideas.

Patti then explained that they would receive similar texts to the one they had just read. For each text, they were to list all the inferences they could make about the characterswhether related to personality traits or physical characteristics. She restated the steps for completing the task and pointed out that the directions were posted on the board for reference.

Afterward, Patti distributed the texts to the students, instructing them to also get their reading notebooks and book boxes so that, once they had finished the assignment, they could transition to independent reading time. She let them know that anyone with questions could remain seated on the carpet.

As the papers were handed out, students collected their boxes and journals and moved to their tables. Several needed to cut their papers to fit into their notebooks, so they began with that step. Patti noticed a few students who started right away and reminded the others that she was waiting for them to begin.

About two minutes later, most students were focused on cutting and pasting their papers into their journals; within five minutes, the majority were reading the passage and starting the task, although a few were still having difficulty getting engaged.

Patti worked with Lucas at the small table, re-explaining the directions and helping him get started. She then noticed that Siu Siu was not yet ready. Patti asked, What are you missing?prompting Siu Siu to remember she needed her journal. Patti also spoke with Albert, reminding him to look for text evidence, before sitting down beside Siu Siu to help her begin her work.

What action might your character do?

Later, I spoke with Ellie, who was designing her cover page in Canva. She explained that she was publishing her narrative writinga story about something real that could happen.

Last year, the carpet was getting very dirty from the art materials and the proximity to the sink and students did not want to sit on it. I ordered a foam mat to try instead but it did not hold up. We used the carpet to meet at the beginning of every class and it was nice to have everyone in a smaller area. 
I had some talks with Virginia about possibly purchasing modular furniture for the space where the carpet was and with Katriona about the space and lesson flow. I wasn't able to come up with a solution that I am entirely happy with, but decided on using the space for more table seating as I have some larger classes this year. It also saves us some precious art time by eliminating a move from carpet to tables. However, I do want to have more flexible seating options for students and when the renovations come to the third floor, am planning to create some different spaces within the enlarged classroom and work areas in the hallway.
For now, I think my best solution is to reinforce classroom agreements and listening skills. I was so happy to see their excitement that I didn't remind them about listening behaviors as I probably should have.

Thank you for your thoughtful question and for highlighting the importance of ensuring continuity in our Upstander work. I completely agree that building upon prior knowledge is key, and its something I keep in mind when designing lessons across grade levels.

I want to clarify that while there may be some familiar elements from the Grade 4 work, the Grade 5 lessons and resources are not a repeat. They are designed to revisit core concepts in order to deepen understanding, while also introducing new layers of discussion and application that are developmentally appropriate for Grade 5. This progression is intentional, reinforcing key messages while extending students capacity to apply them in more complex and meaningful ways.

With regard to assemblies, last years Upstander assembly centered on the theme of being a Bully Buster. On reflection, that message was more focused on how to stop bullying in the moment. This year, the assembly deliberately shifted to a broader lens, encouraging students to SEE, SPEAK, and STAND UP for those who need support. This reframing expands the scope of what it means to be an upstander beyond reacting to bullying, and instead empowers students to act in a wider range of social situations.

The aim is always to revisit and reinforce key concepts while introducing new language, perspectives, and strategies that deepen students understanding and strengthen their ability to apply these skills. I would welcome the opportunity to share how the lessons are structured to build on last years foundation and to explore any additional ways we can continue to develop this important part of our curriculum together.

Students were seated in table groups with laptops open while the teacher displayed a graphic on the screen, asking them to tell me what you think this means. Students whispered to peers to check their understanding. The teacher used a random generator to call on students, creating a safe and fair way to select voices.

When called upon, students were invited to share any observation, even a comparison to a prior graphic. The teacher affirmed contributions while extending them with clarifying questions (e.g., So which ones are at risk? Or, whats safe?). Humor was woven into prompts, helping students feel at ease. Recognizing that one student had been asked several questions through extension and was starting to hesitate with his answers, the teacher shifted to another student, who also participated comfortably.

Connections to prior learning were encouraged without giving away answers, such as reminding students prior learning in G10. Students attempted recall, sometimes with approximate answers that the teacher affirmed while clarifying further. Several were asked to provide specific insights (e.g., one strength, one weakness), and they responded willingly, smiling and engaged.

The discussion transitioned to the Donut Economics Model, again with humor. Students were guided to compare models, connect to social justice concepts, and consider the sweet spot of the donut, though the humor was less effective here. ;). Not all students spoke loudly enough for their peers to hear.  Two students were observed taking notes while others listened but did not appear to make note of anything.

column18: Thanks for coming in Lori!  This was the last lesson for topic 1 for my  DP1 ESS class.  We have a test next class on the entirety of topic 1 (Foundations of ESS). We have been talking about sustainability and how one can measure it.  The previous class we discussed 2 different models and of how sustainability can be measured. We looked at (Ecological Footprint (EF) and the 17 UN Sustainability goals (SDG's) so they have a little experience with sustainability models. The IB ESS course like the kids to be able to evaluate (look at the strengths and weaknesses) of models so I was trying to get them to this as a class before I sent them off on their own to explore more in depth.  After you left, the class, I gave them an assignment where they did a jigsaw activity where they (along with 3 partners) took a deeper dive into 4 of the models.  Each group needed to share a ppt document and be the expert in their model.   At the end of class, for closure, I chose a random student and asked them a question or 2 about a model one of their group members was the expert on.  In general, the kids did a good job with this activity and like working not only with each other, but engaging with the content.   I think in general the most difficult part of IB is giving the kids Agency because the IB curriculum is strict in what it wants the kids to know.  I feel somewhat lucky with ESS because I am able to give them a some room to choose and to take ownership of their learning because of topics like this.  I am able to give them a little background on the content the IB needs them to know then send them on their way to dig deeper into those selected choices.  It's certainly not 100% free choice but the kids are able to at least have some choice of what to dig into.

column7:
G7 INS students were observed sitting in table groups, working quietly and independently, on their GRASPS assessment task: pretending to be aliens and deciding if a society is suitable to receive advanced technology as explained by one student. The teacher monitored progress, sitting or kneeling beside students to share responses at their level and collaborating with the educational assistant to clarify tasks.

Students explained that they had been assigned to regions and then selected specific countries to research. They could explain a need to develop an argument for or against providing advanced technology, using research into government and economic systems. Those I spoke with seemed to be less clear about the research question.  They described needing to identify pros and cons, cite events that illustrate those systems, and consider elements such as political beliefs and distribution of power.

Students reported they would submit a research document by September 18 and a final product (choice of format, e.g., video or presentation) by September 24. While some students spoke clearly about the expectations, others could not fully articulate how their work would be graded or how evidence should be used to support claims. One student described his work simply as a report, with limited detail about expectations.

Two students articulated more fully that they were analyzing advantages and disadvantages of their countrys systems, but they had not yet connected this work to using evidence to support a final assessment. This was consistent with being in the early research stage.

Students appreciated the freedom of product choice, but the large number of class days allocated to independent work raised questions around how to sustain variety, engagement, and forward movement.

I often observe my students at the start of indoor inquiry. I pay attention to their levels of engagement. If they are deeply involved in their play and problem-solving, Ill step back and let them explore independently. However, if they seem stuck or disengaged, stepping in to provide guidance or support can help reignite their interest. Ill also step in when conflicts arise, if one of the Eas are not there already. 

While I observe the students I will also look for teachable moments. If I notice students creating something unique, stepping in to ask questions or encourage further exploration can enhance their learning experience unless they are deeply engaged. Also, stepping back fosters agency and confidence in their abilities. If I do step in like I did at the tuff tray I will observe if the students are engaging positively with my input, and then continue to scaffold. If they appear overwhelmed, then I will step back.

Thank you for observing this session and sharing such affirming feedback. I appreciate your noticing how showcasing student work not only validates individual efforts but also builds collective celebration and community in the classroom. These moments of recognition motivate students to engage more deeply with their sharing.

Your wondering about agency is actually incredibly timely. In a recent conversation with a colleague, I learned about the framing I used to think
 but now I know
 as a way to help students highlight not just their best work, but also the learning that has taken place. Will

Charles began the lesson by demonstrating a vault, emphasizing the importance of sticking the landing and saluting afterward. He then organized the students into four groups to practice the vault. The students quickly lined up and took turns performing the skill while Charles provided individual feedback and encouragement.

Tammy was present in the gym, assisting with student behavior management.

After a few minutes, Charles called the students back and demonstrated a more advanced straddle vault. Many students found this variation challenging, with several demonstrating the previous technique instead. 

Charles briefly checked in with Tammy to inform her of the next skill so she could support the students with him.

Charles gathered the class in the middle of the mat, with Tammy joining. A few students struggled to settle down. Charles redirected their behavior before proceeding. He then introduced the forward roll, adjusting a mat for better visibility. He explained key points:

Avoiding hitting their heads on the mat
Using a tool to help keep their heads tucked
Keeping hands close to their feet
Avoiding common mistakes, such as dropping their bottom too low
Charles demonstrated proper form and asked for a volunteer to perform the skill.  

Charles pointed out to Tammy some tips for supporting the students. Students then formed two lines to take turns practicing the forward roll. Both Charles and Tammy provided hands-on guidance, ensuring proper techniqueincluding a salute at the end.

Many students found the new skill challenging. After everyone had at least one attempt, Charles regrouped the class and gave instructions about the next activity which would be independent practice of the skills they know. He explained how different mats would be used for various skills. He instructed the students to try all the skills during the 10-minute practice session.
column10: You prioritized student safety throughout the lesson, particularly during the introduction of the forward rolla skill with potential risks if performed incorrectly. By giving explicit instructions, modeling correct body posture, and supporting each student personally as they tried the new front roll skill, you ensured that every student had a safe learning environment.

Thank you for taking the time to observe my PE class and provide me with feedback. 

My goal of the lesson structure was to introduce the skills in a progressive manner, starting with a simpler foundation and building to more challenging movements. Student safety is my highest priority, especially with gymnastics skills like the forward roll where proper form is critical to preventing injury. I will continue to emphasize clear modeling and hands-on support for all new skills. I also appreciate you highlighting student agency. I want to providing choice during independent practice to give students ownership and motivation towards PE.

Your wondering about collaboration and peer observation is something I try to integrate in my class. A strategy I use in class is called being the Coach. In partners they take turns being the Coach. One student will perform the skill while the other is coach and gives feedback based on a checklist of cues they have been learning. I encourage them to say something well their partner did and give one helpful tip (1 star, 1 tip). We have done this a few different times but we did not in the class you observed. 

Another strategy I try is when we do stations in gymnastics they stay with a group the entire time to work on different movements. I will go around to different groups to provide instruction but to also ask them for feedback. I like to ask them a question along the lines of what was one thing you saw someone in your group do very well? this keeps the environment positive and helps them look for successes in others. 

I will continue to look for new ways to improve student collaboration in my class. Thank you again for the feedback and feel free to join my class anytime.

Students began the lesson seated on the floor in four groups in the center of the gym. The teacher moved among the groups, reviewing expectations and modeling the activity. Afterward, students went to their positions, with groups arranged on either side of two volleyball nets. As the game began, the teacher circulated around the gym, offering encouragement and feedback.

In the first activity, each group played on its half of the court, with one student serving to their teammates. Every student wore a hula hoop around their waist, attempting to have the ball pass through the hoop when it came to them.

Next, the teacher gathered the students to explain a variation of the activity: this time, team members stood on the opposite side of the net, catching the ball in their hoop. The teacher demonstrated with students, checked for understanding using a thumbs-up signal, and instructed them to begin when the music started. This round was run as a friendly competition, encouraging all students to complete the task.

Afterward, the teacher brought the students back to the middle for a short reflection. Discussion questions focused on the level of difficulty and the communication needed for success. The teacher also prompted students to think about how to find answersoffering examples such as asking an expert or using non-verbal cues.

For the final activity, the teacher introduced a full-court passing game without hula hoops. Students were allowed to catch the ball or let it bounce first. All students actively participated throughout the session.

As I entered, students were in this G7 math class were observed to be enjoying a short brain break with games like Uno and Connect Four. Others were chatting with friends, many up out of their seats and moving around.  One observed with head down no desk, resting.  They returned to their seats in an orderly and timely way when the break ended. Students explained that they had been filling in tables and working on proportions in preparation for a formative.

The teacher introduced a new problem: writing an equation to represent the relationship between the number of chairs (C) and the number of tables (T). He explained slowly, provided visuals, and reinforced the use of meaningful variables (C and T instead of x and y). Some students finished quickly and were encouraged to pause while others caught up.

As students worked, the teacher guided them to use tables to organize their information, called on multiple individuals to provide pieces of the solution, and walked through errors without judgment, saying, Its alright. We all make mistakes. He prompted students to visualize scenarios (e.g., two tables, one table), connected the work to past problems (park and vehicles), and encouraged peer explanation when a classmate was unclear.

Students were responsive, raising hands to show understanding or ask for more time. The teacher used this visual check effectively to pace the lesson. The class was again in transition as I exited, receiving clear directions for the upcoming formative and homework, and students confirmed that they had been preparing for this assessment.  Directions were given to pick up the homework sheet and begin working on it when they finished the independent practice formative.

column18: I learned how important brain breaks are in a lesson. It is next to impossible for students to be sitting at their desks for the full 80 or so minutes. I try to take a brain break after 30-35 minutes or so, but many times I will observe the body language of the class and take a break if needed. It really helps the students regain focus in the lesson after a break and it was really evident in today's lesson. Another brain break that I do is just a simple conversation about a scenario in a word problem. For example, last week we had a question about a singer and concerts, we we spent about 5 minutes talking about concerts that students went to. Students really get into conversations like these and love sharing their experiences.

column18:
Hi DJ, 
Thank you for coming to visit KA yesterday.
1. At the Me level (Individual Responsibility)
Each student is asked to make a personal contribution.
The act of adding their mark represents ownership, accountability, and the idea that my actions matter.
It builds self-awareness: I have something unique to bring.
2. At the Me to We level (Connecting Individual to Community)
Students see how their small part combines with others contributions to create something bigger.

Learners realize that the class identity is shaped by everyones input  no single person can complete the shirt alone.

It teaches interdependence: My contribution has value because it connects with others.

3. At the We level (Collective Responsibility)

The completed shirt symbolizes the class as a whole, a community built on shared effort.Students feel pride and responsibility not just for their own mark, but for the success and well-being of the entire class. It reinforces the lesson: We are stronger together, and what we create collectively represents us all. In add

 How it fits within a Me to We framework:
This activity is a practical metaphor. The shirt starts as a blank canvas (Me), becomes meaningful through individual contributions, and ultimately transforms into a shared product that represents the entire group (We). It helps students internalize that their personal responsibility extends beyond themselves to the success of our learning community. Ultimately, our learners will also grow into transformative encouragers, like Vashti in The Dot, who inspired the boy to simply sign his work.

Upon entry, some students were observed preparing notes at their table groups and others were setting up a pendulum lab with stands and weights of different masses. They explained that they were adjusting variables such as mass, string length, and angle. While some checked their notes to clarify details, they were generally confident in describing their tasks to me.

One pair noted the challenge of measuring the rate of swing and explained that they were timing five cycles to increase accuracy. Another group described their hypothesis: that mass would not affect the pendulums behavior. Though their reasoning about gravity and force was imperfect, they were actively thinking through the concept, adjusting their setup, and testing ideas. Students were observed experimenting with strings of different lengths and using protractors and rulers, phones (with permission) and watches/stopwatches to measure variables.

When asked, students described the objective as both proving or disproving a hypothesis and connecting to the broader unit on mechanical waves. They recognized that the lab also involved analysis, hypothesis testing, and scientific reasoning.

The teacher actively monitored and asked probing questions to extend their thinking, and all students spoken to were able to articulate their hypothesis and intention with varying levels of clarity. Students worked at different paces but maintained focus.

Thanks for coming by our classroom! By integrating structured questioning, conceptual anchors, and opportunities for transfer, I feel that our students can go beyond proving or disproving hypotheses. Additionally, they can see how their investigations supports the scientific principles of mechanical waves that we learned at the beginning of the quarter. By weaving in these additional opportunites, questionings and anchors it nurtures authenticity by allowing them to experience inquiry as scientists doconstantly linking data to deeper understanding.
