Adrienne took a moment to acknowledge that todays cognitive load may have been heavy, and thats okay. It was a reminder to slow down, illustrated by a serene image of Adrienne's childhood farm: a place of calm and simplicity. Speaking in a gentle, unhurried voice, she encouraged the team to check in with themselves.

Adrienne asked, "On a scale of 1 to 10, how are you feeling right now?" This question invited the team  to pause and self-assess. A powerful quote from students who researched mindfulness was shared: "Finding peace in the midst of hard things" - acknowledging that even in the chaos of teaching, moments of stillness are possible.

Adrienne shared the sounds of a singing bowl and asked the participants to raise their hand when they could no longer hear the sound. It was a practice in attentive listening and a metaphor for how we might tune in to our own needs and those of our students.

Mindfulness, Adrienne explained, is about awareness and recognizing who we are and the choices we make each day. A beautiful Canva image was shared, one that teachers could use in their classrooms to foster mindfulness among students. Adrienne introduced the idea of using a toy/tool (perhaps a fidget or sensory object) to ground us in the present. 

The session closed with a breathing exercise, inhaling and exhaling with intention, embracing the moment without judgment. It was a gentle reminder that mindfulness isnt about perfection, its about presence. The overall message of the session: to be kinder to ourselves so we can, in turn, be fully there for our students.

When the observation began, Haley was reminding students, who were seated at the front of the room, that they are drafting body paragraphs and connecting the work to the previous days focus on writing hooks. She reviewed the concept of a hook and explained that students would now continue to engage their readers through their body paragraphs. 

Haley introduced specific craft moves, beginning with Juicy Character Traits. She led a discussion around commonly used words such as nice, helpful, and good, and encouraged students to consider more precise and descriptive word choices. Haley presented examples of stronger vocabulary and asked students to share meanings. Students first discussed their thinking with a partner, and then Haley invited individual students to share their ideas with the class.

Haley connected the vocabulary work to prior morphology lessons, highlighting previously studied words. She asked students to read selected words aloud together and pointed out suffixes within those words. When one student was not engaged, Haley reminded him that he is part of the learning. She then asked for volunteers to share character traits they had observed about the person they were writing about.

Haley modeled sentence construction by sharing an example of a basic sentence followed by a stronger version. She then introduced another craft move, the rule of 3, providing examples and asking students to read them aloud. Haley demonstrated how the rule of 3 could be applied to character traits. During this time, some students became wiggly while seated on the carpet, and a few students got up to get water.

Haley provided students with an opportunity to independently try coming up with a sentence using the rule of 3 before transitioning to work with their accountability partners. Students practiced creating sentences and shared their work with a shoulder partner while remaining on the carpet. Haley noted that the class would discuss their ideas together before transitioning into independent work time.

Hi Ms.  Virginia,

Thank you for visiting the 3D classroom and taking the time to observe our Writers Workshop. I really appreciated your thoughtful feedback and reflections.

Students are currently working on biographical feature articles about adults in our Ersha community who they do not know well yet. They have been conducting interviews and turning that information into engaging feature articles. They are also creating an art piece inspired by their interviews. We are excited that students will soon publish their articles digitally, with a QR code attached to their artwork so others in the community can read their writing.

During the lesson you observed, juicy character traits was a review craft move, while the rule of 3 was a new craft move. I appreciated your wondering about helping students reflect more deeply on how these craft moves strengthen their writing and impact the reader.

One strategy that has worked well is asking students to highlight (with a highlighter) the craft moves they used that day and share how those choices improved their writing. I also enjoy making students famous by screensharing student work from the iPad to celebrate strong writing moves in real time.

I also appreciated your note about movement and transitions during the mini-lesson. While I allow some flexibility in where students sit during carpet time, I often find it challenging to keep mini-lessons truly mini. I also need to revisit expectations around getting water during carpet time or direct instruction.

Your feedback also made me think about using anonymous sample writing pieces and having students place them along a writing continuum to notice what makes writing stronger and identify next steps.

Thank you again for your time, support, and thoughtful feedback.

During a read-aloud, Meagan asked students to listen for nonliteral language and to notice how it contributes to making the story more interesting. Following the reading, she asked students to put their pillows away and gather at the carpet. Students completed these tasks quickly, and Phoebe turned on the lights as the class transitioned. Once assembled, Meagan began a review on writing a hook, noting that many students had started their hooks and that some were close to finishing. She also shared that the class was nearing the end of the unit.

Meagan asked students to indicate where they were in their writing process. She displayed a mentor hook on the board and invited students to study it, then asked them to share why they thought it was effective. She presented two example hooks and asked students to determine which was stronger and explain their reasoning. Meagan then introduced three types of hooks for students to review.

She explained the next steps for the task: students were to draft two possible hooks and then begin their introductory paragraph. A helpdesk list was visible on the board with the names of students who had signed up for teacher support. Meagan referenced this list and communicated when she would meet with each student so they could anticipate support.

Students were dismissed a few at a time to collect their writers folders. They transitioned quietly, retrieved their materials, and began working at the tables. During this time, two students shared with me that one would focus on writing the hook while the other would work on the title page for their article. As work time continued, several students appeared to have difficulty starting the task. Phoebe sat with Alice to provide support, while Meagan met individually with students listed on the helpdesk sign-up.

column18:
Within the workshop model, all students work toward the same genre and craft goals, with differentiation provided through varying levels of support. For students such as Leela, Hubery, Lucas, and occasionally Carter, I may scribe their ideas during brainstorming, encourage the use of voice-to-text for planning and editing, and offer targeted guidance to help them move forward.

To further support students, I create "helper bundles" for each unit, containing sentence stems and other tools taught previously. These are stored in wooden stands at each table. While some students use these resources naturally, othersespecially those who struggle with writingneed ongoing prompting.

Additionally, a pacing chart hidden behind the whiteboard tracks each students progress through the writing process; students move their magnetized picture as they complete each stage.

Given that there are often only Ms. Phoebe and myself available to support multiple students, I also use chatbots (thanks to Haley) to provide immediate feedback. These tools review student work, offer praise, and suggest one or two next steps, helping to keep momentum in their writing.

Typically, students have a 4050 minute writing block four days a week, with mini-lessons of 12 minutes or less to maximize independent writing time. This particular unit was challenging, as it was not closely aligned with our unit of inquiry and therefore could not be leveraged to prepare for the Living Museum. The team has reflected on this and will make adjustments to strengthen connections next year. When we need to borrow time from writing to prepare for a summative presentation, I feel that the writing time we have isn't enough.

Thank you so much for dropping in and for taking such detailed and thoughtful notes on our lesson. In response to your wondering, this unit focuses on the theme of seasons, and we aim to support both Chinese language learners and native speakers through a shared conceptual focus with differentiated language targets. All students are learning key vocabulary related to the four seasons. For non-native speakers, there is an additional emphasis on weather-related vocabulary within each season, as well as revisiting animal vocabulary from the previous unit.

For native speakers, the focus extends further into language development through seasonal poems and songs, including a rhyme about autumn leaves falling like butterflies. This also connects to our previous unit on The Very Hungry Caterpillar, allowing students to build continuity in vocabulary such as butterfly and leaf.
The leaf butterfly activity is designed as a hands-on experience to reinforce shared vocabulary in a meaningful context. At the same time, it provides an opportunity for native speakers to engage more deeply with the rhyme, integrating language learning with creative expression. In this way, the activity supports different proficiency levels while maintaining a common learning intention.

column18: Collaboration between students can be intentionally highlighted in the moment by verbally praising the behavior and alerting the class that it is happening, also during circle time when reviewing photos of what children are doing/making/playing with the students. Intentionally extending collaboration across different activities is an environmental design challenge, the activities and supplies need to lend themselves to group collaboration. I find that at this stage of development, the students who are in the associative and cooperative stages of play continue collaborating with others at different activities by sharing materials, co-constructing, and negotiating dramatic play ideas. The students who are at the solitary or parallel play stages will usually be receptive to invitations to play with a group, but they will stick close to the teacher and not interact with the other students. However, most of the time the students I see not "collaborating" in PK3 are collaborating by the end of first semester in PK4.

~ Differentiate the counting sequence by inviting some students to begin at numbers other than 1, count backward from 5 and later 10, or try counting to 15 or 20 to extend number sense.

Thank you for coming and for the feedback! Response to the wondering: 

- Current Practices (what I am doing during the units)

(1) Following independent character and pinyin writing tasks, student worksheets are collected, reviewed and marked. Highlighted errors are returned to learners for self-editing. During the correction process, students are prompted to draw on earlier lesson experiences to review key content, recognize their mistakes, and reinforce their learning through prior multi-sensory inputs.

(2) Upon completing all literacy and writing activities, students share their finished work on Seesaw. This showcase allows children to present their learning outcomes, while guiding them to reflect on the entire learning journey and recognize how different types of practices supported their character learning and writing development.

- Additional Strategies to Enhance Metacognition

To further strengthen students metacognitive awareness, short guided reflective discussions can be added at transitional moments of the lesson. Organize quick pair sharing or whole-class questioning, encouraging students to verbalize how singing, physical movements and choral repetition helped them memorize new words and characters. This will help students consciously reflect on their own learning strategies and develop basic self-managing skills.

Students were seated at the front of the room as Joshua introduced the structure of the lesson, explaining that they would be working in stations. He referenced current learning around adding a one-digit number to a two-digit number and wrote a number on the board. Joshua asked students to raise their hands if they remembered where to begin when using a number line to solve the problem.

Joshua shared that he and Ms. Eva had observed that some students number lines were difficult to follow due to organization. He highlighted specific strategies used by students, noting that Phoebe used a ruler and finger spacing to organize her work, Darren used jump lines that supported readability and allowed for checking, and some students circled their answers on the number line. Joshua invited Gaby to the board to help create a map key representing these strategies.

Joshua then introduced a 100 chart board, explaining that some students were using the blank side for an added challenge. He informed students that if they completed their station activity before the 10-minute rotation ended, they could repeat the activity. Students were then directed to move to their assigned stations.

At the Headbands station, Ms. Eva supported student pairs as they asked each other questions to determine a number. Students used number lines to support their thinking, and sentence stems were available to guide questioning.

Ive been thinking about how to make collaboration within stations more purposeful so that students are not just working together, but actively learning from one anothers thinking. One idea I took from the PD with John Hattie is the importance of feedback as a driver of learning, especially when students are both seeking and receiving it.

To build on this, I could expand my station structures by explicitly modelling how to give effective peer feedback during a math task. For example, I would demonstrate how to respond to a partners strategy by asking clarifying questions, identifying strengths in their thinking, and offering suggestions for improvement.

Then, students would be supported with sentence starters such as:

I noticed that you
 Can you explain why
?
Another way to think about this might be

I agree/disagree because

One question I have is


This would shift collaboration from simply completing tasks together to engaging in meaningful mathematical discourse. It also aligns with Hatties idea that errors become opportunities to learn when students receive timely and specific feedback.

After meeting briefly at the carpet with Mr. Neufeld, students transitioned into literacy stations. Two students joined Ms. Ash for guided reading, while another group worked with Mr. Neufeld in a separate guided reading group. During guided reading, Ellie expressed a desire to read first. Ms. Ash asked her to put the book down so all participants could see the words. Elroy listened as Ellie read aloud. When Ellie finished a page, Ms. Ash paused the reading to point out a missed word and drew attention to the punctuation in the word Good, noting the presence of an exclamation mark. Both students attempted to recall the name of the punctuation mark. Elroy identified quotation marks but referred to them as commas. Ash wrote an exclamation mark on a whiteboard and introduced the term by writing it out.

Ellie showed eagerness to continue reading the next part of the story. When she encountered difficulty with the word did, Ash prompted her by looking toward the alphabet chart. Ellie followed the prompt, identified the letter D, and explained her thinking when asked. Ash then asked both students to sound out the word did and blend the sounds together. She revisited the word dance and explained that it was written in the past tense.

As the session progressed, Ash informed Ellie that her reading time was ending and that it was Elroys turn. Ellie showed limited interest in listening while Elroy read, and Ash encouraged her to follow along in the text. During Elroys reading, Ash asked him to explain why his voice changed at the end of a sentence. He responded that the duck was small and the horse was big. Ash then asked how he knew the sentence was a question.

At the end of the session, Ash asked Ellie, who had identified herself as the leader, whether the group had done a good job and reminded her of the responsibility to clean up.

Students were preparing for an upcoming writing celebration. Cat introduced the activity by sharing a slide outlining how students would introduce their character to a partner from another class. She referenced a previously completed paper and modeled what she might say about her own character. Sentence stems were projected on the board, and Cat guided students through practicing their introductions. During this practice, she circulated and provided support to individual students before bringing the group back together.

Cat then prompted students to expand their sharing by including their characters likes, dislikes, and strengths, reminding them they could use their paper as a support. She introduced a new slide explaining that students would also share their writing pieces, showing all the books they had written before selecting a favorite to read aloud. Sentence stems were again provided to support this sharing. Cat facilitated a discussion by asking students for tips on how to make their sharing engaging for their partners, restating and rewording student contributions for clarity. Students suggested that it is more engaging when partners can see both the story and illustrations.

To model expectations, Cat read a story using a robotic voice, prompting students to respond. She then explained that reading is like a performance and modeled expressive reading with clarity and appropriate pacing. After thanking students for their contributions, she introduced available materials, including book stands, and reviewed the three components students would share during the celebration.

Cat explained that students would first practice independently and noted that she prefers to practice out loud. She invited questions, acknowledged and validated student inquiries, and then dismissed students to gather materials and find a space to practice. A 10-minute timer was displayed as students began working independently. During this time, Cat pulled one student to the carpet and guided her through an individual practice.

Our Realistic Fiction writing unit proved to be incredibly engaging again this year. To start, students drew their character, brainstormed a description, chose some possible settings and problems, and then followed specific story writing steps. After breaking it down slowly for their first book, they independently followed the steps to write more books for their character and turned it into a book series. At this point in the year, they were ready to write a lot and had stamina during the unit. It could have continued longer. Near the end, they had the option to continue writing by themselves or collaborate with a friend to write a partner story for their characters. Most chose to work with a partner and it was interesting to see how they collaborated. Some chose to alternate writing and illustrating each page, while others designated one partner the writer and one the illustrator. 
Last year, we were able to connect this writing unit to our Where We Are in Place & Time unit, but after changing the unit this year, there wasnt a natural connection. Since we were ultimately unhappy with our new unit, Im hoping the tweaks next year will make it possible to again connect to writing, as it was another way for students to show what they learned.

Students entered the gym and immediately began running laps as part of a warm-up routine. The gym had been set up in advance for the lesson. Charles called the students to gather in a circle, and students responded by quickly running to the designated area and sitting down. Charles explained that the class would be divided into two groups, with one group practicing catching a frisbee. He invited students to raise their hands to demonstrate ways to catch a frisbee and reinforced techniques such as grabbing it or clapping hands together around it. He then reviewed throwing techniques, reminding students to place their thumb on top of the frisbee and move their arm across their body.

Charles introduced the second activity, which focused on throwing at a target. He asked for a student volunteer to help model the game and explained that students would throw the frisbee toward a target, retrieve it if they missed, and leave it in the target if successful, with the overall goal of filling all targets. He clarified that the activity was not a race. Students were then divided into two groups. Ms. Jasmine supported the group at the target activity while Charles worked with the catching group in another area of the gym.

Music was played during the activity as students began practicing. In the catching group, each student had a frisbee. Students lined up, and Charles threw their frisbee for them to run and catch. When students successfully caught the frisbee, Charles and peers responded with cheers. When students did not catch it, Charles acknowledged their effort and continued the activity. Students in both groups remained engaged and focused on practicing the targeted skills. Charles signaled the final round for the catching group, stopped the music, and directed students to switch groups.

Virginia, thanks for coming to watch part of my class and taking the time to write thoughtful notes. 

Routines is a huge emphasis I spend lots of time on for all the reasons you mentioned. I think it also reduces the anxiety in the younger children and builds the class culture for students to feel safe to try things. They are used to the entry routines but also working in split groups, as you saw. Splitting into groups is a core part of my routines. Many times, whole group instruction can have low repetition and high wait time for the students. They stand in long lines, get one turn every few minutes, and can lose focus. I find small-group rotations with routine allow me to increase each student's active practice time. Splitting the group also lets me differentiate in real time  I can give extra support to any struggling students in my group.

I like your wondering question. It made me realize that I was mostly just giving technical feedback to the students, and not shifting some of that to the students. My intention was to put them on teams for one activity, to develop more collaboration and peer feedback amongst themselves, but I didnt clearly state that to them as a goal. Something I will certainly do in the future.  I can give them points to look for in their team that they can help give feedback to one another on. Such as remember to watch where your partners thumb is, pull frisbee across body before throwing ect. 
For my catching group, I can instruct the students to try and find one piece of feedback to give to the person behind them in line each time they are waiting in line. Give them a few things that can specifically look for. This suggestion will definitely support the critical thinking and caring culture I try to create in my classes.

Thank you again for coming and please come again any time!

Amelie gathered students and engaged them in a discussion about Rammy's Choices. She began by focusing on the strategy of saying stop, reminding students they can use an assertive voice while also speaking in a kind way. She then introduced the idea of saying sorry, explaining that when they say sorry, they take a problem and help make it smaller. Students used their arms to model a big problem becoming smaller. Amelie emphasized that even when something is accidental, students should still say sorry and check in to make sure their friend is okay.

Amelie continued by discussing sharing and taking turns. She asked students to repeat the phrase, take turns and share. A few students contributed ideas, including lining up as a strategy. Amelie listened to student responses and validated their thinking. During the discussion, she highlighted a student who was looking at Lydia while she was speaking and noted to the class that listening to others and taking turns are important.

She then introduced the Rammy's Choice of Talk it out and invited students to share strategies for how they might do this. Amelie explained that students would practice all of the Rammy Choices during a game. She stated two goals for the activity: to have fun and to use Rammys Choices. She used a call-and-response attention signal (if you are ready) to gather focus before transitioning to the activity.

The game involved using a pipe cleaner to move a ping pong ball. Amelie first attempted the task independently, and the ball fell. She asked students why this happened, and they identified that two people were needed. She then invited a student to demonstrate working together to move the ball. Amelie posed a question about what to do if the ball drops, suggesting sitting down and crying and never playing that game again; students responded by laughing and saying they would try again.

Students were then invited to work with a partner to move a ball from one side of the room to the other. Amelie prompted them to think about what they could do if the ball dropped, connecting back to the Rammy Choices. She called students in pairs and provided them with the materials needed for the game.

Students were seated in the corner teaching space as Joe introduced the lesson. The word Fitness was written on the board along with four activities: strength (being strong), endurance (not getting tired quickly), speed (moving fast), and agility (changing direction quickly). Joe briefly explained each of the four stations and then asked for a volunteer to lead the stretching activity. Kinlee volunteered, and Joe directed him to the middle of the gym while the other students stood around him and followed his lead.

Students engaged in the stretching activity mostly silently while Joe supported by providing feedback. When Kinlee forgot a movement, Joe prompted him and continued to guide the group by counting and offering reminders as needed. Brendan, who had a broken foot, remained seated at the sidelines reading a book during this time. The stretching lasted approximately 34 minutes.

Following the warm-up, Joe directed students to move to four activity stations based on their color teams. He began by supporting the group working on strength through squats and lunges, then transitioned to the agility station where he provided tips as students navigated the course. He later moved to the speed group and reminded them to sprint. Throughout the lesson, students were mostly engaged in their tasks. Groups receiving direct support from Joe demonstrated increased levels of active engagement, while intensity decreased in groups when he transitioned to another station.

After several minutes, Joe instructed students to rotate to the next station. During the second rotation, he continued to check in with each group. At the sprint station, he introduced the use of fast feet as preparation before a short partner sprint. During this time, one student requested a break, and Joe responded that a break would be provided shortly. Joe blew the whistle, signaling the end of that rotation. He told the students they could take a 3-minute water break and then they would move to the next station in their rotation.

To help keep students engaged and active even when I'm working with another group, I plan to add clearer roles within each station (e.g. leader, timekeeper, technique coach), so everyone has a specific responsibility. Thank you for the thoughtful observation and feedback. The wondering about collaboration highlights an area for continued growth in practice.

Opportunities to share guidance lesson ideas with grade-level teams are currently limited and tend to be informal. There is not yet a consistent structure for communicating lesson objectives or offering strategies for how teachers can reinforce learning between guidance lessons. Strengthening this area is an important next step in supporting continuity for students.

One potential approach is to increase involvement in grade-level meeting spaces, such as joining unit kick-off meetings. This could support two-way collaboration by aligning guidance lessons with the language and concepts of the unit of inquiry, while also identifying ways classroom teachers can reinforce social-emotional learning within their daily instruction.

There is also an opportunity to gather teacher input on how they would prefer to receive information about upcoming guidance lessons. Understanding these preferences could help ensure communication is effective, relevant, and actionable.

Currently, having teachers present during guidance lessons provides a shared understanding of the content and language used, allowing for informal reinforcement in the classroom. A next step would be to build on this by offering simple, practical follow-up activities or prompts that teachers can easily integrate outside of guidance time.

Collaboration with grade-level teams around guidance lessons is an area I would like to continue developing. Establishing more intentional and consistent collaboration structures could extend the impact of guidance lessons and support a more cohesive student experience across settings, ensuring that social-emotional learning is reinforced through shared language and practices in the classroom.

I would happily do games on a smaller scale more regularly. I love it. I think even just having a day where the kids were doing a certain relay for a small chunk of time, and in mixed groups would be so fun. For example, making 4 teams: numbers 1-6, 7-12, 13-18, 19-23 in each class joining up to make 1 larger team. Or somehow doing a "sorting hat" type of activity one day to determine teams... I also love the idea of houses or building off dynasties, to group the kids into cross class groups or teams. I think doing that and coming together for different games more regularly, and on a smaller scale, would be so much fun. 

In terms of sensory and ability, it depends on the groups. I think knowing their sensory needs helps, and allowing kids to have the space to sit out and take a break if they want or need is important. I think there were kids on both days that did that. But also, the games are chosen and designed to allow the kids to have various levels of involvement, based on what works for them. I think in retrospect, maybe making "lives" in poison would make it last a little longer. I think for grade 4 the timings worked really well, but in grade 5 they were over a lot quicker, even with the added challenge of including the pin to also be knocked down. (honestly, that was a quick last minute decision this morning when I was setting up for round 2). 

I think arranging for games, on a smaller scale more often would be really good for the kids. Always keeping their "team" the same would bring some larger scales of teamwork across the grade level, and make it easier to get them sorted each time the games happened. 

The choice of the games are important- making sure everyone can access them in some way is key. I miss the component of the small sided games, and having your class champion you, like we had last year, but on the flip side of that, it also gave the kids down time to be upset if they had gotten out or lost their own game. This year we kept it moving faster and smoother.

During the observation, students were seated at the front of the room while Will projected a passage from a chapter of an autobiography he planned to read aloud. Will explained that students had a MAP test scheduled for the following day and that, instead of reviewing previously learned skills directly, they would think about concepts through the chapter reading. He introduced the term autobiography by writing the word on the board and breaking it into parts: auto, bio, and graphy. He explained the meanings of each part and asked students to share additional words beginning with auto. Students shared several examples, and Will guided them to connect the word parts to the meaning of autobiography as writing about someones life. Before reading, Will reviewed expectations for listening, asking students to remain at a level zero, stay comfortable while keeping their heads up, and raise their hands if they had questions.

As Will read aloud, most students listened quietly. Some students followed the projected text on the screen, while Patrick held a copy of the book and silently read along. After the first few paragraphs, Will paused and asked students to identify any connections they could make to the text. He then created a chart on the board and directed students to listen for inside and outside character traits. Following the next paragraph, Will used a jar of popsicle sticks to randomly select students to share a character trait and determine whether it was an inside or outside trait. As students responded, Will recorded their ideas on the chart. When one student shared an idea but struggled to explain his thinking, Will encouraged him to elaborate and, after noticing the difficulty, told the student he would return to him later. Throughout the discussion, Will guided students in distinguishing between inside and outside traits, acknowledging that some traits could fit into more than one category and prompting students to think through their reasoning. Will then continued reading and explained that the class would move on to another review topic.

Ive been trying to think more intentionally about how students access texts in different ways, especially during whole-group lessons where reading stamina and processing needs can vary widely across the class. I also appreciated your comments around agency and reasoning. One of my goals each year is to push students beyond identifying an answer and toward explaining the thinking behind it, even when the reasoning feels uncertain or incomplete.

Your wondering about supporting students with more nuanced character traits is something Ive been reflecting on as well. One strategy I want to continue developing is giving students more opportunities to compare traits that may overlap or shift depending on context. During this lesson, students began noticing that some traits could reasonably fit into both inside and outside categories, which led to richer conversations than if there had only been one correct answer. Moving forward, I would like to incorporate more partner discussions and short written justifications where students defend their reasoning using evidence from the text. I think these opportunities will help students become more comfortable with ambiguity and strengthen their ability to explain increasingly complex thinking independently.

Thank you for all of your observations and feedback. This lesson was a great example of intentional co-planning and co-teaching in 5A. The story that students used was one they had reviewed before, however, I had assumed that some students had access to a bilingual version I had made that actually was not available to them. This was an unfortunate oversight that complicated the task for my highest needs students, but we were able to work around it. 

Regarding co-planning partnerships, trust is the most important factor. I feel fortunate to have developed a trusting relationship with Taralyn over the last two years. It has made it easy for us to co-plan lessons like today when we are both clear on our objectives going into our planning meetings.

The most effective co-planning sessions are ones where both teachers are able to pre-plan so that they are both prepared and focused on a common goal. Before this lesson, Taralyn and I were both aware of the goals of the unit. She had already been planning for the next days lesson, and I came in with some preplanned ideas for next steps. 

The best advice I have for other co-teaching partners is to consider concentrating co-planning on RAMs days. This was a huge benefit when I experimented with the practice last year. It led to much more consistency of co-teaching than Day rotation-based planning, and also helped generate increasted horizontal alignment across rooms. Unfortunately, Grade 5s schedule no longer allows for this practice, but other grades at AISG could consider it. Andrea Honigsfeld details this planning arrangement in one of her books and calls it 4+1 scheduling (4 teaching days and 1 planning day).

column18:
I think one of the biggest factors in making a strong co-planning partnership successful is having a shared understanding of the purpose and progression of the learning. Jake and I spend a lot of time discussing not only the learning intention itself, but also the possible student responses, misconceptions, scaffolds, and questions that could move student thinking forward. We try to anticipate where students may need clarification or extension so that we are both prepared to support students fluidly throughout the lesson.
 
It also really helps when a team has a clear direction with standards already identified, as well as a shared understanding and agreement around mentor texts, lesson progression, and the overall goals of the unit. Having those foundations in place allows co-planning conversations to focus more deeply on student learning, differentiation, questioning, and instructional decisions rather than starting from scratch each time.
 
I also think trust and flexibility are essential within co-planning and co-teaching. Over time, Jake and I have developed a rhythm where we are comfortable building off one anothers ideas, stepping in naturally during discussions, and adjusting based on what students need in the moment. We both view all students as shared learners, which helps create consistency and shared ownership within the classroom.
 
An effective co-planning session for us usually involves unpacking the learning goal together, discussing differentiation and support strategies, planning key questions, and determining how we can best support students during each stage of the lesson. We also reflect afterward on what worked well and what adjustments we may want to make moving forward.
 
One piece of advice I would give to others who are co-planning is to approach planning collaboratively rather than simply dividing responsibilities. The strongest co-planning partnerships come from open communication, shared ownership, and ongoing reflection focused on improving learning for all students.

Brittany, Chay, and Amelie, prepared and facilitated a workshop for caregivers focused on transitions, with 10 caregivers in attendance. Brittany opened the session by introducing the topic and inviting caregivers to reflect on a time when they experienced transition or change, prompting them to discuss with their table groups what made those experiences challenging. During these conversations, Brittany, Chay, and Amelie each joined a table group to engage directly with caregivers and contribute to the discussions.

Following the table discussions, Chay invited volunteers to share reflections with the larger group. When participants were initially hesitant, Brittany contributed by summarizing themes from her tables conversation, including challenges participants identified as well as positive outcomes that emerged through transition experiences. Brittany highlighted that there can be growth and learning gained through change. Amelie then shared an additional perspective from her table discussion, emphasizing the importance of supportive relationships and friendships during times of transition. Chay also summarized key ideas from her group before facilitating a myth buster true-or-false activity addressing common misconceptions related to transitions.

Brittany later addressed the caregivers by emphasizing that no one in the room was an expert, but that everyone brought valuable experiences that could support collective learning. She discussed the complexity of transitions and the importance of preparing for the process. Amelie shared examples of behaviors children may demonstrate during transitions and explained that children may communicate emotions behaviorally when they do not yet have the language to express their feelings directly. She also provided caregivers with strategies to support children in processing emotions during periods of change.

Amelie introduced the RAFT model before Chay unpacked and explained each component in greater detail. Chay then transitioned the final part of the model back to Amelie, who explained the affirmation component of RAFT and emphasized the value of helping students and children use specific affirmations. Brittany facilitated the F component of RAFT by discussing the importance of farewells, not only to people but also to places, routines, and experiences. Chay concluded the workshop by discussing the T component, Think Destination, and shared practical strategies caregivers could use to help familiarize children with upcoming transitions and environments.

The wondering around caregiver engagement and participation is an important area for reflection. While the smaller group size allowed for more personalized discussion and interaction, it also raises questions about how caregiver workshops can continue to remain relevant and engaging for a broader range of families.

One area to consider moving forward is whether workshops could become more differentiated and responsive to caregiver needs and interests. Collecting caregiver questions and wonderings beforehand through the sign-up process could help tailor the presentation to the interests and needs of the attending audience, making the session more targeted and relevant.

Another consideration is incorporating a station-based format within caregiver workshops, where each counselor facilitates a smaller discussion space focused on a specific topic. This structure could create more intimate and interactive conversations while also allowing for greater personalization. It may also create opportunities for collaboration with other departments and members of the school community. For example, in this caregiver coffee, one station could involve librarian sharing literacy resources related to transitions, while another could involve a digital champion discussing ways children can maintain connections with peers through different digital platforms. There may also be opportunities to invite teachers or community members with personal experiences as Third Culture Kids to share perspectives and strategies that supported them during transitions.

I am also curious whether caregivers could provide more direct feedback regarding the types of caregiver workshops they would find most meaningful for the upcoming year. Gathering this feedback could help ensure future sessions remain responsive, engaging, and aligned with the evolving needs of families within the school community.

Appropriate footwear is something we take seriously from a safety perspective, and we already have a consistent expectation which are shared first thing when we meet students for the first time and are shared all across within the PHE department.

Students are not permitted to participate in running or other high-movement activities if they are not wearing appropriate athletic footwear. Footwear such as platform Crocs, slides, sandals, or other shoes that do not provide adequate stability and support are considered unsuitable for these types of activities due to the increased risk of slips, trips, and ankle injuries.

- Students are asked to reflect on their own six wellness dimensions and come up with examples (e.g. healthy diet, enough sleep, etc.)
- Teacher shared some personal examples so students better understand what is required

column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10:
The teacher created meaningful opportunities for students to personalize their learning by connecting the six dimensions of wellness to their own lives and experiences. The students reflected on their own wellness routines and identified personal examples such as diet, sleep, physical activity, and spiritual health. The teachers own examples helped model the reflection expected of students (and added some vulnerability, too).

column14: n/a
column18:
Thank you for stopping by my classroom and for the observations and feedback. Yes, I did add goal setting after you left. I asked students to pick one wellness dimension they wanted to improve and write a small step they could take. For example, one student who struggled with spiritual health committed to two minutes of quiet reflection before bed. It worked because the goals were based on their own examples.

Regarding adding a cultural dimension: Great point. It's a wonderful way to incorporate culturally responsive teaching into the classroom. I could ask students: How does your family take care of mental or emotional health? This would let students share cultural practices (like family prayer or gratitude circles) and find common ground. Ill add this next time. Thank you for contributing and for sharing how you practice spiritual health.

column7:
- Grade 6 English L&L class
- 15 students (7 girls and 8 boys)
- Teacher is displaying the 16 Key Concepts of the MYP programme (which makes me very happy as a MYPC) and asking students to make connections between the subject (Lang. and Lit.) and the concepts displayed. Teacher asks clarifying questions, such as 'Why do you think communication is a central key concept in this subject.'
- Teacher presents the KC of this unit 'Communication' and asks students to discuss in their table groups to share ideas and come up with a common definition. 
- Teacher walks around and checks in with the individual groups to check their thinking.
- Afterwards, students are allowed to share their answers in a plenary setting. Teacher asks follow-up questions so students can clarify their thinking and add onto each others ideas.
- Teacher then discusses the Related Concepts and goes through the same exercise so students can commonly define the RCs of 'Structure' and 'Purpose'. It is clear that the foundation of this unit of study is properly introduced to the students. 
- Afterwards, the teacher showed a variety of different terms and asked the students to move through the room depending on if they feel it connects to 'Communication', 'Structure', or 'Purpose'. For example, 'Writing a letter to a friend without telling them why you are writing'.
column9: How do we help students generalize a mindset or strategy from one subject or setting to another?
column10:
Rather than simply being told what the concepts mean, students considered how concepts such as Communication connect specifically to their subject. The teachers follow-up questions helped students explain and deepen these connections. This supports the TLF focus on helping students transfer ideas and understanding across different contexts, especially as these KCs connection among subjects.

Tip: perhaps explain how the KC of Communication is also present in other subjects, e.g. VPA and Design. I think that would allow students to real see the interdisciplinary connections between subjects.

Also appreciate how the teacher explains how these RCs appear in the unit (e.g. Structure is evident in when we're writing by the use of paragraphs).

column7: Yesterday, I visited Audrey Boettcher's Grade 7 English Language in Literature class at the end of the period. Students were working in small groups as Audrey circled around to conference with each of them. Student had directions on the screen that gave partner's explicit roles in the task. For each of the advertisements, the students were expected to determin the topic, audience, purpose, and appeal for each ad. I circled around and spoke to the groups. column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: The Sentence Frames for Analyzing Advertisements provided a purposeful linguistic scaffold for the range of English learners in the classroom. The frames helped students organize their analysis of brand and purpose, audience, visual design, and appeal into coherent sentences without reducing the intellectual demand of the task. Students ability to explain the task, articulate why they were learning it, and make progress independently suggests that the support increased access while preserving meaningful thinking.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: The partner work was intentionally structured rather than simply placing students together. The displayed directions assigned complementary responsibilities: Partner A recorded notes, Partner B synthesized the groups thinking on paper, and students then switched roles. This structure supported equitable participation and shared responsibility, connecting closely to the TLF question, To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning? As Audrey circulated and conferred with groups, students remained calm, focused, and able to explain their thinking, providing evidence of a trusting learning environment in which collaboration had become a productive classroom routine.

column7:
At the time of the observation, Steph was team teaching with the EAL teacher during a reading lesson. The focus of the lesson was helping students unpack what the Practice component of a lesson looks like. Students had explored the Mini-Lesson component the previous day and were scheduled to explore the Reflection component the following day. 

The question displayed on the screen was: What do you think the teacher and the students should be doing during the practice part of a lesson? A collection of student-generated ideas was visible on the screen. During the observation, students shared ideas that included focused body, ears listening, and raise your hand. Steph then asked students to take a moment to reread their brainstormed ideas and consider whether anything was missing. 

As Steph prepared to transition into reading expectations, she introduced a seven-minute brain break, providing students with an opportunity to move before beginning the next part of the lesson. 

Following the break, Steph introduced a Book Tasting activity. She began with an image from Goldilocks and the Three Bears and asked students to recall what Goldilocks was searching for - something that was just right. Steph connected this idea to selecting books that are just right for the reader. She then shared a slide outlining indicators that a book might be too easy for a student.
column9: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column10: You created space for student voice by inviting students to contribute to and then revisit a shared understanding of what happens during the Practice portion of a lesson. Rather than simply presenting the expectations, you asked students to read the collective brainstorm and identify anything they believed was missing. This positioned students as contributors to the development of the classs understanding of the learning process and began to make their role within that process more visible.
column12: Do students have access to strategies for self-care and emotional well-being?
column13: You intentionally incorporated a seven-minute movement break before beginning the Book Tasting activity. This provided students with a concrete opportunity to regulate their bodies and attention before transitioning into a new learning experience. The move also aligns with UDLs Engagement principle, which identifies embedded self-regulation strategies, including brain breaks and flexible pacing, as ways of reducing barriers to sustained participation.
column14: The Goldilocks connection helped students understand the idea of choosing a just right book. How might individual students think about what makes a book just right for them, including their interests, reading level, language needs, and the support they may need?
column16: In what ways are students have opportunities to pursue their interests and passions?
column18: Thanks for visiting the class DJ and for your thoughtful notes on the lesson you observed. For the first few weeks, we have been using the time in lessons to set up expectations for students during different parts of their day. It is notiecable that these students have experienced strong routines and expecations in their Grade 2 classes as they have a lot of background knowledge and they are already putting into place the behaviour that should be seen. This year has been easy to jump into co-teaching with Jake as we have a strong working relationship and we have co-taught many times already. I like being able to teach alongside Jake as I find we compliment each other and offer ideas that the other person might not have thought about. It has been especially important at the beginning of the year to add in movement breaks for the students. Some of the lessons have been a lot of listening and talking as we set up expectations and develop agreements. Providing a break has given all students a chance to reset their bodies so they are focused for what is to come. Since beginning readers workshop we have been talking about just right books. Students were asked to share their ideas and then we shared some with them: reading at a good pace and understanding it, being interested and slightly challenged, having a little knowledge about the topic. Students also knew about using the 5 finger rule. Over the next few weeks, my job is to get to know my students as readers, develop goals with them, hear them all read and practice conferences. Through this individual time, I would like to discuss interest of topics, and learn about how I can support them. I am intentionally trying to slow down the way I normally begin the first part of the year so students can get into routines and have enough time to practice, for example during independent reading time. This way I am hoping that I set myself and the students up for success and routines are cemented early in the year.

column7:
Jake was team teaching with Steph during a Grade 3 reading lesson focused on unpacking what the Practice part of a lesson looks like. This lesson was part of a sequence in which students had explored the Mini-Lesson the previous day and would explore Reflection the following day. 

Jake was part of the shared facilitation of the lesson as students considered the question, What do you think the teacher and the students should be doing during the practice part of a lesson? Students contributed ideas about expected behaviors during practice, and were then asked to reread their collective thinking and consider what might be missing. 

As the lesson transitioned toward independent reading expectations, Jake participated in the seven-minute brain break alongside students. His involvement positioned him as an active member of the 3A classroom community and reinforced the sense that he was part of the learning environment rather than working separately from it. 

During the introduction to the Book Tasting activity, Jake had translanguaged the Goldilocks and the Three Bears slide into Korean and Chinese. He shared this with students and explained that translanguaging would be used as part of their learning in these lessons. This made the use of students home languages visible and positioned multilingualism as a resource for learning. 

Jake also introduced students to a quiet reading strategy using a telephone. He showed students how the tool could allow them to hear themselves read while maintaining a whisper voice, providing another strategy they could use during independent reading.
column9: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column10: You introduced the reading telephone as a practical strategy students could use to support themselves during quiet reading. Rather than the support sitting only with the teacher, you gave students access to a tool they could use themselves to hear and monitor their reading. This begins to build students awareness that they can select and use strategies that help them become increasingly independent readers.
column12: How might assessment models be adapted to accommodate students from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds?
column13: You made multilingualism visible as an expected part of the learning by translanguaging the Goldilocks slide into Korean and Chinese and explicitly letting students know that their languages would be used during these lessons. You also introduced the telephone as another reading strategy students could use to support themselves during quiet reading. Together, these moves provided students with additional ways to access and participate in the reading experience.
column14: What did the co-planning process with Steph look like in developing this lesson, and how has that process looked across your work with the other Grade 3 teachers this week? How are those conversations helping you identify opportunities to intentionally build multilingual strategies and supports into classroom learning from the outset?
column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18:
Thank you for coming to observe me today, DJ. I am glad you were able to see how I use a UDL approach and add translanguaging tools to our slides. I have been including Chinese, Korean, and English translations, and possibly Japanese soon! Last year, I realized that including an English definition and having students say it aloud was helpful even for native English speakers. We can easily forget that being a native speaker does not mean a student understands every word or how it functions.

I ordered the reading phones for the team last year, but they were not being used much. As we explore Who We Are as Readers, this felt like the perfect time to take more initiative and lead their use. Once one student tries one, they all want to try one! They are a simple way to build reading skills and confidence. I have enjoyed taking more initiative this year and switching leadership roles naturally during lessons.

To answer your question about co-planning, the lesson you observed showed how our planning comes into the classroom, from the multilingual supports to the way Steph and I shared the teaching. We co-plan Thursdays with 3C/3D and Fridays with 3A/3B, but also check in before school, at lunch, and during meetings. These conversations help us build language and visual supports into lessons from the beginning.

We are also intentional about students seeing the HR and EAL teachers as equal teachers. When possible, we start and end lessons together and share the teaching throughout. Our UDL supports are available to everyone without calling out particular students, and I am already seeing students naturally look to them for support. We also include our EAs in these conversations so we can build strong habits as a team from the start. Our co-planning and co-teaching are off to a great start, and I feel our collaboration is even stronger than in years past.

column7:
At the time of the observation, Will and the EAL teacher had students engaged in a Turn & Talk around the question, What do you love reading about? As the activity concluded, Will used popsicle sticks to randomly select students to share ideas from their conversations. As students shared, the EAL teacher scribed their contributions on the whiteboard. Will also invited other students to make connections to what their classmates were sharing. 

The class then transitioned to a translanguaged slide featuring Goldilocks and the Three Bears. Will used the idea of Goldilocks looking for something that was just right to introduce the concept of selecting books that are the right fit for each reader. 

After providing students with thinking time, Will asked, What do we need to consider to help us find the right-fit book? Students contributed ideas that included checking whether they knew the words, looking in areas of the library connected to subjects that interested them, and considering recommendations from friends. Will scribed their ideas on the whiteboard before sharing some additional considerations from the slide. 

Will then introduced the Book Tasting activity. Students were asked to move around the classroom, sample different books, and use a recording sheet to capture their thinking and rate each book they explored.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You began the lesson by asking students what they love reading about and then carried the idea of personal interest into the conversation about selecting a right-fit book. Students themselves identified finding topics that interest them as one consideration when choosing a book. This helped position book selection as something personal to each reader rather than as a single definition of what everyone should be reading.
column12: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column13: You invited students to help construct the criteria for selecting a right-fit book rather than providing all of the criteria yourself. Students contributed strategies such as checking whether they could read the words, considering their interests, and using recommendations from friends. The Book Tasting then gave students an opportunity to put this thinking into practice by exploring books and recording their own responses. These moves begin to equip students to make more informed and independent decisions as readers.
column14: As students complete the Book Tasting, how might the recording sheet invite them to explain why a book is or is not just right for them, rather than only rating whether they liked it?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column18:
Thank you for the feedback, DJ! I appreciate you highlighting the connection between personalization and agency in this lesson. One of my goals with the Book Tasting was to move away from the idea that a just-right book is determined only by reading level and help students recognize that interest, purpose, recommendations, and personal connection all play a role. Having students generate much of that criteria themselves was also an important part of the lesson for me.

Your wondering about the recording sheet is a good one. Looking back, a key limitation was that I used a pre-made resource that didnt fully align with the main idea of the lesson
 that selecting a book is about more than reading level and includes interest, purpose, and personal connection. Because of that, the sheet emphasized whether students were interested in a book, but not why it might be a good fit for them as readers. A next step would be to design my own resource that better reflects these ideas, including a prompt such as, Is this book just right for you? How do you know? This would ask students to apply the criteria we developed rather than simply rate the book.

I also see value in revisiting these recording sheets later. After students have more experience choosing books independently, we could return to their original choices and reflect on how their thinking about just right books has evolved. This would help make the Book Tasting less of a one-time activity and more of a starting point for developing independence and self-awareness as readers.

column18:
Thanks for coming by!

Students take agency in the investigation by making purposeful decisions about their roles, procedures, and future trials. Working collaboratively with a lab partner, students determine how to divide responsibilities such as conducting procedures, measuring variables, making observations, and recording data. column7:
Students were working on a conversation/interview task connected to identity, asking classmates questions about their identities and what makes them who they are. Students were working on their computers and were able to use a variety of languages to respond to the questions. EAL support was clearly embedded in the class.

Students needed to collect responses from three classmates for two questions before moving on to an individual written summary. Students were at different stages of the task, with one student already working on the final summary while others were still collecting responses.

At the time of the observation, Brittany was beginning her first guidance lesson with Grade 3D. She opened the lesson by introducing balloon breathing as a self-regulation strategy. Brittany first modelled taking a deep breath in through the nose and slowly exhaling through the mouth before inviting students to follow along. As students practiced the breathing technique, she offered positive affirmations to students who were following the process. 

Brittany then connected the lesson to Grade 3's current Who We Are unit by explaining that she wanted students to learn more about who she is. Using photographs displayed on the screen, she shared six facts about herself, including information about her family, favourite hobbies, and favourite food. Students were invited to ask questions and make connections to what Brittany shared. 

To continue building familiarity with her while incorporating movement, Brittany introduced a Would Ms. Brittany Rather
? activity. Students responded to prompts such as choosing between the mountains or the beach, reading a book or watching a movie, and solving a problem or planning a party by moving to indicate their choice. The final prompt, which highlighted Brittany's preference for solving problems, provided a transition into a discussion about her role as the school counsellor. 

Brittany used a Mrs. Potato Head model to make different aspects of the counsellor role more concrete for students. As students selected body parts for the model, she connected each part to an aspect of her work. For example, when a student selected the feet, Brittany explained that she uses her feet to walk to classrooms for guidance lessons. When another student selected the hands, she explained that part of her role is to lend a helping hand and to provide care and reassurance when students need support.

Beginning your first guidance lesson in this way also positioned emotional well-being as a natural and valued part of students' learning experience. Your positive affirmations reinforced the routine as students practiced it and helped establish the guidance space as one in which students can develop tools for managing their emotions and well-being.

Thank you for your thoughtful observation notes. The wondering about agency made me reflect on how I can build on the opportunities students already had to participate and give them greater voice in shaping future guidance lessons.

Although the main activities in this lesson were teacher-planned, students had additional opportunities to share their own ideas and questions. Later in the lesson, students were invited to use Seesaw to ask me any questions they had. They will also respond in their guidance journals to the question, What would you like Ms. Brittany to know about you? I see these as important ways for me to learn more about students while also giving them a voice in our guidance space.

Moving forward, I would like to create more consistent opportunities for student input. For example, I could include check-in questions in Seesaw activities where students can reflect on their guidance learning and share topics or situations they are interested in learning more about. I can then use their responses to help inform future lessons and topics.

As I plan to open each guidance lesson with a mindfulness activity, I could also invite students to suggest activities they are interested in trying or have learned elsewhere and would like to share with the class. This would give students an opportunity to contribute to our learning community and take greater ownership of our guidance time. Ultimately, I would like students to see guidance as a space where their questions, interests, and experiences can help shape what we learn together.

At the time of observation, Haley and the 3D students were engaged in Writers Workshop. Students were seated on the carpet as Haley read The Word Collector. On the screen, she displayed guiding questions including, What did the word collector do that helped him become a better writer? and What is one thing we can do like him? As she read, Haley paused to allow students to make connections and contribute their thinking. 

Following the read-aloud, Haley explained that students would begin collecting their own ideas and words around the question, What do I care about? The purpose was for students to develop a personal bank of ideas they could draw upon during future independent writing. To support their thinking, Haley displayed possible categories such as food, hobbies, people, sports, and art. She also connected the activity to the Grade 3 Who We Are provocation from earlier in the morning, during which teachers had shared aspects of their own lives. 

Before students began, Haley asked them to indicate, on a scale of 15, how well they understood the instructions. Most students indicated a 4 or 5. Students then transitioned to their tables to begin independently generating their lists. Haley worked more closely with students who had indicated that they needed additional support, while three students worked with the EAL teacher. The EA circulated among the remaining students and provided support as needed. Haley explained that students would have ten minutes of individual writing time before returning to the carpet to share.
column9: In what ways are students have opportunities to pursue their interests and passions?
column10: You created a writing experience that was responsive both to who students are and what they needed as learners. By inviting students to build a bank around What do I care about?, you positioned their interests, relationships, hobbies, and experiences as legitimate sources for writing. You also used the 15 understanding check to identify students who needed additional support and then adjusted the learning environment through your support, the EAL teacher, and the EA.
column12: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?

Although all students were working toward the same goal, each student determined which people, interests, experiences, and passions would populate their personal idea bank. This begins to shift students from receiving writing topics toward seeing themselves as people who have their own ideas worth writing about.
column14: When students return to the carpet to share, how might they be able to learn from one anothers collections - for example, hearing a peers idea and adding a new word, category, or connection to their own bank?

column18:
Hi DJ,
Thank you for visiting the 3D classroom and taking the time to observe our first official Writers Workshop of the year. Since this is a brand-new group of students and we are only in week 2, we are still building routines and getting to know each other as a community.

As a grade level team, we are trying a writing process unit this year, which is a new experience for me. This lesson was really about helping students see that everyone is a writer and beginning the pre-writing stage by collecting inspiration from the people, experiences, interests, and things they care about.

I really appreciated your wondering about how students could learn from one another's collections. We actually built this into the lesson after the observation. Once the ten minutes were up, students did a silent walk around the classroom to notice each other's lists. They then had a few minutes to add any new ideas to their own lists after seeing something a peer had written. I would like to continue building on this idea and make these opportunities for students to inspire one another a more intentional part of our writing process.

We will also be closely connecting this writing unit to our Who We Are UOI as we explore our common and unique interests and what makes each of us who we are.

Thanks again for visiting and for your thoughtful feedback!

column18:
The lesson you observed was the second lesson of our Fitness Volleyball Unit. In Lesson 1, students were introduced to the setter position, which serves as a primary focus during the gameplay component of the unit. From there, we explored the setter role in greater detail and identified three key fitness components that contribute to being an effective setter: cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, and agility.

As part of their Criterion B summative assessment, students will develop a personal fitness goal connected to their role as a designated setter during gameplay. They will then design a fitness plan aimed at improving the specific fitness components needed to become more successful in that role.

The lesson you observed was designed to build on the learning from Lesson 1 by deepening students understanding of these fitness components through inquiry-based activities. Rather than simply being told why each component is important, students were given opportunities to explore, discuss, and make connections between the fitness activities and the physical demands of the setter position.

The unit is intentionally layered so that students gradually develop an understanding of what is expected of them and, importantly, why it matters. As the unit progresses, students will implement their own designed workout plans and drills, evaluate their effectiveness, and have opportunities to adjust and adapt their plans before completing the final summative assessment.

Students were seated in a circle with a hand drum in front of each student. Phillip sang a song while students performed a drumming pattern they had previously practiced. At the conclusion of the song, Phillip asked students if they would like to try a game that incorporated bean bags into the song. Students responded that they wanted to try the game. The pattern shifted from striking their own drum and then a neighbors drum to striking their own drum and then passing a bean bag to the next person.

Students practiced the new pattern briefly before Phillip sang the song while they played the game. When the song ended and the bean bags were not evenly distributed around the circle, Phillip asked students to identify what had happened. As one student shared an idea, Phillip reminded the class to listen, explaining that the student was sharing something important. Phillip then restated that the pattern had broken because people were not staying on the beat.

Phillip told students they would try the game again and reminded them to keep the beat. After a few beats, he stopped and provided support to a student who was having difficulty with the pattern. Once students resumed the pattern, Phillip sang the song again while they played. He then asked students to place the bean bags in the middle of the circle and practice the pattern again without them.

Following another round of the song, Phillip asked students to move to the carpet. When one student jumped over the drums during the transition, Phillip reminded the student not to jump over the drums and invited him to move through the space correctly.

At the carpet, Phillip asked students to recall where the song came from. Several students recalled that it came from Africa. Phillip then asked students to consider and guess what the song might be about.

As students entered the classroom in the morning, they completed their pack-up tasks and gathered in a circle on the carpet. Visuals containing information related to the morning meeting were displayed on the TV screen. As students settled into the circle, Taralyn asked several students to change places so that the group could be seated in a boy-girl pattern, directing specific students to sit between others to complete the pattern.

Taralyn joined the students in the circle and asked who would like to begin the greeting. She reminded students to look one another in the eye as they greeted each other. Ms. Joyce was seated outside of the circle and was not included in the greeting activity. When a couple of students laughed at something that was said during the greeting, Taralyn provided a quick redirection.

After the greeting was completed, Taralyn shared that she had noticed some laughter and possible discomfort. She invited students to share what had caused the laughter or discomfort and asked them to consider how it felt to be greeted without a genuine smile and how that might affect the community. Initially, the class was silent and no students volunteered to respond. Taralyn then used name sticks to randomly select students to share their thinking. After several students responded when called upon, additional students volunteered to build on the group's thinking. Taralyn connected their comments to an earlier class conversation about the "ripple effect."

Taralyn invited the class to try the greeting again. When one student delivered his greeting in a silly way and several students began to giggle, Taralyn used a quiet hand gesture to reduce the laughter. After the second greeting was completed, Taralyn asked students how the experience had felt different. She then shared a quote about kindness and asked students to share their thinking about the quote. Several students raised their hands and waited to be called on to contribute their ideas.
