column18:
When I learned that Ms. Joyce had been sitting outside of the circle and was not included in our greeting, I was really upset that I had not noticed it in the moment. I was so focused on the students, the greeting routine, and how students were interacting with one another that I missed something important happening within our community. This wondering made me reflect on how inclusion is communicated not only through what we say, but also through the choices we make and the way we create space for others. Moving forward, I will be much more intentional about noticing who is fully included in our circle and helping students develop that same awareness.

This also provides an authentic connection to our Who We Are unit and our learning from the first week of school about the ripple effect of our choices. At our next morning meeting, if someone is sitting outside of the circle, I will use it as an opportunity for students to pause, notice, and reflect: What choice are we making? What message might that choice send? How could it affect the person outside the circle and our community as a whole? I will connect this back to our class agreements of being respectful and kind and ask students to consider whether we are truly living by the agreements we created together. I want students to understand that even small choicessuch as making space for someone in a circlecan have a ripple effect on whether people feel seen, valued, and included in our community.

Thank you for the feedback, particularly the Wonder around student agency. It has encouraged me to reflect on how agency develops across the wider learning sequence rather than within a single stage of the lesson.

The observed part of the lesson was intentionally more teacher-guided, as students were revisiting foundational poetic and literary terminology that many had limited or no previous experience learning in Korean. This built on their Quizlet practice and an online knowledge check from the previous lesson. Using English and Chinese alongside Korean was also an intentional scaffold to help students connect unfamiliar Korean terminology with their existing linguistic knowledge.

My learning sequence is designed as a gradual release of responsibility. Following teacher modelling and guided review, students work collaboratively to identify and discuss poetic devices and stylistic choices, before moving into individual close reading and analysis. They then present and justify their interpretations to the class, eventually applying these skills independently in an analytical essay for their summative assessment.

Your Wonder has made me consider how I can make student agency more visible even within the earlier, scaffolded stages of this process. For example, students could have greater choice in which resources or linguistic supports they use, which textual features they investigate, or how they initially demonstrate their understanding. At the same time, I would like to retain the structured modelling needed at this stage and gradually increase student independence as their confidence and disciplinary knowledge develop.

This unit is a little different from our regular Design units, as it was added to help support the Grade 6 technology transition requested by the school rather than being part of our regular Design curriculum. Because of that, we have been trying to make sure it still fits meaningfully within the Design cycle and develops skills that are useful beyond just learning individual tools.

Students come into Grade 6 with very limited laptop experience, as laptops are not really used in Elementary, so we are starting with skills that we cannot assume they already have. Last year we moved the unit from Criterion C to Criterion A, which I think was much more appropriate. Students are still very much doing, but the doing is through primary research. They explore the tools themselves, ask questions, try things out, and record their findings rather than simply being shown what to do. This fits much better with Criterion A and with the main ATL focus of the unit, which is developing more independent learners.

We have continued to adjust the unit this year based on what students actually need. We added ManageBac, for example, as well as more explicit practice with typing, using a mouse, file management, and checking announcements. Many students are currently typing at around 1520 WPM, so some of these basic skills need more attention than we originally expected.

One challenge has been that there is still not always clear information about what systems students are expected to use or when they will be ready. For example, the Grade 6 groups were not available until the end of the first week of school. Since this unit is supporting a wider school transition, having the systems, expectations, and tools ready proactively would make it much easier to plan effectively rather than having to adjust reactively once the unit is already underway.

At the time of observation, KC students entered the elementary gym and sat along the sideline, where Charles welcomed them and explained that the lesson would begin with a warm-up. Students were invited to run or walk along the blue section surrounding the basketball court. After approximately two laps, Charles blew the whistle and students gathered in a circle at center court. 

Charles asked students to place their hands on their chests and notice their heartbeats. He explained that their hearts were beating faster because they had been running and introduced long, deep breaths as a way to help their bodies slow down and recover. Students then moved to an extended circle marked by colored mats and continued the warm-up with hip circles, knee circles, arm circles, and shuffling movements. When Charles used the whistle, he reinforced the established expectation that students should stop, look, and listen. 

After approximately eight minutes of continuous movement, Charles gathered students again to introduce a chasing game. He clearly explained the parameters and modeled how the game would work: students holding a small hoop became the wolves and attempted to catch classmates moving through their cage. Students then participated enthusiastically in the game. Throughout the observed portion of the lesson, students spent a significant amount of time physically active and consistently responded to Charles established signals and behavioral expectations.

DJ, 
thank you for taking the time to observe my PE class. I appreciate the notes and feedback you provided.
In response to your observations about student engagement and their response to the signals, my goal is to always maximize movement time. So I am glad to see that the structures in place (floor markers, modeling, and the whistle protocol) are already  helping create a smooth-running and active environment. Many students are returning from last year so a lot of routines have been review for them. 
I intentionally try to connect the physical and the cognitive aspects of PE, and try to help them understand the "why" behind what they are doing - like how their bodies react to exercise and how they can self-regulate. Hopefully they leave my class not only stronger, but more self aware.
Regarding your wondering about collaboration, I tend to focus on maximizing activity time during games, and can occasionally miss this opportunity. You are right that a brief pause for peer-to-peer converstion about strategies could improve the depth of the lesson. At the time of observation, Angela and the 1C students were engaged in a math lesson. Following a warm-up activity on the carpet, Angela introduced the next phase of the lesson. She shared the problem, I have the number 8 and I want to subtract 2. How can I do it? Each table had a copy of the question, one marker, and a 2 × 5 array. 

Angela emphasized that the focus was on thinking, sharing mathematical thinking, and making that thinking visible. She asked each group to select one person to act as the scribe while students discussed their ideas. Angela reminded students that there were many ways to show their thinking and encouraged them to draw on strategies they had used during the previous days lesson. 

Students worked in four groups. Initially, some groups were slow to begin discussing the problem. Angela and the Educational Assistant circulated and checked in with each group, and students gradually began sharing and recording their ideas. Different representations emerged across the groups, including mathematical expressions and diagrams. 

Angela then brought students together for a gallery walk to examine the different ways groups had represented their thinking. At the first stop, she highlighted that she could see thinking and perseverance, while also noting that answers did not always need to be correct because everyone was continuing to grow and learn. To support respectful mathematical discussion, Angela provided students with the sentence stem, I respectfully disagree. Maybe you could try


Students used mathematical expressions, diagrams, and strategies from the previous lesson to communicate how they were thinking about 8?2. This gave Grade 1 learners multiple entry points for expressing their understanding and reinforced that mathematical thinking can be represented in different ways.
column12: How are strong, trusting relationships cultivated as the foundation for peer learning and conflict resolution?
column13:
You intentionally structured the task around shared thinking by placing students in groups, assigning a scribe, and then using a gallery walk so students could see how their classmates approached the same problem differently. The sentence stem, I respectfully disagree. Maybe you could try
, was an especially useful support because it gave these young learners concrete language for responding to another persons mathematical thinking with respect and curiosity.
column14: Since some groups were initially slow to begin their conversation, what structure might help every student contribute - for example, giving individual think time followed by each student sharing one strategy before the scribe begins recording - so that the groups representation reflects the thinking of multiple learners?

column18:
Yes, I agree that adding more structure to the collaboration process could help ensure all learners have an opportunity to contribute before recording their thinking. Providing individual think time followed by each student sharing a strategy could help amplify a wider range of ideas.

Reflecting on this week, some of the challenge came from this being only our fourth Illustrative Mathematics lesson. Students are still building confidence with the routines and collaborative structures that support mathematical discourse, and I am already seeing growth in their willingness to share ideas and work together.

To be transparent, students were working in groups of four because the Building Thinking Classrooms work was intentionally left displayed on the whiteboards for Back-to-School Night. While this reduced the number of available boards, it also gave families an authentic glimpse into students mathematical thinking.

Looking back, I would have benefited from spending a few additional days engaging students in Building Thinking Classrooms tasks before moving into Illustrative Mathematics. A recent BTC activity with random pairings showed students becoming more willing to take risks, share ideas, and engage in mathematical conversations. As we continue using Illustrative Mathematics as our primary resource, I would be more intentional about grouping structures while continuing to build students confidence and collaborative skills as mathematicians.

Moving forward, an important consideration will be determining which lesson components are best suited for whole-group instruction, Individual  think time  and which lend themselves to a Building Thinking Classrooms approach.

At the time of observation, the 3C class was seated in rows while Joe shared expectations for the lesson. He asked the four team captains to collect the beach balls that would be used for the first activity, and the remainder of the class soon joined them. 

Joe used the whistle as a signal for attention. When he first blew the whistle, several students stopped and listened immediately, while a few needed additional time to respond. Continuing to explicitly teach, reinforce, and hold all students accountable to this routine would help make transitions more efficient and ensure that instructions are heard by everyone. 

Students then moved into four groups and formed circles, working together to keep a beach ball in the air using volleyball-style passes. After approximately four minutes, Joe blew the whistle again, and most students stopped and attended. He brought the class together to discuss strategies for keeping the ball in the air for longer. Joe modeled with a student how adjusting the amount of force used when striking the ball could improve control, and several additional strategies were demonstrated. 

Joe then reorganized the class from four groups into two larger groups and asked students to continue practicing. He remained with one group and provided ongoing coaching. After approximately three minutes, he gathered students again for a whole-group debrief. Students then returned to their original four teams for a new cooperative challenge in which they needed to transport a ball together without using their hands.

They also had to identify why the ball was dropping, consider the importance of synchronized movement and communication, and compare which strategies were more effective and why.

Students were seated in table groups working on All About Me flipbooks. An image of a completed book was displayed on the TV screen, along with a timer showing the remaining work time. A group of five students worked on the same task at the teacher table with Meagan, while Phoebe circulated among and supported students working at their table groups.

As students at the teacher table worked, Meagan provided feedback and asked clarifying questions. She encouraged one student to add drawings to accompany his writing and prompted students to move on to the next part of the task as they were ready. When students were ready to write sentences, Meagan supported them by having them practice saying their sentences aloud before writing them. When a student asked what personality meant, Meagan asked him to think about what people see when they think of him and provided examples from the All About Me book she had created. She then asked students to picture in their minds what they might draw to represent their thinking.

Throughout the observation, all students were working on their books, with some students quietly talking with peers as they worked. At the end of the work period, Meagan called for students attention and waited until everyone was listening and looking toward her. She explained that students would have three minutes to tidy their tables and that anyone who had not completed the task would have additional time later in the afternoon. She shared that once the room was tidy, the class would have a movement break, which was met with cheers from many students. Students cleaned their tables and moved to the carpet. Meagan then offered students a choice of which movement break to do.

column18:
Thank you for observing my lesson. I selected those five students to work at my table based on my initial observations of their independent work during the writing task. These students appeared to need the most targeted support to access the learningsome required additional explanation of the task itself, others needed sustained support with task initiation and focus, and a few needed both. By bringing them together, I was able to provide the scaffolding and encouragement they needed to move forward with confidence.

What was particularly interesting was how students responded differently to the small-group setting. Shirley, for instance, used the afternoon session to work independently, which showed she had internalized what she needed and was ready to apply it on her own. In contrast, Raz and Anthony were genuinely excited to continue working with me, which tells me they benefited from the one-on-one attention and are building positive associations with seeking help when they need it.

I see the small-group table as a responsive toolone that allows me to meet students where they are and adjust my support based on what I observe in real time. It also sends an important message that we all need help sometimes, and that asking for it is a strength.

When the observation began, students were working in three different groups. Ms. Celia was supporting students working on iPads, while another group of students was browsing books in the library corner. Mike was working with a group of six students who were writing sentences on marker board strips.

As students worked on a sentence, one student asked whether the word pool had one l or two. Mike wrote the word on his marker board and asked students which version they thought looked right. Once all students had finished the sentence, Mike provided a second sentence for them to write: The kid ran down the hill. The marker board strips were too short for some students to fit all of the words. Students worked at their own pace while Mike provided individual suggestions and encouragement. He reminded students to think about what goes at the end of a sentence.

Mike then asked the group to practice writing the word down with him. He noted that ow sometimes makes the sound heard in down and asked students to think of other words containing that ow sound.

When the timer on the board ran out, Mike checked in with the different groups, directing students to turn off iPads, put books away, or move to the teacher table. He then set a new timer for 11 minutes, and students transitioned to their new areas. Mike reminded students who were unsure where to go that they could check the directions on the whiteboard. One student had difficulty finding a book he wanted and interrupted Mikes teacher table group on two occasions. Mike told the student that he would help him find a book later.

Mike then began working with the next group of students, providing sentences for them to write on the marker boards.

At the time of observation, the PK4 Foxes were completing indoor play when Amelie played a song. Students began singing along and gathered in a circle on the carpet. Once they were seated, Amelie displayed a visual showing that eyes are watching, ears are listening, voices are quiet, and bodies are calm, reviewing each expectation with the class. To further focus students attention, she invited them to imagine holding a birthday cake, smell it, and then blow out the candles. 

Amelie then revisited the self-portraits students had created the previous week, sharing that she had noticed how different they were in features such as hair, eyes, and face shapes. She introduced a guessing game in which a small section of a students face, such as their eyes or mouth, was shown on the screen and classmates guessed who it was. Each student was included in the game. Once identified, the student used the sentence stem, Its me, and classmates responded, Its wonderful. Students participated enthusiastically throughout the activity. 

Amelie transitioned to a Sesame Street poster titled Were Different, Were the Same. She showed images of different characters noses and asked students what they noticed about how they were different before discussing what all noses can do, such as smell or sneeze. She repeated this process with mouths and skin, reinforcing the idea that parts of our bodies can look different while having similar functions. 

To connect the idea to students own experiences, Amelie invited students to place their hands on the carpet and notice how they were different. She then showed photographs of AISG students using their hands to demonstrate caring actions, including helping one another pick up toys.
column9: How might we ensure students are given voice and choice in the curriculum to reflect their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences?
column10: You intentionally created opportunities for students to affirm their identities and recognize differences as something to value. Revisiting each childs self-portrait, ensuring every student was represented in the guessing game, and establishing the repeated response, Its wonderful, positioned individual differences as assets within the class. This provides avenues for students to affirm their identities and supports an environment that values diversity and inclusivity.
column12: Do students have access to strategies for self-care and emotional well-being?
column13: You provided several developmentally appropriate ways for students to access and participate in the learning: music, visuals, photographs, movement, verbal discussion, sentence stems, and the concrete experience of examining their own hands.
column14: I wonder how students might have opportunities to make small choices within this learning - for example, choosing a feature of themselves they would like classmates to notice or share.

column18:
I appreciated the feedback about the intentional ways I affirmed each students identity and provided multiple entry points into the learning. This is one of the key areas thats on CASEL standard - to get to know oneself and feel affirmed. Including every child in the guessing game and using the response Its wonderful helped create a classroom environment in which differences were noticed, celebrated, and valued.

I had a similar reflection about providing students with more opportunities to make choices. At times, I become focused on covering the concept I have planned and move through the lesson too quickly. As a result, I may not give students enough time to process the idea, make personal connections, or contribute their own thinking.

Moving forward, I would like to slow down and create more space for student agency. For example, students could choose a feature they would like their classmates to notice, select a photograph or self-portrait detail to share, or decide how they would like to express what makes them unique. I could also pause more often to invite students observations and questions. These small choices would help students take greater ownership of the learning while giving them more time to connect the concept of difference and belonging to their own identities and experiences.

Thank you!

When the classroom visit began, students were working independently on a variety of writing tasks. Some students were creating heart maps, while others were writing about their summers or finishing an activity focused on how the class will treat others. Leighanna circulated around the room, checking in with students, answering questions, and providing feedback. She used a practiced call-and-response to gain the classs attention and reminded students that they could use their home language on their heart maps if they could not remember how to say or write something in English and translate it later. After checking in with one student, Leighanna asked whether he needed anything else before she moved on. When he said no, she told him she would check in with him again later.

A few moments into the visit, nearly all students were engaged in their individual tasks, while a couple of students were having difficulty getting started or sustaining their work. When one student shared that she was hungry and became distracted from her work, Leighanna directed her attention to the timer on the board, noting that three minutes remained, and encouraged her to finish the work period. When the timer ended, Leighanna asked students to put their materials away and return to their seats.

Before students left the classroom, Leighanna facilitated an on-task check-in using a thumb vote. She asked students whether they felt they had accomplished a lot during literacy time. When a couple of students asked what accomplished meant, Leighanna explained the word. She reminded students that everyone needed to participate in the thumb vote and invited students who showed a sideways or down thumb to talk with her about strategies that could help them be more successful. She also shared that she had not observed any thumbs-down behaviors during the literacy work time.
column9: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column10: The visible timer, individual teacher check-ins, feedback, and reminder that you would return to check on a student provided students with information and support for managing independent work. These practices connect with UDL guidance around optimizing challenge and support and offering action-oriented feedback.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?

This aligns with the Being goal of building self-reflection and goal-setting and with UDLs emphasis on enhancing learners capacity for monitoring progress.
column14: How might the invitation to use home languages be intentionally supported in the coming weeks so that translanguaging becomes an ongoing option as students plan, draft, discuss, and communicate their thinking, while also providing intentional supports that help students increasingly balance their use of multiple languages and build confidence and proficiency in sharing their learning in English?
column16: What structures support students in practicing self-regulation or collaboration beyond the classroom?
column18: To move translanguaging from an occasional fallback into an ongoing, intentional practice, I'd like to start by getting a clearer picture of my students' language strengths and areas for growth, whether through observation, conversations, or student sample work, so I can be more purposeful about how I pair language partners going forward. From there, I could form partnerships with intention: sometimes grouping students who share a home language so they can think and discuss freely before drafting, and other times pairing students with complementary strengths so English gets modeled and practiced together rather than one student just translating for another. I also want to continue to build in structured supports, like sentence frames, visuals, and sentence starters, especially at the point where students move from thinking in a mix of languages to writing in English, so they can carry their ideas over with confidence. Over time, this would help translanguaging become more than just a stopgap for a missing word. It could grow into a real tool for thinking and collaborating, while still supporting students as they build balance and confidence in English.

At the time of observation, the 1B students were transitioning into a mathematics lesson. Students were seated on the carpet while Sonia displayed the title Sort and Count Shapes on the screen. She presented a range of shapes and colors and invited students to respond to the prompts, What do you notice? and What do you wonder? 

Students were eager to contribute observations and questions. One student wondered why a hexagon had a line through the middle, and another student responded that it was because the hexagon was made of two trapezoids. Another student made an observation about quadrilaterals. Sonia facilitated the discussion for approximately four minutes, allowing students to build on the mathematical ideas that emerged. 

Before moving into the next phase of the lesson, Sonia reviewed the norms and behaviors of the 1B Mathematical Community, which appeared to have been co-created by the class the previous week. Sonia then asked students whether they had ever participated in a race. Following a short discussion, she posed the problem: What happens if a circle and a square race? 

Students were placed into random partnerships and moved to vertical whiteboards, where they began discussing the problem and recording their thinking. Sonia and the Educational Assistant circulated between pairs, checking in and offering support as students worked.
column9: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column10: You created meaningful space for student thinking at the beginning of the lesson through the Notice and Wonder routine. Rather than immediately explaining the shapes, you invited students to identify mathematical relationships themselves. The exchange about the hexagon being composed of two trapezoids was particularly strong evidence that students were contributing ideas and responding to one anothers mathematical thinking.
column12: How might assessment models be adapted to accommodate students from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds?
column13: You provided several entry points into the mathematics by combining visual representations of shapes, oral discussion, connections to students experiences with racing, partner talk, and recording ideas on vertical whiteboards. These different modes gave Grade 1 students multiple ways to access and begin expressing their thinking rather than relying on a single form of participation.
column14: I wonder how the learning intention for the circle and square race problem was made visible to students. What mathematical idea were students intended to investigate, and how might making that purpose more explicit help them understand what they are trying to discover as they discuss and represent their thinking?

column18: After reflecting on the lesson, I realized that my students werent sorting and organizing the way I had anticipated. My goal was for them to create some form of structure that would help them recognize patterns, but they ended up focusing more on the attributes of the shapes rather than the patterns themselves. Looking back, I should have guided them through sorting with two shapes first, then had them work in pairs to explore other possible outcomes, this would have given them a clearer sense of what I was aiming for. In tomorrows lesson, theyll be working with shapes again and sorting them into different groups.

- Grade 7 Science (14:15 start observation - P4)
- 21 students
- Students are engaged in a lab related to temprature and energy transfer
- One student, when asked, could explain the experiment in her own words
- After conclusion of the experiment, students are asked to answer questions on the whiteboard tables. Teacher is directing what they need to drawn on their table (two lines, fire, and particles)

Following lunch, students returned to the classroom and were seated at their tables with their notebooks open. Leighanna worked to gain the classs attention while Jon checked in with students. As Leighanna introduced a discussion about parts of speech, Jon wrote parts of speech on the board and recorded the different parts of speech that students identified during the group discussion.

Students initially had difficulty recalling parts of speech beyond nouns. One student identified verb but did not remember its meaning, and another student explained that verbs are action words. Jon wrote a sentence on the board and asked students to identify the action verb in the sentence. Students then talked with partners about other action words. Leighanna asked students to share words their partners had identified, and Jon recorded additional examples of verbs on the board.

A student identified adverb as another part of speech but did not know its meaning. Leighanna asked whether anyone in the class knew what it meant. When no students responded, she told the class that this was okay. Another student identified adjective but did not know its meaning, and another student attempted to contribute. Jon connected the discussion to the sentence on the board, asking students, if an adjective describes a noun, what the adjective might be in the new sentence he had written. He then asked students to suggest other adjectives that could be used in the sentence.

As students began calling out answers, Leighanna reminded them that their goal for the week was not to blurt out. While Leighanna spoke with the class, Jon approached a student who needed redirection related to seated behavior. Leighanna then directed students attention to a sentence that was already printed in their open notebooks. She guided students through questions about the parts of speech in the sentence and asked them to underline the nouns in green. As students worked on this task, Jon circulated among the tables, checking on individual students and their progress.

Thank you for the detailed observation and notes.  This mini-lesson will recur throughout the year as students learn to break down mentor sentences, label parts of speech, and develop their understanding of sentence complexity. We plan to implement a color-coding system that will follow them from these weekly mentor sentences directly into their small guided reading groups.

For this specific block, we planned three components: whole-class grammar instruction, UFLI, and literacy rotations. Currently, the first two components are taught whole-group. However, we are discussing transitioning to a parallel teaching model in the future. By splitting the classroom, we can deliver the same instruction while providing more targeted support to learners who benefit from smaller groups. For now, we are co-monitoring the whole class together.

The third component of the lesson was literacy rotations, where we each lead a station that connects back to the grammar and UFLI patterns. My focus is leveled guided reading. Throughout the week, we will reinforce and extend these concepts during our rotations. During the observation, my small group worked on starting a new book. We integrated the new phonemic pattern and plan to use a mentor sentence from this guided reading book to extend our parts-of-speech discussion across multiple readings of the text.

Following lunch, students met on the carpet and participated in movement and focus activities led by a video. After approximately five minutes, Naomi stopped the video and asked students to sit in a circle for math time. Naomi displayed dots on the board and asked students to engage with the dots in different ways. When students went to the board to count the dots, she asked them to demonstrate different ways of counting them.

Naomi then read a story about four little speckled frogs. She asked students to identify how many frogs there were at the beginning of the story and how many remained at the end. She invited four students to volunteer as frogs and read the story while the students acted it out. A second group of four students then acted out the story. Following the activity, Naomi asked the students who had participated to pat themselves on the back for being good frogs.

Naomi told students that they would next complete an activity at their tables. She asked students to check whether there were enough pencils for everyone at their table. After checking, students returned to the carpet. Naomi then asked whether there were enough pencils for everyone to have two. Students returned to their tables to check and then came back to the carpet. Next, she asked students to determine whether there were enough erasers for everyone to have one, again having them return to the circle after checking. Most students returned to the carpet quickly each time. When students did not walk or follow another expectation, Naomi redirected their behavior.

Back on the carpet, Naomi asked students how they knew whether there were enough materials. Students responded that they had counted the items. When students asked about counting additional classroom materials, Naomi also invited them to check the scissors and glue sticks. With each direction to check objects, all students engaged in looking at the materials and coming back to the carpet. Responses to the questions were answered largely in whole group response.

column18: Thank you for coming in! As I read over the observations, two things stood out to me. First, when two students wanted the same color and I suggested Rock, Paper, Scissors to resolve it, I wondered if this was a missed teachable moment. I did ask, "What could you do to solve this?" when they couldnt come up with something right away I could have shown them the Rammy Makes a Choice poster to help them decide. However, I also considered that stopping the lesson at that moment might have taken away from the math lesson. I believe it was a teachable moment, but perhaps one that could be addressed during a class discussion or reflection time rather than in the moment. Second, I reflected on my use of a timer during centers. I realized I need to be more consistent with using a timer so that students understand the routine, transitions are smoother, and I am not managing everything myself. Going forward, I want to use a timer consistently to support student independence and allow myself to focus more on observing and supporting their learning during centers.

At the time of observation, Jessie was introducing students to the phone strategy, in which each student used a replica phone handle to speak quietly and listen closely to their own pronunciation. On the screen, Jessie displayed a range of vocabulary words with corresponding images. The words were intentionally selected to highlight similar sounds that differed according to the tonal marks written in Pinyin. The focus of this portion of the lesson was for students to recognize and accurately produce these tonal differences. 

Jessie asked students to use their phones to practise saying each word as she pointed to it on the screen. It took several moments for students to settle into the routine and use the phones purposefully. As students pronounced each word, Jessie reinforced the connection between the spoken sound and the four tones displayed on the whiteboard. After approximately three minutes, she introduced a second set of words featuring a different sound and repeated the practice. 

Jessie then asked students to put their phones down and returned to the first set of vocabulary. Individual volunteers used the microphone to pronounce the words and tones for the class. During this phase, several students continued playing with their phone handles, which created a noticeable level of distraction. As Jessie began introducing the next part of the lesson, she stopped and collected the phones before continuing. Students then received their notebooks and moved into written practice. Jessie pronounced words from the screen, and students recorded each word in Pinyin with the corresponding tonal mark.

Thank you for this thoughtful observation. 
Your "wondering" resonates with me: I understand the power of creating space for them to explain why they chose a particular answer, making their reasoning visible and strengthening not only their ownership of the learning process, but also helping other students to develop strategies for language comprehension. 
When students explain or justify their thinking, they demonstrate and reinforce comprehension strategies such as recognizing cognates, using prefixes and suffixes or using context. It is beneficial for students to share these strategies with one another. I often design my lessons to encourage this. For example, when we practice reading strategies in preparation for formative and summative reading assessments, or when we reflect on those strategies, I have students work in pairs or small groups. They help each other arrive at answers and are expected to explain their reasoning. We also discuss the strategies used, so that students can apply similar approaches independently. However, incorporating this into Quizlet Live would be somewhat difficult because, as a friendly competition, speed is key.
One concern however, is that the use of the target language in the classroom (by myself and the students) is imperative. However, for Phase 2 students to explain their thinking, they will need to use their native language (English/Chinese/Korean.) I struggle to find a balance, though ultimately the goal is that they become capable of expressing such ideas in Spanish. 
A brief reflection routine would not interupt the flow of the game. Students could share which match was the most challenging and how they figured it out. This would encourage metacognition and allow students to hear diverse strategies, fostering a classroom culture where reasoning is valued alongside accuracy. By making their thinking processes visible, students become active participants in their own learning rather than simply receivers of correct answers.

Thank you again for your support and insights!

After using the washroom, washing their hands, and having a drink of water, Yilan lined students up at the classroom door and invited them to find their bubble  a laminated leaf displaying their photo and name. When one student ran to his bubble, Yilan calmly stopped him, reminded him that students walk in the Teddy Bear classroom, and asked him to return to the door and try again. This provided an immediate opportunity to reinforce the classroom expectation in a clear and consistent way. 

Once students were settled on the carpet, Yilan played a Hello song to begin the morning meeting. Students enthusiastically danced and sang together before returning to their bubbles. Yilan then introduced a chart displaying images of feet, a car, a bus, and a train and asked students to identify how they travelled to school that morning. One at a time, students placed their photograph beneath the corresponding mode of transportation. Yilan extended their responses with follow-up questions such as, Who drives the car? When students had difficulty expressing their ideas in English, the Educational Assistant supported them through translanguaging. Yilan also invited the adults in the room to share how they travelled to school, further connecting the conversation to the students classroom community. 

After approximately seven minutes, Yilan used the completed chart to transition into a counting experience. She first asked students how many classmates had walked to school, and students responded, One. One student then selected the magnetic numeral 1 to place on the chart, while another was invited to write the numeral. Yilan repeated this process for each transportation category. Students then stood and counted to ten together while clapping, followed by counting to ten while jumping. As the observation concluded, Yilan was preparing to read a story to the class.

column18:
Thank you for this thoughtful wondering. After reflecting on your question, I recognize that by asking students "Which group has the most? Which has the fewest? How do you know?" I can intentionally shift their focus from simple counting to deeper mathematical thinking and reasoning. However, since my students are still developing their English vocabulary, I need to consider how to make these concepts accessible to them.

To support my students' understanding, I plan to:
Use Visual and Gestural Support: Rather than relying on words alone, I will use hand gestures, pointing, and visual demonstrations to show "most" and "fewest." I can physically move between groups and use exaggerated motions to help them understand the concept.

Simplify Language: I will use shorter, simpler sentences paired with visuals. For example: "Look. This group has more. This group has less" while pointing and comparing.

Incorporate Home Languages: I will ask my EA to support by using comparison words in my students' home languages to support understanding.

Repeat and Reinforce: I will use the same comparison language consistently so students become familiar with these terms over time through repetition and context.

Explore Measurement Through Hands-On Activities: we will explore our height in the class using different measurement methods. Students will build with blocks to match their height, use beads strung together to measure their length, and use ribbon to measure as well. These hands-on activities create natural opportunities for students to understand non-standard measurement, compare and notice differences, build mathematical language, develop fine motor skills, and explore measurement concepts.Through these measuring activities, students encounter words like "tall," "long," "same," "different," "taller," and "shorter." Repeated exposure to these terms in context supports our learners.
