column12: How are strong, trusting relationships cultivated as the foundation for peer learning and conflict resolution?
column13: Your response to the emerging conflict supported students in developing the language they needed to begin resolving the situation themselves. Providing language stems rather than simply solving the disagreement for them equips students with conflict-resolution strategies and developing the trusting relationships needed for peer interaction. Reinforcing nearby examples of successful cooperation also made positive collaborative behaviors visible to the group.
column14: I wonder where the idea to paint leaves originated. Was this primarily an adult-designed provocation, or had it emerged from something students had noticed, collected, discussed, or shown interest in?
column16: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column18:
Yes, the leaf painting was a teacher-planned provocation. Since it is still the beginning of the school year, I am still getting to know the students, what they are interested in, what skills they are bringing, and how they play and work with different materials and with each other. I planned the leaf painting as an open-ended activity so students could explore natural materials through watercolor, texture, color, and conversation.

My goal was not for everyone to make the same finished product. I wanted the leaves and watercolor to be an invitation for students to explore, and also a way for me to learn more about them. I was watching to see what they noticed, how they used the materials, what they talked about, and what interests might come from the experience that we could build on next.

column7:
At the time of observation, the PK4 Tigers were engaged in indoor play. Karen was highly mobile throughout the classroom, moving between individual students and small groups as they engaged in a range of experiences, including creating artwork, using play dough at the sensory station, and imagining they were refurbishing a home in the loft. 

Karen sat alongside one student who was creating artwork and drew with her while engaging her in conversation. She asked questions about the students work, responded to her ideas, and ensured she had access to the materials she needed. At the painting easel, Karen supported several students as they finished their paintings. Rather than completing the routines for them, she provided just enough guidance for students to move their own paintings to the drying rack and clean the easel independently. 

A similar approach was evident when a student wanted to use a stapler to create a book. Rather than stapling the pages herself, Karen asked the educational assistant to show the student how to use the stapler so the student could complete the task independently. Later, when several students working in the loft announced that they had finished refurbishing their home, Karen responded, What else can you add to make it better?, encouraging them to return to their ideas and continue developing their play. Throughout the observation, the educational assistant actively documented students play by taking photographs with the class iPad.
column9: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column10: A particularly strong aspect of your practice was the way you consistently supported students without taking over their work. Whether students were moving paintings, cleaning the easel, using a stapler, or developing their play in the loft, you positioned yourself as a scaffold rather than the person completing the task. This models respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior and creates opportunities for students to become the primary drivers of their work.
column12: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column13:
The indoor play environment provided students with meaningful opportunities to design, create, make, and add something unique to their play. Students were creating artwork, making books, experimenting with materials, and collaboratively transforming the loft into their imagined home. 

Your response when the student announced they were finished -  What else can you add to make it better? - was particularly effective and encouraged him to act. Rather than suggesting what they should add, you encouraged them to revisit their own ideas, extend their thinking, and continue the creative process.
column14: The educational assistant was actively taking photographs throughout the play period. I wonder whether students also have opportunities to use the iPad themselves to photograph their play, creations, or moments they consider important. How might giving students greater ownership of the documentation process further strengthen their agency and reflection?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column18:
Thank you! I agree that giving students more ownership over documentation can be a powerful way to increase students agency and reflection. Its something Ive been thinking about and I plan to introduce this idea as the year progresses. 
Right now, we are still in the early stages of settling into routines and building a shared understanding of how our classroom works. Once I feel that students have a solid grasp of our daily rhythms, expectations, and how to use materials safely and respectfully, I plan to invite them to take on more active roles in documenting their own play and learning through using the iPad to take photos, record videos, or capture moments that matter to them. 
In the past, in preparation for student-led conferences, we have had the students create a photo story of the things they like best about AISG. It has been interesting to see how some children really connect to this kind of reflection and Im sure if I start this kind of documentation earlier in the year they will show me even more of their amazing wonderings.
I also want to be aware of ensuring that the technology tool becomes an extension of their curiosity rather than a distraction to their play.

column7: AH initially entered the classroom with intention of a quick pop-in, but the interactions with students during their brain break, in which they showed me their I&S Notebooks provided an opportunity to highlight strong classroom practice that was targeted to the developmental needs of pre-teens. Furthermore the brain-break from learning about still challenged students with some brain-teasing puzzles that partners and small groups were working on withing the classroom. Students took me through their notebook to explain the expectations for the L&R page system for each topic, how each topic must be contained within those two pages, expctations for annotations, highlighting, and pasting in relevant artifacts givn by the teacher. Each time a new topic is introdiced, the students write it in their index, so they can easily refer to the numbered pages. The notebooks were tidy, well-organized, legible writing, and no loose papers. All resources are in this notebook. The majority of students I spoke with shared they were very happy with this system and said it was nice they didn't have to use their computer.
column9: How might assessment models be adapted to accommodate students from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds?
column10: The structured L&R notebook system was highly responsive to the developmental needs of Grade 7 learners. Containing each topic within two indexed pages, alongside clear expectations for annotations, highlighting, and attached resources, gave students a concrete system for managing increasingly complex learning. The brain break also provided a thoughtful change of pace while keeping students socially and cognitively engaged through optional puzzles with partners and small groups.
column12: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column13: Students did more than follow the notebook system, they could independently explain its purpose, expectations, and organization. Their tidy, complete notebooks, updated indexes, and ability to locate resources quickly showed that they had internalized responsibility for maintaining their learning. Students positive comments about having everything in one place, and not needing their computers, also suggested that the system helped them feel more organized and in control.
column14: This is my soft encouragement to perhaps share this approach with your peers in I&S, and perhaps across PLC's. The notebook system appeared to be successfully developing organization and resource-management habits within I&S. How might students periodically reflect on which elements of the system most support their learning, and consider how strategies such as indexing, visual annotation, or consolidating resources could transfer to other subjects and future learning contexts? Can I sign you up for a future Teachers Teaching Teachers (TTT)?
column18: Thanks for the feedback, Andrew.  I am truly sorry for the delayed response, and it will not happen again, as I now know exactly what is expected.   Regarding "wondering," I would be more than happy to share the interactive notebook with departments/colleagues.  I would like to wait a little longer, however, as I would like to present a student notebook to the faculty later in the year when the students have completed a bulk of the course.  I believe this approach would have a positive effect, as they would be able to better see the utility of notebook.

column7:
22 students in class. Students were working through a linear function problem about weekly savings, with the problem and supporting prompts displayed on the board. The display reminded students to read the question, annotate, analyze the information, write an equation, and include units and show their work. Both standard form and point-slope form were provided as possible approaches, with y = mx + b written on the board and students asked to identify x, y, m and b.

Students talked through the problem in pairs and at their group tables. Four students sitting in the individual seats along the side worked independently rather than with another student. One student was using a calculator. An online random name selector was used to select students to answer questions. There was quite a lot of side conversation from students while Esteban was talking.

Looking at one students notebook, they had recorded and were working with y = mx + b, slope, point-slope form and coordinate pairs. There were a number of attempts, corrections and crossed-out working as the student worked through the problem.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: The learning experience provided students with different ways to access and work through the problem. The prompts on the board broke the process down clearly, while also giving students the option of using standard or point-slope form. I also noticed students approaching the mathematics in different ways in their working, with the student notebook I looked at showing several attempts and corrections as they worked towards a solution. Students had space to work through the problem at their own pace, while you circulated and provided support where needed.
column12: What structures support students in practicing self-regulation or collaboration beyond the classroom?
column13: Students had clear opportunities to collaborate, with time to talk through the problem in pairs and at their tables before answers were shared with the class. I also liked the reminders on the board to read, annotate, analyse and show working. These gave students a clear process to follow and reinforced habits they can use when working through problems independently.
column14: I wonder how we might build on tasks like this to help students see themselves as capable mathematicians, particularly those who may lack confidence or need more support to get started. How do you help students recognise their own progress and develop confidence that they can work through challenging problems, even when they dont immediately know what to do?
column16: How might this task shift students beliefs about their potential or their ability to influence outcomes in their lives?
column18:
Thank you for the observation John. I appreciate the feedback on collaboration and personalization.

The strategies I used are consistent with my usual approach: giving thinking time before solutions, encouraging different approaches, and focusing questions on process rather than quick answers. I also try to build on valid ideas students share during discussion. I do recognize that with 22 students, keeping everyone fully focused during whole-class moments can be challenging, and I will continue working on that. Using the wheel of names creates a moment of excitement (some students really want to be selected, while others absolutely do not), and that bit of tension helps keep them engaged, but at the same time will rise the excitement and creates some disorder, that can be good to some point, but needs to be controlled.

Regarding the confidence question, definitively group work helps. Next week we (with Ms. Crosby) have planned a stations activity with different formats (papers, puzzles, manipulative) that will help to develop confidence and independence. I will circulate giving them support, but mainly,  I will be in a particular station where I will offer direct support to selected students. That dynamic may give them space to practice on their own, which I hope will build their confidence and sense of capability.

column7:
13 students in class, with three students sitting individually and the others sitting in pairs. Mario was at the front working through an example on the screen using his iPad to demonstrate how to find the inverse of a function. He worked through the process step by step on the display, using different colors to show the different parts of the working.

The class was quiet and focused while Mario was explaining. One student asked a question, which Mario answered and demonstrated on the screen. One student in the back row was explaining part of the process to the student next to them in Chinese.

There was very little student talk during the teacher-led part of the lesson. Mario then moved from finding the inverse algebraically to graphing the inverse. Following the demonstration and explanation, students moved into working on the task themselves.
column9: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
column10: The calm and supportive learning environment you have created was good for your students to focus. Students were comfortable asking questions when they were unsure, and I noticed a student quietly explaining their thinking to a classmate in Chinese. Both are good indicators that students feel safe to seek clarification, test their understanding and support each other without worrying about getting something wrong.
column12: To what extent is student work authentic and reflective of that done by experts outside of school?
column13: I like the use of a problem that asks students to apply their understanding of functions rather than simply follow a procedure. Finding and graphing an inverse requires students to move between different representations and make sense of the relationship between them. This is also building the kind of mathematical thinking and confidence with functions that students will need as they move into IBDP Mathematics, where they will increasingly need to select and apply their understanding in less familiar contexts.
column14: I wonder how you determine, during a teacher-led explanation like this one, where individual students are in their understanding before moving into independent work? How might that information then shape the level of support, challenge or next step that different students receive?
column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18:
Thank you for visiting my class and the observations you noted.

To answer the questions from the wondering part, during a teacher-led explanation, I can gauge individual student understanding by incorporating a few low-stakes, quick checks for understanding. For example, I might pause after each key step and ask students to show a thumbs-up, thumbs-down, or a specific number of fingers to indicate  their condiecne level.

I also watch for non-verbal cues such as students who are fidgeting, looking away, or not writing anything compared with those who are nodding and writing along.

The environment is created so that when students do ask questions, it gives me the opportunity to ask the class and check for their understanding.

I also utilize IXL for a quick quiz (entry slip) at the beginning of the class to check for student understanding on the content covered prior to the class. We do this 1-2 times a week depending on the content covered.

This information allows me to gauge our students confidence level and their ability to understand what was covered, which then allows me to further differentiate the instruction/work that the students will do.

column7:
17 students in class. The class started with quiet reading, with the timing for the opening part of the lesson clearly displayed on the board: reading from 13:5514:15 and then writing from 14:1514:20. One student was sitting independently, one pair together and the other students were sitting in groups of three or four.

Students were reading books of their own choice and making notes about what they had read. The room was very quiet during this time, although some students quietly talked with each other about the task. Looking at student work, students were keeping a reading record including the book they were reading, time spent reading, pages read and a short response to their reading. One student was reading a Chinese graphic novel and had quite detailed handwritten notes alongside their reading.

Pearl worked individually with one student and gave feedback on their work. She then circulated between the tables, checking in with students as they completed the task.

Pearl brought the class back together at the front and students looked and listened as she spoke. She used the board to explain the next part of the task and asked prompting questions as she worked through it. A number of students responded to her questions. Pearl then moved back to the board and continued explaining and modeling the correct way to complete the task before students moved on with their work.
column9: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column10: You created space for students to bring something of themselves to the learning through their independent reading. Students were reading different texts and, through the short reflection, were asked to make their own meaning from what they had read. I particularly liked seeing the range of texts students were engaging with and how their individual responses captured something different from their reading.
column12: How might personalized learning experiences foster a sense of community?
column13: You created a calm environment where students were able to engage with texts that were meaningful to them, while still being part of a shared reading experience. I particularly liked seeing students reading different texts and working independently, while also having opportunities to quietly share and talk about their reading with others. Your circulating and checking in individually with students added to the sense that each student and their learning was valued within the class.
column14: Thanks for having me in your class today. I wonder how we might give students opportunities to explore and share the different experiences that exist within Chinese culture. Could students draw on their own family histories, regional backgrounds, different Chinese dialects, or the experiences of Chinese communities around the world and connect these to the texts they are reading? What might this look like in your class?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to document and share cultural histories?
column18: Thank you for the observation and insightful feedback. Your questions has given me a lot to think about connecting with students' Chinese background. Here are my some thoughts. Before independent reading, I could provide students with a simple prompt which is related to themselves, such as culture heritage, family histories. After reading, they could respond to the prompt, which will link the text to students' personal world. Students can write it down on their reading journal or we can do pair sharing. Besides, I will continue to expand the classroom library to include about Chinese communities.

column7:
Grade 10 I&S working on the Family History Task, a summative assessment that included a self-reflection. The class was split between study boxes, with one table of four and one table of three, and other students working in the spaces outside. Students were working individually on their laptops. One student asked Ron a clarifying question about the task.

Three students were speaking to each other in Chinese and the volume increased for a short period. Ron went out to check on students working in the study boxes. Students had an accountability partner and were asked to check their partners work.

Ron asked students to close their devices while he gave the next set of instructions. He then asked students to turn and talk with a partner about the next steps for the task.
column9: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column10: The Family History Task gave students a clear opportunity to reflect on their own work and progress. I particularly liked the combination of individual self-reflection and the use of accountability partners to check each others work. The turn and talk around next steps also gave students space to think about where they were in the process and what they needed to do next, rather than simply moving on with the task.
column12: How might we ensure students have opportunities to learn from each other's cultural backgrounds and experiences?
column13: I liked the use of accountability partners and the turn and talk, which created opportunities for students to learn from each other rather than working entirely in isolation. This felt particularly relevant for the Family History Task, where students are bringing their own family and cultural experiences into their work. Giving students space to share and discuss these experiences allows the diversity within the class to become part of the learning.
column14: Thanks for having me in your class. A wondering for me is how the Family History Task could be used to go even further in bringing diverse perspectives and experiences into the learning of the whole class. There is a really rich opportunity here for students not only to explore their own family histories, but also to learn from the different histories, experiences and perspectives represented by their classmates, particularly those that may not usually be visible in the curriculum. How might you create opportunities for students to share aspects of what they discover through this task so that their individual family histories and experiences become a resource for the learning of the wider class?
column16: How might we design lessons to highlight diverse contributions to fields that may not often be highlighted within the mainstream curricula?
column18:
Thanks, John. I appreciate the feedback and the wondering. I really like the idea of extending the Family History Task so that some of the individual learning can become part of the wider class learning as well.

One possibility could be giving students an opportunity at the end of the task to share something from their family history that theyre comfortable sharing. With the diversity we have in the class, I think there could be some really interesting connections, similarities and differences that come out of that.

Something for me to explore as I continue developing the task. Thanks again for coming in.

column7:
Six students were present in the class.
The teacher used a thumbs-up/thumbs-middle check-in to gauge students' perceptions of the usefulness of the presentation task. Four students indicated a thumbs-up, while two responded with a thumbs-middle.
The teacher invited students who responded with a thumbs-middle to elaborate on their thinking, prompting a discussion about the value of learning from both preparing their own presentation and listening to the presentations of others.
The teacher clearly outlined the timeline for the task, explaining that presentation slides were due by Tuesday and that students would present in pairs. The teacher also connected the task to students' preparation for Paper One on September 8, helping students understand the purpose and relevance of the learning.
The teacher checked assigned homework before transitioning into the paired work.
Students worked collaboratively in pairs to develop their presentations.
Throughout the lesson, the teacher circulated around the room, offering encouragement, checking for understanding, and conferencing with students about how their chosen topic connected to the identified global issue. The teacher used questioning to clarify students' thinking and support their understanding.
column9: How do we help students generalize a mindset or strategy from one subject or setting to another?
column10: The teacher explicitly connected the current learning to future assessments and learning experiences. Students understood that their paired presentations would prepare them for Paper One on September 8, helping them see the relevance and purpose of the task beyond the immediate lesson. By making these connections, the teacher reinforced that the presentation skills and analysis students were developing would transfer to future learning.
column12: To what extent are students encouraged to explore diverse global perspectives on historical and contemporary issues that extend beyond the dominant culture?
column13: The teacher regularly checked for student understanding and encouraged reflection throughout the lesson. Students were invited to evaluate the usefulness of the task using a thumbs-up/thumbs-middle check-in, and the teacher followed up by asking students to explain their thinking. As students worked in pairs, the teacher circulated, provided encouragement, and checked students' understanding of how their topic connected to the identified global issue, offering timely support where needed.
column14: Students worked collaboratively in pairs and responded to teacher prompts throughout the lesson. I wonder how students might have additional opportunities to make decisions about the direction or format of their presentations, or to co-construct the success criteria. How might increasing student ownership further strengthen engagement and investment in the learning process?
column16: How might we ensure students are given voice and choice in the curriculum to reflect their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences?
column18:
Thank you for the detailed feedback on this lesson.

It is useful to know that an observer can see my intention to make explicit connections between course content, formative activities and assessment tasks. I want students to feel as though the work in class is purposeful and meaningful. Sometimes this relates to an assessment, but it also relates to what kind of learning tasks feel relevant and useful. For example, I think that students can sometimes find peer presentations a little tough to sit through.

I wanted to check that most students got something out of peer presentations and I often use things like thumbs up/thumbs down to help me take a quick survey during lessons. 

In terms of how I could then make the peer presentations more useful, I could have provided feedback sheets for students to fill out during the presentations. In the past I have selected different students to do these (not all students have to give feedback every time) and this is a good way of personalizing learning. I.e. I can ask a student who struggles with close reading to give feedback to a student who is strong in analysis to help them identify what might be missing in their own work. Generally, giving feedback helps students to attend to what their peers are saying and make connections back to their own learning. 

In relation to the wondering, it would have been useful to have students co-construct the success criteria for the presentations because it would require them to identify what learning needed to come out of the task. Also, in this small class, it would help them feel more ownership and engagement. As there are only 8 students, I need to think carefully about how to create learning experiences that cater to the very different individuals in this class (especially as only one student speaks English as their mother tongue).

column7:
At the time of observation, the 1A students were transitioning from snack break and their morning specials into a mathematics lesson. As students returned to the classroom, Lovina played a calming video, which supported them in settling quietly onto the carpet. Once students were ready, she rang a bell to signal the transition into learning. 

To begin the lesson, Lovina displayed a model graph titled Favorite Fruits and revisited key vocabulary students had been exploring, including survey, data, information, category, organize, and sort. She then shared the learning intention for the lesson: students would work with a partner to create a survey question that could be used to generate data from their 1A classmates. 

Using the graph as a model, Lovina reinforced learning from the previous week. She reviewed the idea that categories help organize and sort collected information, using different fruits such as apples, pears, and strawberries as examples. She then posed a series of questions that required students to interpret the graph, including identifying the most and least popular fruits and determining how many students preferred particular choices. 

After reiterating the partner task, Lovina used popsicle sticks to randomly pair students. Before releasing them to work, Lovina and the Educational Assistant modeled how partners could approach the task together, including what to do if they had different ideas about which survey question to pursue. Their demonstration explicitly showed students how to listen to one another, negotiate ideas, and compromise when making a shared decision.
column9: How are strong, trusting relationships cultivated as the foundation for peer learning and conflict resolution?
column10: The modelling by you and the Educational Assistant was a particularly strong example of intentionally preparing students for collaborative learning. Rather than simply telling students to work together, you demonstrated what collaboration could sound and look like when two partners have different ideas.
column12: In what ways do students have opportunities to engage with their community through their learning projects?
column13: The task itself provided an important opportunity for student decision-making: rather than simply responding to a teacher-generated survey, pairs were being asked to develop the question that would generate their own data.
column14: What opportunities will individual students have to develop survey questions around things they are genuinely curious about?
column16: In what ways does authentic learning promote a sense of connection to the broader world?
column18:
Today's lesson connected to the data handling component of Illustrative Mathematics Unit 1. Students had the opportunity to create their own survey questions, and tomorrow we will focus on gathering and organizing data. This learning also links to our UOI, where we are exploring our community and encouraging students to be curious about the people and places around them.

In our daily classroom routines, students regularly participate in voting to make fair and collaborative decisions. For example, one of this week's exploration stations focuses on origami. Students voted on activities they were curious about and interested in exploring during exploration time. We are already seeing students become experts in different areas and confidently teach and support one another in their learning, fostering a classroom culture of curiosity, collaboration, and shared discovery.

column7:
At the time of observation, the 1D students were seated on the carpet as Cat facilitated a Writing Workshop mini-lesson. At the outset, she shared the learning intention: students would practice adding more detail to writing they had already started. Cat used her own writing about going to the movies as a model text, displaying it on the screen and rereading it with the class. She then asked, What other details could I add to my writing? before introducing the carrot strategy, demonstrating how writers can mark a place in their draft where they want to insert additional information. 

Cat modeled the revision process by adding details such as the name of the movie and who she attended it with. As she wrote the movie title, she explained that she was unsure of the exact spelling and would stretch it out and write it as best she could. This modeled for students that, at this stage of the writing process, communicating ideas takes priority over having every word spelled accurately. Throughout the modeling, Cat consistently sounded out words and phrases as she wrote, providing students with an audible and visible example of how writers can independently work through unfamiliar words. 

Cat also explained that she wanted to make her illustrations clearer for her audience and modeled adding labels to important parts of her drawing. On the following Your Turn slide, she clearly outlined the expectations for independent writing: students would select one of their pieces from the previous week, reread it, use the carrot strategy to add additional details, and add labels to their illustrations. She also provided a clear extension for students who finished before the timer ended: they could revisit another existing piece and continue revising rather than beginning a new piece of writing.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You made the revision process highly visible by combining oral explanation, a visual model, the physical carrot marking, sounding out unfamiliar words, and labels on illustrations. Particularly effective was your willingness to model uncertainty around spelling and demonstrate how to stretch a word rather than allowing accuracy to interrupt the flow of ideas. These concrete strategies provide your students with practical ways to continue working independently when they encounter a barrier.
column12: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column13: Rather than simply telling students to add more detail, you explicitly modeled a strategy they could later apply without adult assistance. Your directions positioned students to manage their workshop time independently: select an existing piece, reread it, identify places to add information, add labels, and move to another piece if time remained. This helped make the process of revising something students could begin to manage for themselves.
column14: Are there opportunities for students to reflect on which revision strategy helped make their writing clearer for their audience?
column16: In what ways are students creating products or performances for authentic audiences?
column18: At the end of writing time, students shared what they added with a partner. Today, we focused on adding more details to our illustrations. At this point in the year, we are just trying to develop our writing stamina and independence, so these strategies support that. In the future,  we will continue to look at writing samples and offer feedback about what could be added to improve them.

column7:
At the time of observation, the 1D students were beginning a 15-minute Quiet Time. The Homeroom Teacher set a timer and played soft music in the background while students worked independently to set up their Unit of Inquiry notebooks. Kyle distributed the notebooks, and students were expected to write their names and paste or tape in a cover sheet entitled My First Day of Grade 1. During this time, the Homeroom Teacher worked one-on-one with a student at the carpet while Kyle took responsibility for supporting the rest of the class. 

There was clear coordination between the Homeroom Teacher and Kyle in how the learning experience was structured. Kyle moved throughout the classroom, checking in with individual students while providing more targeted support to two or three students with developing English proficiency. With one student in particular, he combined simple, accessible language with total physical response to clarify the steps of the task. This enabled the student to understand what was expected and successfully complete the notebook setup. Kyle simultaneously continued to monitor the wider class, including supporting another student who appeared unsure of what to do after completing the initial task.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You responded intentionally to students differing linguistic needs while maintaining the same learning expectation for the class. Your use of simple vocabulary, total physical response, and individual check-ins gave students additional ways to understand what was expected. In particular, your scaffolding enabled one multilingual learner to understand the steps and successfully complete the task independently.
column12: How are adults modeling respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior?
column13: You provided support without taking ownership of the task away from students. As you circulated, students were largely responsible for organizing their materials, completing the notebook setup, and moving through the task themselves. With the student who needed additional language support, you scaffolded his understanding while still leaving the actual work in her hands.
column14: How is regular co-planning with homeroom teachers helping you anticipate the linguistic demands of upcoming learning experiences and intentionally build in support such as visuals, simplified language, modeling, from the outset?
column16: How might we ensure students are given voice and choice in the curriculum to reflect their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences?
column18:
Hi DJ,
Thanks for popping into 1D yesterday afternoon. I really like the 15 minutes of quiet time that Cat has implemented to get her students ready for the afternoon and it doubles a a means of catching some students up or completing tasks to get ready for the afternoon, ie. we used the UoI notebooks for the first time in the next class.
Co-planning thus far in grade 1 is going quite well, though it was interrupted by the WIDA testing during the previous week, we were still all able to plan for this week and have clear goals for the students in the class (not just EAL roster). The team is hard working, so we are now planning ways to be very intentional in our co-teaching and ensuring we cover all aspects of the model. It will take some time for them to adjust; however, so far they are very receptive to my ideas and how I want to ensure we are helping all students in the class access the curriculum. There are over 30 students on the EAL roster, so given the class sizes, this means close to half, but on top of this, most are multilingual learners, so I am prioritizing what helps (EAL roster) learners, will help all learners access the learning and be successful. 
Again, the team is doing well with adjusting to my style of doing things and I look forward to how I can strengthen this team and how we can work together to ensure success for all grade one students throughout the year!

column7:
Twenty-one students were present.
Students rotated through five stations during the lesson. A countdown timer was displayed on the board to indicate the time remaining at each station.

Entered the class at 14:25. Grade 6 students are seated and listening to Duncan introducing details of the new unit, which is designing a free-standing dwelling for a fictional character in one of three distinctly different biomes - arctic, rainforest, or desert. The positives are noted and appreciated - there is genuine excitement about the unit and it is perfect for this grade level, incorporating complexity, agency some clear learning and much learning by stealth where they learn through engagement and doing and dont even realise it. Your wondering is one I am exploring further with the Grade 6 design team. What scope is there for them to embellish their designs once they have met the formal requirements? This lesson built on the previous lessons, where we investigated wave properties, what produces waves, and some calculations. I like to start the lesson by giving the students a chance to recap the previous lesson, if possible. This allows them to recall some details about our topic as well as helps me identify any students who may have missed the previous lesson.

I like the suggestion about having students bring in their own pictures related to the phenomenon. This will build on an earlier assignment where we had them share summer pictures of themselves doing science. This may encourage them to look more deeply into the concept and possibly notice it in situations where they otherwise might not.

Something I am still struggling with with this grade is differentiation. Some days, I have a better plan to help students who grasp the concepts quickly by providing an extension. However, in a lesson like this one, some students struggled to complete a few of the stations, particularly my data analysis activity. I have been working with the LIT team and the EAL team to get ideas and strategies to ensure that all students are able to access and learn the material.

To your question, I like the idea of extending the use of family data beyond blood groups. Students could select a number of inherited traits and collect phenotype data from family members, then use these data to generate their own questions or hypotheses about possible patterns of inheritance.
Despite the early hour, I felt that the students were, for the most part, engaged with the content and responded well to the Genetics Detectives activity. I had not asked students in advance to find out their family blood groups, so there was inevitably some uncertainty in the information they were able to provide. On reflection, asking students to bring this information to the lesson could have allowed the activity to be more structured and student-led.
For example, after modelling one or two examples as a class, students could have worked through the remaining genetic problems themselves. If the family blood-group information had been collected digitally beforehand, I could also have used it to prepare a table of anonymized examples for students to analyse independently.
In general, I felt there were points during the lesson where I spent a little too much time presenting information. Although working through the problems together as a class was effective, with some additional front-loading and guidance I could have reduced the teacher-directed component and given students more time to practise applying the concepts themselves.

Students were seated on the carpet as Maria introduced a problem focused on determining how many students were in the classroom. Students were asked to use a counting mat to represent the number of students present. One student chose dinosaurs as counters. When the student lost track of which classmates had already been counted, Maria invited other students to share ideas that might help. A student suggested using popsicle sticks to keep track. Maria asked the student to get the sticks and work with the classmate. As student names were called and popsicle sticks were pulled, the other student added dinosaurs to the counting mat.

After four student names had been called, the student put the dinosaurs away. Maria asked whether the student no longer wanted to use the counting mat, and the activity shifted to counting the popsicle sticks that had been lined up on the carpet. Students then included their teachers in the count and noted that there were no popsicle sticks representing the teachers.

Maria asked students to return to their seats and noted that one student had another idea for representing the class. She invited the student to share, and he pointed to the water bottles. Maria identified his idea of using the water bottles as another way to represent the students in the classroom. She then displayed a visual on the screen showing five-frames that students could use to represent the number of students in the class. A second question on the board asked, What do you notice about the different ways that we showed how many of us are here?

Students were asked to work in pairs. Different groups selected different materials to represent the class. One group used water bottles, another used popsicle sticks, and another used name tags. Many of the materials students selected did not fit within the five-frames. Maria checked in with the group using water bottles and asked whether they could use other tools to show their thinking. While one student continued lining up the water bottles, his partner selected smaller counters to use with the representation. Maria asked the students whether they knew which classmates the counters represented and how they would keep track so that a student would not be forgotten.

Students returned to the classroom from recess and gathered on the carpet at the front of the room. Kenya reminded the class that the previous day they had talked about ways people are alike and things they have in common. She asked students to think about how they can make friends. Students shared ideas, including being kind to friends. Kenya then asked students to think about what they already knew about their friends, such as things their friends like or information about their siblings and families. When Kenya asked one student what he knew about his friend, he shared that his friend did not have any siblings.

Kenya returned to the question of what makes a good friend, and students shared ideas including playing together, helping, and being kind. She then asked what students could do to learn more about their friends. When one student shared that he could make Lego by himself, Kenya asked whether he knew if his friends could make Lego and followed by asking what someone could do if they wanted to know something about a friend. One student suggested teaching a friend, and another shared that they could ask questions.

Kenya displayed a Venn diagram on the screen and explained that she and Ms. Helen would model how to complete the Getting to Know My Classmate diagram. She explained that Ms. Helen would record things she liked on one side and Kenya would record her own responses on the other. Kenya and Helen took turns asking one another questions and recording their answers. When they identified something they had in common, they recorded it in the center of the diagram. During the modeling, Kenya asked students what letter the word brother begins with, and students responded, B.

Kenya continued modeling how to ask questions of Ms. Helen. When they discovered another similarity, Kenya asked students where the information should be recorded, and many students responded that it belonged in the middle of the diagram. Kenya then reviewed the information she had learned about Ms. Helen through their conversation.

Kenya explained that it was now the students turn and that they would get to know someone other than the person they usually played with. She showed students partner cards that would be used to identify a random partner. Students stood, and Kenya distributed a card to each student. As students found their partners, Helen gave each pair a paper containing the Venn diagram. Kenya then asked students to sit with their partners on the carpet.

Thank you for your feedback. This exercise was specifically meant to help students do a description of a picture. 
But the task had 3 purposes : 
1  give students the opportunity to practice how to describe a picture, using targeted structures and vocabulary for that purpose. (Describing a picture is an exercise used for Criterion C of MYP)
2  give students the opportunity to practice the vocabulary of the unit (The unit is about celebrations  in this case the celebration of a birthday).
3  give students the opportunity practice using the language with accuracy - for example sentence structures and look at what they need to work on more specifically (for example : agreement of adjectives with nouns (masculine / feminine / plural forms)).
This exercise is important as students will use this task and re-use these sentence structures for their writing (writing on the unit about celebrations).
So students will hopefully be able to transfer the skills learned further in this unit, but also in the next units.
This exercise was also important to me to see what students are able to do and how they would handle the exercise. (Some students only talked about the people, for example, and not the situation. This gives me the opportunity to redirect).
I am actually wondering about the little abbreviations I give the students: is it too detailed ? Students say it helps them but I often think that this is helping them too much and might take away some of their critical thinking skills. (Although the feedback that I had in previous years, showed that students found it helpful).
Again, thank you for the feedback! If you have any questions, let me know!

Kylie discussed the response with the student and asked whether she knew what additional information she could share. Similar interactions occurred with several students as they submitted an initial response, received feedback from the app, and then checked in with Kylie about their next steps. When asked about the experience, one student shared that they liked using the app because they could learn a lot from it. When students reported that they had not gotten everything correct, Kylie told them that it was OK to not be perfect. When another student shared that she had received a strong response, Kylie celebrated with her. When a student needed help interpreting the feedback he had received, Kylie directed him to a classmate who could help him understand what to do next.
column9: How are adults modeling respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior?
column10: Through this activity, you positioned students as the primary users of technology rather than having technology used primarily by the teacher. Students independently accessed Snorkl, recorded their mathematical thinking, received feedback, and made decisions about how to respond to that feedback. This aligns closely with AISG's Transformative Learning Framework, specifically in the personalization and agency facets with its emphasis on students owning their learning and using digital technologies in empowering ways.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13: The Cool Down created a cycle of respond ? receive feedback ? reflect ? revise or seek support. You reinforced this process by asking students what they understood from the feedback rather than immediately interpreting it for them. This connects strongly with UDL's emphasis on offering action-oriented feedback and enhancing learners' capacity for monitoring their own progress.
column14: You directed one student to a classmate who could help him interpret his feedback. What might happen if students regularly had opportunities to discuss their feedback and mathematical reasoning with a peer before seeking teacher support?
column16: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column18:
Thank you for coming to observe my lesson and sharing your feedback and observations of the lesson. I really appreciated how you noticed the different things happening in the lesson, particularly around student agency and personalization.

Agency is something I really value in my classroom. I want students to feel that they own their learning and understand that it is okay not to get the correct answer straight away. Making mistakes, receiving feedback, and having another go are all important parts of the learning journey.

I really like how Snorkl supports this. As this was only the second time they had used the program, I was really pleased to see that they were already beginning to understand this feedback cycle.

I also like your wondering around collaboration. I think pairing students to share their response and feedback with a partner could be a great first step before coming to the teacher. It could provide another opportunity to talk through their thinking and make sense of the feedback. 

Thank you again for your thoughtful observation and feedback.

column7:
Students were seated in the teaching space on the second level of the new library. Adrienne projected photos of the library and introduced students to auditory cues that would be used during their library time. She played a clip of music and asked students to use their listening ears to identify the instrument they heard. One student guessed that the instrument was a violin. Adrienne told the student that the response was close and invited the class to listen again. Another student identified the instrument as a cello. Adrienne explained that hearing the cello would signal that library time was almost over and that it was time to check out books. She then played a second clip and asked students to identify the instrument. Students identified the piano, and Adrienne explained that the piano music would signal that it was time to line up.

Adrienne then invited students to browse and check out books and told them they could choose to use the slide to travel from the second level to the main floor. All students lined up to use the slide, with Adrienne monitoring students at the top and Lovina monitoring at the bottom. A few students became noisy while waiting for their turns, and Adrienne reminded them to wait quietly. While students browsed, Adrienne checked in with individual students and helped them locate books they were looking for. When it was time to check out, Adrienne played the cello music and reminded students who were still upstairs to go down and check out their books. As students moved through the library, they were animated and excited, and reminders were provided to walk and use quiet voices in the space.

column10: You introduced distinct musical cues for two different library transitions and gave students an opportunity to listen, identify, and learn the meaning of each cue before they were expected to respond to it independently. This aligns with UDL's emphasis on providing multiple ways to perceive information and using multiple media, while also supporting students in developing strategies that allow them to engage in their library space with increasing independence.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13: Students were given space to browse the library, select books, seek individual assistance when needed, and choose how they moved from the second level to the main floor. You also responded individually to students who needed support finding particular books, giving them a sense of support and comfort in the library space.
column14: UDL specifically identifies nurturing joy and play as part of engagement while also emphasizing emotional capacity and awareness of self and others. What other structures do you hope to establish which might allow students to maintain their enthusiasm for features such as the slide while developing an understanding of when and how their movement and voice affect others using the shared library?

column18: Yes! I am thinking we can use Zones of Regulation as a guide to help the children identify their zone before and after sliding. I am hoping to partner with Brittney and use some of the same mindfulness / self-regulation tools so children can practice strategies of calming themselves. Eventually I would love the space under the stairs to be a calm down corner as well. column7:
At the time of observation, Joshua and the 3B students were engaged in Morning Meeting, seated together in a circle on the carpet. On the screen was a collection of student responses beginning with the sentence stem, What matters to me
 

Joshua began with an emotional check-in, asking students to indicate how they were feeling by holding up between one and five fingers. He then invited students to share how they were feeling, why, and something from their weekend. Before beginning, Joshua reminded students that the person holding the ball had the opportunity to speak. Students raised their hands to indicate that they wanted to share, and Joshua passed the ball to individual students. As students spoke, Joshua periodically reinforced the use of past tense and reminded the class of the agreed-upon speaking and listening protocols. Students who made a connection with something being shared could signal this nonverbally using their thumb and pinky finger rather than interrupting the speaker. 

When one student was particularly eager to speak and explained that he wanted to tell Joshua something, Joshua acknowledged him while reinforcing that they could speak together after Morning Meeting. He reminded the class about the power of the ball and explicitly connected the routine to the self-management skills they were developing. 

After approximately five students had shared, Joshua transitioned into the more active portion of Morning Meeting. Students were asked to respond to the question, What do you value? using a musical-chairs-style protocol. Students would move around the room while music played and, when the music stopped, share with the person beside them using the sentence stem, I value
because

column9: How are adults modeling respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior?
column10: You made one of the purposes behind the Morning Meeting routines explicit rather than simply expecting students to follow them. When a student wanted to speak outside the established protocol, you acknowledged his desire to contribute while reinforcing the power of the ball and directly naming self-management as the skill students were developing.
column12: How are strong, trusting relationships cultivated as the foundation for peer learning and conflict resolution?
column13: You created clear structures that helped students practice listening to one another as members of a community. The talking ball protected each students opportunity to speak, while the nonverbal connection signal allowed classmates to show that another persons experience resonated with them without taking over the conversation.

because
 with different partners, how might they also be encouraged to respond to or build on something their partner has said as a way of facilitating deeper community connections?

column18: My next step will be to begin explicitly modeling some of the thinking routines that the Grade 3 team focused on developing last year. The team has been introducing me to the hand signals they used to help students respond to, connect with, and build on one anothers thinking. I would like to intentionally incorporate these into Morning Meeting so students move beyond simply sharing their own ideas and begin engaging more deeply with the ideas of their classmates.

column7:
At the time of observation, the 3C students had just completed their Morning Meeting and were transitioning into their math lesson. Once students were seated and ready, Will directed them to the math paper, Represent and Solve Multiplication Problems, which had already been placed on their tables. Students were asked to independently solve two problems centered on the questions, How many dots do you see? and How do you see them? Will set a two-minute timer, and students immediately began working, suggesting that the routines and expectations for this type of mathematical thinking were well established. 

As students worked, the Educational Assistant prompted one student to explain their thinking, while Will circulated and affirmed the use of labels, diagrams, and operations to represent mathematical ideas. When the class came back together, Will asked one student to share an answer. When the student found it difficult to fully explain their reasoning, Will invited another student to build on the initial response. A third student was then asked to extend the conversation by sharing a different way of seeing the problem. This process was repeated with the second problem, with students contributing different strategies and building on one anothers mathematical thinking while Will scribed and represented their ideas on the whiteboard. 

Before moving on, Will provided an additional minute for any students who wanted to come to the whiteboard to make a connection between the two problems or contribute an idea they had not yet had the opportunity to share. 

The lesson then transitioned to a partner problem-solving task using the vertical whiteboards. Will explained that one student would initially act as the scribe and the other as the thinker, with students regularly exchanging the marker. He emphasized that the student holding the marker needed to listen carefully to their partner and modeled with a student how the class would transition to their assigned partners. 

Before students began, Will reinforced that finding the answer was the easier part; the more challenging work was showing their thinking. Students were encouraged to use numbers, diagrams, labels, and words and were expected to demonstrate their solution using two different representations.
column9: How might we ensure students have opportunities to learn from each other's cultural backgrounds and experiences?
column10: You intentionally structured the discussion so that mathematical understanding was developed collectively rather than through a sequence of disconnected student answers. When one student struggled to fully articulate their reasoning, you invited another student to build on the initial idea, followed by another student contributing a different way of seeing the problem. By recording these contributions on the board, you made the progression of the classs thinking visible. Students were therefore not simply sharing answers with you; they were being positioned to listen to, extend, and learn from the mathematical thinking of their peers.
column12: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
column13: You consistently communicated that mathematics was about making thinking visible rather than simply obtaining the correct answer. Your statement that the answer was the easier part and that showing their thinking was the more challenging work reinforced the value of reasoning and productive struggle. Asking students to represent solutions in two ways - and explicitly legitimizing numbers, diagrams, labels, and words - created space for students to approach the same mathematical idea from different perspectives.
column14: Students already had flexibility in whether they used numbers, diagrams, labels, or words. How might students decide which representations best communicate their particular strategy - and explaining why those representations make their mathematical thinking clearer?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column18:
Thank you for the feedback, DJ! I appreciate you highlighting the collaborative nature of the math discussion. Ive been working on moving away from students simply sharing individual answers and toward having them listen to, build on, and make connections between one anothers thinking. I also want students to see mathematics as something they can communicate and make visible, rather than simply arriving at an answer.

Your wondering about agency gives me an interesting next step. While students have flexibility in how they represent their thinking, I could be more intentional about asking them why a particular representation works well. Questions like, What does this model show more clearly than the equation? could help students move from simply having a choice of representations to intentionally selecting the one that best communicates their mathematical thinking.

column7:
As students entered the classroom, they took seats at tables and sang hello songs along with videos displayed on the screen. Jean then asked students to stand and sing the greetings with different partners. The class followed this with a goodbye song. The goodbye song contained more words, and students appeared less familiar with the lyrics. Helen was in the classroom supporting Jean and the students and sang along with the class.

Following the songs, Jean displayed different visuals on the board and led students in practicing a variety of greetings. Jean greeted individual students and asked each student to respond with the appropriate greeting. During this practice, one student indicated a need to use the restroom with a hand signal. Jean acknowledged the signal with a nod, and the student left the classroom without interrupting the lesson. Jean continued by introducing and practicing paired expressions, including thank you and youre welcome, followed by Im sorry and its okay. Jean prompted individual students to respond orally, and each student attempted the responses when asked.

Jean then showed a short video featuring cartoon characters using the expressions students had practiced. The video presented the language in different situations to demonstrate when the words and phrases might be used. Following the video, Jean distributed cards and asked students to work with partners to match words with the corresponding responses. During the partner activity, students looked at the written words and practiced saying the expressions and responses to one another.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You provided opportunities for students to practice the greetings and responses through songs, teacher modeling, visuals, a video, printed words, movement, and oral practice. This aligns closely with UDL guidance to provide multiple means of representation and to illustrate through multiple media, as well as multiple means of action and expression.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: Students moved from whole-group practice and individual teacher-student exchanges to practicing the language with peers. The partner matching activity required students to communicate with one another rather than only identify matching written language. This supports the Collaboration facet of AISG's Transformative Learning Framework, cultivating teamwork and communication through collaborative learning.
column14: What opportunities might allow students to recognize and use these expressions spontaneously outside the structured language activity, and how might you build opportunities for them to share these experiences once back in the classroom?

column18:
Thank you for your thoughtful feedback. I encourage students to notice and use these expressions during authentic moments throughout the school dayfor example, when greeting classmates, receiving help, sharing materials, accidentally bumping into someone, or saying goodbye. I also greet students at the door every day and intentionally use the greetings we have learned in class, helping them become more comfortable using Chinese in real-life contexts.

I occasionally use a Hot Potato activity for students to share when and where they have used authentic Chinese outside the classroom. This will help students make connections between classroom learning and their everyday experiences.

column7:
When the observation began, students were seated at table groups working individually on worksheets with privacy folders in place. Jenny circulated around the room, checking in with students, answering questions, and providing support as they worked. As students completed the worksheet, they left their seats to hand their papers to Jenny and then put away their privacy folders. The characters for yi and wu were displayed on the board. Students who had finished their worksheets transitioned to the carpet, where Jenny began asking questions about the characters displayed.

Jenny modeled how to write the pinyin with tone marks on the board and then wrote several different characters underneath the pinyin. She reminded students to use their eyes to notice the small details within the characters and asked them to check her work closely. Jenny also discussed the order of the strokes used to form the characters. She then invited a student to the front of the room and wrote a character on his back. The student then wrote a character on Jennys back, and each tried to identify the character the other had written. Jenny explained that students would work with partners and challenge one another by writing characters on each others backs. During the activity, the observer joined one partnership and drew the character for yi on each students back. When asked to identify the character, both students responded, one. Students continued working in pairs, taking turns writing and identifying characters. Jenny circulated among the partnerships, checking in and providing guidance. After several minutes, Jenny used a countdown to gain students attention and gave the next set of instructions while showing students their workbooks.
column9: To what extent are students utilizing authentic research, inquiry, and information literacy strategies?
column10: Asking students to look carefully at the small details within characters, check the modeled work, and notice stroke order provided explicit opportunities to notice patterns and distinguishing features. This connects with the UDL guideline of highlighting and exploring patterns, critical features, big ideas, and relationships as learners build knowledge.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: Writing characters on one anothers backs created another mode for students to practice character recognition beyond paper-and-pencil work. By adding in this quick activity, you also provided an opportunity for students to connect with their peers and have a meaningful movement break before heading back into another individual written task.
column14: What is the intended purpose of having all students use privacy dividers during independent work, and how might their use affect different learners? Could students develop greater awareness and agency by learning to identify when a privacy divider supports their focus and when it creates a barrier to their learning?
column16: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column18:
This is an individual check task, I can not run it one on one, so I use the divider to have all students do it at the same time. I only use the privacy dividers when I want students to work by themselves and not help each other. 
Before using it, I told my students that this is a chance for them to show me and themselves what they have learned. So they do not feel left out, and they want to try their best alone.
But dividers are not good for every student in the same way. For some kids who get distracted easily, dividers help them focus. For other kids who have a hard time with reading, dividers may make them feel nervous because they cannot get help from friends. So in other learning time, I dont use a divider. I design activities where children can work with their classmates so that they can learn with each other. But they are welcome to use a divider if some of them want to work quietly on their own.
As time and routines go on, students will know when they need to work on their own and when they can share.

column7:
As students entered from their classrooms, Delissa invited them to find a seat that would help their learning. Some students chose to sit in the bean bags, and Delissa reminded them to have their bodies ready; this meant sitting up rather than lying down.

Delissa began by showing students flash cards with letters. Students were asked to say the corresponding sound and form each letter by writing it in the air. Delissa reminded students that letter formation matters. As students responded as a group, Delissa asked individual students to respond when she could not hear their voices.

Delissa reminded students of previous work examining what happens when the short vowel a is paired with different letters and drew attention to the difference between the short a and short e sounds. Students were then asked to get their whiteboards and organize them according to the sounds displayed on the board. Delissa used a countdown as students prepared for the task. When she reached zero, she asked students for the Chinese word for zero and thanked them for teaching her the word.

Delissa modeled on her own whiteboard how students should draw the columns. She then said a series of words and asked students to write each word in the appropriate column. After writing their responses, students held up their boards. When one student began drawing on his board, Delissa reminded him that the markers would be used as tools during the lesson. As additional words were presented, each student recorded responses on a whiteboard, with most responses demonstrating accuracy in the task. Delissa transitioned from asking students to hold up their boards to walking around the room and observing their work as they wrote.

Following the whiteboard activity, Delissa asked students to put down their boards and markers. She reminded them that they had worked with structure words the previous week and asked them to recall different ways they could describe a picture. Delissa displayed a visual reminder and asked students which part of their brain they needed to use and which part of their body they might use when describing a picture. Students had difficulty identifying that they could use their eyes to gather information about the picture. Delissa also noted that they would need to use their brains.

Delissa returned to the concept of structure words and asked students to recall and share what they could see. She identified the categories of what, size, color, quantity, shape, where, and movement. Students were asked to show a quiet thumb on their chest when they had an idea they wanted to share. One student shared, the big black one dog catched the yellow ball on the green grass. Delissa responded to the student's thinking and then asked the student to identify which structure words had been used in the description.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You created opportunties for students to encounter letter-sound and language concepts through flash cards, oral responses, air writing, visual models, whiteboards, and a visual reminder for structure words. They also demonstrated their understanding through speaking, physical movement, and writing. These approaches align with UDL's emphasis on supporting multiple ways to perceive information and using multiple tools and media for communication and expression.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13: You consistently connected new learning to concepts and strategies students had encountered previously. By prompting students to recall earlier learning and then apply it in new tasks, you supported students in building on what they already knew rather than thinking in isolation. The use of visual reminders and questions that encouraged students to explain their thinking further supported students in recognizing patterns and making connections across learning experiences.
column14: To what extent was this lesson focused on establishing and reinforcing routines and foundational skills? As those routines become more established, what opportunities might emerge to increase complexity, independence, and productive struggle?
column16: How do learning experiences connect to students long-term goals or sense of purpose?
column18:
In the past week, the group focused on establishing a positive climate for learning. As part of this routine, we identified the parts of our bodies that support learning as we grow as readers and writers. Students were invited to reflect on and engage specific body parts: eyes for seeing words or attending to the mouth, ears for listening, mouths for responding or sharing ideas, hands for touching words, and the brain for thinking and making connections. This routine helps refocus students' attention and serves as an effective self-regulation tool when used consistently. Moving forward, it would be helpful to have a visual reference of this routine displayed in the roomespecially on sleepy Mondays!

The primary goal of the first few weeks is to ensure students have a solid foundation in letter-sound correspondence and letter formation. While some students may find this work easy, anecdotal data and observations suggest that many are struggling to apply these skills (decoding and encoding) across different contexts. Therefore, we emphasize the importance of correct letter formation and accurate pronunciation of sounds (e.g., /m/ rather than muh) when sounding out words. As foundational skills become more secure, we expect to see transfer of learning, evidenced by phonetic spelling that aligns with students growing knowledge.

The structured activity was designed to strengthen speaking and, later, writing skills by encouraging students to expand sentences through careful observation. I will model how to structure sentences so that students practice using correct sentence structure as well.

Looking ahead, we hope to move toward more independent tasks and application in writing.

column18:
