column7:
Children are in different spaces aruond the classroom engaged in a variety of play and exploration.  KR is sat near a table with some children. There is a small basket with envelopes.  Each envelope has the child's name and photo on the front and inside is the name cut into strips.  KR is inviting the students at the table to pick out thier puzzle.  She guides them to find a suitable space and gives instructions on what to do.  
As the children engage KR is observing and asking questions ("How many letters in your name?" Which comes first?" "Do you know some of the letters?") When they finish, she says the name of the letter, pointing to each one and then says the child's name (Go Loulwah!).

column10: This exploration of letters started with the letters most relevant to each child, those of thier own name.  Each puzzle therefore would be different and unique to them.  This not only made the engagement relevant, it was accessible to everyone and opened up more conversation by noticing similairities and differences both within the name and between names.  A simple puzzle opened up a rich dialogue around numbers and counting, revealing both prior knowledge and misconcpetions of each child who engaged.
column12: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column13: In the observation the engagemtn in the puzzle was open and fully a choice.  No-one was called over to comeplete the task, but KR was ready to support those who wanted to engage.  She provided options for extension (choosing another envelope) and questions to prompt thinking, but if they wanted to move to something else, the only direction was to put the pieces back. This meant that those who were ready or intersted could do so and had options to extend thier thinking.  L, who stayed and took a second name  and through the conversation with KR, was able to explore different letters and numbers, thus taking her learning further.
column18:
Thank you for visiting! Reading your reflection where you noticed personalization and agency embedded in our activities was very affirming. Those were some of the outcomes I intended when I set up the name puzzles.
Each child's own name contains the most relevant letters for them and is the most easily accessible entry point for every child. I wanted them to feel connected to their own names, and each other, through a simple, yet powerful invitation. Personalizing each child's puzzle with their photo and name made the engagement immediate and authentic. Over time, I hope everyone will try this activity because it was their name, and their letters.
I also really appreciated your observation about agency. I try very hard to let children choose when and how to engage, and to trust that when they're ready, they'll come. Seeing Loulwah stay for a second name game and then watching her thinking turn towards comparing letters and numbers with me was a reminder that when we step back and offer options, children often take their learning exactly where they need it to go. This activity can become open-ended when we ask questions to extend a child's thinking and really listen to what they are noticing.
Pointing to the letters as we count and showing fingers as a manipulative helps young children who often need a concrete, visual anchor to understand abstract concepts like "more" and "less." 
Thank you again for noticing the depth in what might look like a simple puzzle. I'm glad the intentionality came through.

Hi John, thank you for dropping by and for the observational feedback. To answer your question; how can I help students see that their choices, effort, and response to feedback directly influence their progress; I would:

Add a "What did I do?" prompt to the Exit Ticket. After selecting their level, students write one action they took that helped (e.g., "I focused on my elbow position after the teacher feedback") and one thing they'll try next time (as suggested, thank you for that). Additionally, I would start the next lesson with an anonymous example by sharing a student's reflection from a previous class to show how a specific choice led to improvement, normalizing the idea that progress comes from intentional effort. Or I could show them their own exit ticket from the previous class and have them set a small goal to improve in the lesson. This would allow me to end each lesson with a "Choice and Consequence" sentence; students write: "I chose to ............ today, and that helped me .........."
This helps students see that improvement isn't accidental; it's a direct result of their own actions and how they respond to guidance.

11 students were seated in four groups, with two or three students in each group. Amy began by explaining the upcoming speaking and writing assessments.

The class then moved into a Jeopardy review activity. The categories included Subject-Verb Agreement, Relative Clauses, Present Perfect, Past Perfect and Passive Voice. Questions were organised from 100 to 500 points.

Amy distributed a small whiteboard to each group. Students discussed the questions within their groups and wrote one answer per team on their whiteboard. Amy asked groups to show their answers and then revealed the correct answer on the screen. Points were awarded to teams with correct answers.

For some questions, Amy paused to review the grammar being tested. For example, relative clauses were reviewed using a slide showing the formula, examples, defining and non-defining clauses, and the use of who, which, that, where and whose.

Students also had a packet of worksheets covering the grammar being reviewed. One student at the front-left table did not join the Jeopardy activity during the observation and continued working independently on the worksheet packet.

The review packet students had, and were working on when you entered the classroom, also included additional practice for each of the grammar skills. This allowed students to target areas where they needed more support and complete additional practice based on their individual needs. 

As a next step, I could further personalize a review like this by using grammar stations. Each station could focus on a different skill, such as relative clauses, present perfect, past perfect, or passive voice, with different levels or types of practice available. Based on formative assessment results and their own confidence, students could spend more time at the stations that address their individual areas for growth rather than completing the same amount of practice for every skill. Students who are already confident with a particular grammar point could complete a more challenging task or move on to another station.

How might students develop and use their own short set of team norms for communication and conflict resolution, giving them greater responsibility for managing competitive situations independently?
column18:
Moving forward, I plan to preface small-sided games by encouraging teams to hold brief team huddles before matches begin. During these huddles, students will develop a short set of team norms around communication, positivity, and conflict resolution so that everyone is on the same page before competition begins. This could include agreeing on the type of language they want to use with one another, what staying positive should look and sound like during challenging moments, how they will respond when disagreements occur, and even developing a team cheer or other way of encouraging one another. By allowing students to create these expectations themselves, I hope to give them greater ownership and responsibility for managing competitive situations without immediately relying on the teacher to resolve every issue.
I would also like to extend the discussion of conflict beyond disagreements with opponents or teammates. Students can also experience internal conflict when they become frustrated with themselves, make repeated mistakes, or begin to lose confidence during competition. As a class, we can identify some of these situations and discuss strategies students can use to regulate their emotions, reset mentally, and persevere. I would also help students recognize that these types of internal challenges are not limited to sports such as volleyball but can occur in many aspects of everyday life.

At the time of observation, Jake was engaged with the 3A students in a reading activity using a text that appeared to have been introduced the previous day. Jake read the text aloud, pausing regularly for students to chorally supply the next word before he continued reading. This routine was repeated throughout the text, requiring students to listen carefully, follow along, and clearly articulate the missing words as Jake modelled fluent reading and pronunciation. 

After completing the text, Jake drew students attention to the words they had supplied, explaining that these were words they could use in their everyday communication as well as across different subject areas. 

Students then transitioned into a partner-reading activity using the same text. Partners alternated reading after each sentence, with five minutes provided for the activity. During this time, Jake, the Educational Assistant, and the Homeroom Teacher circulated among the pairs, monitoring students reading and providing support where needed.

Students were seated at the carpet as Mitch introduced the focus of the lesson: Developing research questions that move beyond finding individual facts. He asked students to read the learning objective, We can form questions to help us find information beyond just facts. Mitch shared an anecdote about communicating facts about golf and then presented two different statements for students to compare. Students discussed the statements with a partner through a turn and talk. Following the discussion, Mitch commented on students use of turn and talk so far this year, specifically noting that students were adding on to one anothers thinking. He invited Ms. Ashley to contribute to the observation, and she shared that she had also seen students engaging in conversations with one another.

Mitch asked students to indicate which of the two statements they thought was better by using sign language to select A or B. He then invited students to explain the reasoning behind their selections. The discussion transitioned to the characteristics of closed questions. Mitch explained that closed questions generally focus on one small fact and can often be answered quickly, and he provided additional examples. He asked students to identify the opposite of a closed question before introducing the characteristics and examples of open questions. He discussed with students how open questions provide different possibilities for thinking.

Mitch then displayed a series of questions and asked students to determine whether each was open or closed. He introduced sign language for O and C so students could communicate their responses. As each question was read, students displayed their answers while Mitch scanned the group to view individual responses. After completing the questions, students returned to their talk partners to discuss the first question. Mitch checked in with several groups while Ashley and Jojo each talked with a group. Mitch then brought students back together and asked what they noticed about the question displayed on the board.

As the whole-class conversation continued, Ashley created an Open and Closed T-chart on the board. Mitch revisited previously discussed characteristics of open and closed questions and facilitated further discussion about the nature of the questions. Ashley pointed out that one question began with how but functioned as a closed question. She added who, what, when, how, and why to the T-chart as the class continued examining how questions are constructed.
column10: By using sign language as a response strategy , you provided an efficient and inclusive way for all students to share their thinking simultaneously. This allowed you to quickly scan the group, identify students who might be experiencing difficulty or holding different understandings, and gather timely formative feedback to inform instruction. The strategy also aligns with UDL principles by varying and honoring methods for student response and expression.

I was pleased that these materials and the collaborative tasks encouraged students to think actively as both writers and examiners.

For the article, students spent ten minutes annotating the text before comparing their ideas with the official examiner notes. For the comic, I removed this scaffold and asked students to create examiner notes as if they were IB paper setters. This encouraged them to apply their understanding independently and prepared them for their upcoming Paper 1 assessment (which, will be using two comics of which the students select one--although the students are unaware of the fact that these will be the text type used).

I've already worked to revise the essay-reconstruction activity. Cutting the essay into sentence strips created too many possible combinations, which overwhelmed several students. Next time, I would label each strip with a code such as A1, A2, B1, and B2 (with the letter identifying the paragraph, but the letters [and numbers] not arranged sequentially). Haley then transitioned the lesson to multiplication expressions. After introducing the meaning of the word expression, she explained that each student would receive a card containing a drawing, diagram, or situation. Students were tasked with matching their card to one of the multiplication expressions posted around the room and being prepared to explain their reasoning. 

Students were eager to begin, and Haley reinforced the classroom expectations before releasing them to the task. At her signal, students moved to the vertical whiteboards displaying the expressions that matched their cards and began discussing why their representations belonged with that expression. 

Haley then gave each group one marker and challenged them to show different ways of representing the same expression beyond the model provided on their cards. Students were given three minutes and engaged in purposeful mathematical dialogue as they generated representations, with one student in each group recording the groups thinking. Haley and the Educational Assistant circulated between groups, prompting students to explain their ideas and identify the representations they were creating, including tally marks, word problems, and bar models. 

After three minutes, students returned to the carpet and shared the different models their groups had generated. Haley invited the class to respond positively after classmates shared their mathematical thinking.
column9: How might we ensure students have opportunities to learn from each other's cultural backgrounds and experiences?
column10: You designed the whiteboard task so that students had to move beyond simply finding the correct expression and build mathematical understanding together. Giving each group one marker encouraged discussion before ideas were recorded, and students contributed different representations of the same expression while one student scribed the groups collective thinking. The strongest evidence of collaboration was that students were not merely working beside one another; one students representation could become part of the groups shared set of models, allowing students to learn with and from their peers.
column12: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
column13: You extended the task beyond matching cards to expressions by asking students to generate additional ways to model the same mathematical idea. Students responded by creating representations such as tally marks, word problems, and bar models rather than reproducing only the model they had been given.
column14: Students had considerable ownership of the mathematical conversation once they reached the whiteboards. Are there opportunities to extend that ownership by asking students, after seeing several possible models, to individually select the representation they believe communicates the multiplication expression most effectively and explain why?
column16: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column18:
Thank you so much for coming in and for the thoughtful feedback. It has been so great to see this group of students collaborate and share their mathematical thinking with one another. They are still getting used to sharing their ideas in larger groups, but Im finding that the Building Thinking Classrooms protocols are really helping them make that transition. The small-group structures give them more confidence to develop and explain their thinking before bringing it to the whole group.

I also really appreciated your wondering about agency and having students think about which representation communicates an expression most effectively. We actually built on this in the following lesson. After working through a few expressions in small-group math talks, we started noticing and discussing how different representations can be more useful for different expressions. For example, expressions with larger factors and sums can be much easier to represent with a bar model than by drawing equal groups.

This has been an interesting part of the unit because students are often excited to show that they know how to do multiplication. These tasks are helping them move beyond just getting an answer and think more about why a strategy works, how representations connect, and which representation might be most helpful for a particular expression.

Thanks again for coming in and sharing your feedback!

column7:
At the time of observation, the 3A students had just returned from morning recess. Steph took time to ensure students were regulated and ready for learning, reinforcing expectations before transitioning into mathematics. 

Steph began a Math Talk connected to the Illustrative Mathematics lesson, Lets Represent Equal Groups. Using a Notice and Wonder routine, she displayed an image of six pairs of socks and invited students to look at it through their math minds. Three students shared observations, including noticing that there were six groups of two and identifying a connection to even numbers. When Steph shifted the conversation to wonderings, one student shared curiosity about how many socks there were altogether, followed by three additional students contributing their own questions. 

Steph then displayed a picture graph and again invited students to notice and wonder about the mathematical information represented. Throughout the discussion, she frequently paraphrased, clarified, and amplified students language, helping make their ideas accessible to the wider class and supporting students in connecting mathematical vocabulary to the thinking being shared. Students then engaged in a turn-and-talk about the graph before returning to a whole-class discussion to share their ideas. 

Steph transitioned students into the next task by explaining that they would each receive a set of cards containing different diagrams, pictures, and words. Students would first cut out and independently sort and match their cards based on the mathematical relationships they noticed. They would then work with a partner to compare their matches and check their thinking.

Particularly effective was the way you paraphrased and amplified students responses rather than simply replacing their words with your own. This helped preserve student thinking while making mathematical ideas and vocabulary more accessible to the wider group.

column18:
Thank you for your notes on the observation last week.
I feel that I have become more comfortable with teaching Illustrative Math and adapting lessons before they begin and also in the moment to fit my students needs. The warm up is a great time to get students bodies and minds focused for math. I like the opportunities for sharing, for voices to be heard and to hear how students are working through different problems placed in front of them. I also like to use the randomiser so that all students could be asked to share, therefore everyone needs to have thought through what their answer would be.
During the lesson, I adapted the part where students were sorting cards and then discussing their answers with each other. Originally this was designed for students to work alongside a partner. My reason for adapting this was I wanted to see if their knowledge from earlier in the week had transferred over and this task enabled me to see if they could make connections. I ensured there was still had a partner element to the lesson to see if they could explain their thinking and work through any differences they might have had. What I found was that all students were able to complete this task with little difficulty. 
I have been adding in opportunities to use the vertical whiteboards and Building Thinking Classrooms so that students are working collaboratively to solve problems together. I find this requires more collaboration from students, as they discuss and solve problems together. I also notice that the trust and understanding of our classmates builds through these opportunities as they learn to support and work alongside people with differing strengths.

column7:
At the time of observation, Charles welcomed the PK4B Owls into the gym. Students sat along the sideline while he clearly outlined the opening sequence: two laps around the half-gym, followed by meeting together in the corner. Once gathered, Charles took a moment to settle and regulate the group before revisiting learning from the previous lesson. He reminded students that they had been making shapes with their bodies and invited them to recall examples. Individual students contributed ideas including a star, egg, and pencil. 

Charles then previewed the learning for the lesson, explaining that students would practise creating these shapes again, but with a variation in how they would make them. He also clearly explained the sequence leading up to this task: stretching, playing the warm-up game Apples and Bananas, and then returning to body shapes. 

Students independently removed their shoes and socks and moved to individual mats arranged in a circle on the main gymnastics mat. Charles led approximately three minutes of stretching before bringing students into a close circle. He reviewed the expectations and rules for Apples and Bananas, after which students participated enthusiastically. 

Throughout the observation, the clarity of routines, transitions, and expectations was particularly noticeable. These very young learners appeared to understand where to go, what to do, and what would happen next, allowing the lesson to move calmly and efficiently from one experience to another.
column9: Do students have access to strategies for self-care and emotional well-being?
column10: You created a highly predictable learning environment for these young learners through clear routines, explicit expectations, and a carefully sequenced lesson. Taking time to regulate the students before discussing previous learning, previewing what would happen next, and consistently gathering students into defined spaces reduced uncertainty and helped them successfully manage several transitions. Their ability to move from the sideline, to running, to the corner, to removing shoes and socks, and then to their individual mats suggests that these routines are well established. For PK4 students in particular, this kind of structure supports both self-regulation and readiness to participate.
column12: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column13: You connected the lesson back to students' previous experience of representing ideas physically by making shapes with their bodies. Inviting students to recall shapes such as a star, egg, and pencil activated their prior thinking and prepared them to return to the idea in a new way. Your preview that they would make these shapes again with a variation creates the potential for students to explore how their bodies can represent the same idea in different ways, which is an age-appropriate pathway into creative expression and movement.
column14: I acknowledge not seeing this portion of the lesson, but I wonder how you might build a small amount of student decision-making into body-shapes while maintaining the strong routines and structure you have established?
column16: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column18:
Hello DJ,

Thank you for taking the time to observe my PE lesson. I always appreciate your feedback and the positive presence you bring to the gym.

Im glad you recognized the smoothness of routines. We have spent lots of time practicing and reviewing them, which gives me more lesson time to focus on subject matter rather than management. Each lesson builds from the last so they can develop new skills, find more challenges, and more have more opportunities for independence.

To answer your wondering about student agency, this is something I actively build into our gymnastics unitespecially once students have established a strong foundation of skills and terminology. Later in the lesson you observed, I set up learning stations where children could freely choose which skills to practice. I offered a balancing area, a rolling area, and a jumping area. Each area had clear parameters, but flexibility within for student choice. This structure allows them to work on what they enjoy most, what they feel they need to improve, or what they feel most confident in.
Thank you again for your time and insights. I look forward to seeing you in the gym more often.

Charles

At the time of observation, the 3D students were seated in the corner of the gym as Joe introduced the expectations and learning targets for the PE lesson. He invited one student to lead the class through the stretching routine while he modelled alongside her. Most students followed the routine independently. When one student became disruptive and dysregulated at the back of the group, Joe calmly changed the students position, bringing him beside himself so that he could remain connected to the lesson. 

After approximately four minutes, Joe used the whistle to bring students to the centre of the gym mat. He then introduced and modelled the three activity stations: walking across the balance beam using specified movements, practising somersaults, and completing a jump and turn from an elevated mat. Joe demonstrated each activity, highlighted important safety expectations, and provided students with an opportunity to ask questions before dividing them into three groups. 

Once the rotations began, students moved into their activities while the Educational Assistant supported primarily at the balance beam and jumping stations. Joe positioned himself at the somersault station, where students required more direct technical instruction and physical support to successfully complete the movement.
column9: Do students have access to strategies for self-care and emotional well-being?
column10: You responded effectively to differing social-emotional and cognitive needs throughout the lesson. Moving the dysregulated student closer to you allowed him to remain part of the learning rather than being removed from it, while your decision to provide more intensive support at the somersault station responded directly to where students required the greatest level of technical assistance.
column12: How are adults modeling respectful, autonomy-supportive behavior?
column13: You created an authentic opportunity for a student to take responsibility for part of the learning by having her lead the stretching routine. Rather than being entirely teacher-directed, this placed a student in a visible leadership role while you supported from alongside her.
column14: As students become more confident with the routines at each station, how might they begin to support one another's learning rather than relying primarily on adult feedback? For example, could students occasionally work in pairs as performer and observer, using one simple success criterion to notice and share feedback before switching roles?
column16: How are strong, trusting relationships cultivated as the foundation for peer learning and conflict resolution?
column18: Thank you for the feedback and for taking the time to observe my lesson. I already give students opportunities to support and give feedback to each other quite often, especially in some of the other units where this is easier to menage.  In gymnastics, I tend to be more cautious as it requires students to be more responsible and aware of safety when helping each other. I usually do this once I am confident that they are capable and responsible enough to do it appropriately. I will continue to look for more opportunities to use this approach in gymnastics as well, while making sure that students understand how to support each other safely and that there is no risk of anyone getting hurt.

4C - EAL Co-taught class. Focus: Developing effective talk partners / accountable conversation - 4th September

Jessica explicitly introduces and unpacks the behaviours of an effective talk partner. Students were invited to think about what good talkers and listeners do, with expectations including:

These are also available on the TV screen. (minimal and clear, readable font)
Quiet body
Taking turns talking and listening
Eyes on your partner  described as using kind eyes; showing interest rather than staring
Brain awake  actively thinking about and focusing on what a partner is saying

Jessica spends time unpacking what it might mean to have your brain awake, rather than simply presenting the phrase as an expectation.

Jessica and Narelle model a partner conversation for students. Before beginning, students were given a clear purpose for watching and were asked to notice evidence of the talk-partner behaviours.

The modelled conversation centred on libraries. Jessica used highly expressive body language, facial expression and gesture while speaking, providing additional visual support for meaning. 
Jessica and Narelle demonstrate taking turns, asking questions and building on what the other person had said.

Following the model, Jessica returned to the success criteria and asks students what they had noticed:

Were the speakers moving like robots, or were their bodies mostly still?
How did you know that Ms Yakkas had her brain awake?
What did she say that showed she was listening?

A student shares that Ms Yakkas had made connections to what Jessica had said. Jessica paraphrases and expands on the student response, providing a further example.

Jessica acknowledges that learning how to be a talker and listener takes practice and reinforceds that this was something the class would continue to develop.

Students were then given an opportunity to practise with partners. Jessica, Elaine and Narelle supported the organisation of pairs and a group of three, helping students position themselves so that they were facing one another.

Adults circulate and supporte students during the discussion. Elaine also used translation support with students, including opportunities for students to share in Korean. This appeared to provide an additional access point for participation while they are learning the process.

Jessica continued to monitor the whole class, gave time reminders and used familiar attention signals to bring students back together.

Some partnerships struggle with the two minutes was quite a long time for some students to sustain conversation on the one topic, (even though it was an accessible topic) without interrupting or shifting to dialogue.

Explicit modelling made the learning highly accessible.

The clarity with which you unpacked the behaviours of an effective talk partner, followed by an actual teacher model, gave students a concrete picture of what successful partner talk could look and sound like. Asking students to observe the model with a specific job and then identify evidence of listening and connection shifted the expectations from something they were simply told to do into something they could see, notice and begin to understand.

Students are moving towards applying understanding of volume through independent practice. Previous to this that have been working collaboratively on vertical whiteboards around the room, solving volume problems and giving and receiving feedback to each other. 

The transition from the whiteboard work into independent practice is calm and respectful. Students help clean and tidy the spaces and appeared comfortable taking responsibility for their classroom environment.

Laurie gave clear instructions for the independent task. 
Students are sharing question cards but completing the work independently. 
Laurie reminds students that if they received the same question they had just completed in the collaboration, they should exchange it for a different one.

The lesson title and task question are displayed clearly on the TV.

Students work independently in their workbooks while Laurie and Ashley (EAL) circulated and support students. 
Ashleys role within the lesson appeared integrated into the learning, with both adults available to respond to students as they worked. Ashley connecting with Noah. 

The steps for calculating volume, including the formula, are visible on the TV as a step by step check list for students to refer to.

Laurie has observed that some students appear to be moving quickly to just plug the numbers into the formula rather than first making sense of the problem. 
Laurie reminds students that not every question is asking them to calculate volume and explicitly reinforces the need to read the whole question and identify what was actually being asked before beginning the calculation.
 
Observations of student work show that some students are mixing up length, width and height when interpreting the visuals. In one example, the orientation of length and width within the diagram seemed to create some uncertainty for students.

Some students are fast calculators and solving the problem quickly, however their layout / steps are not as clear or explict as will be needed as the maths gets more complex. Eg:

2 × 3 × 4
12 × 2

Rather than
2 x 3 x 4
2 x 12

As the end of the lesson concludes. Laurie calls for end of the lesson and leaves to go to supervision and leaves Cherrie to support students in their transition for recess, which is managed quickly, calmly and respecfully.

5A  Writing Lesson
Students are continuing a writing task from the previous day, following earlier learning around subjectverb agreement.
Instructions are displayed clearly on the TV screen, with the main message:
Your main job is to write


Students continue from where they finished yesterday.
A yellow dot is used as a visual marker to show the point in their writing from which they are now expected to apply the learning about subjectverb agreement.

Ms. Ashley has given further guidance and examples on whiteboard tables for each table group.

Students are working in a range of formats. Some are writing extended pieces, others are drawing or developing comics. Some students have a strong creative flow of ideas.

There is also a lot of erasing, correcting and rewriting happening, suggesting that students are actively reviewing and changing their work as they write.

Taralyn conferences with individual students.

Ashley works alongside Richie, initially supporting with redirection and then helping him identify a next step.

Some students, including Louis and Jeffery, remain primarily focused on drawing rather than writing. At this stage there is little evidence of transfer of the subjectverb agreement learning into their work.

Taralyn revisits an example around the word family, explaining that it can be treated as a single unit and prompting students to think about what this means for subjectverb agreement.

Ashley supports Shirley with capital letters while also helping her access the reflection task.

Taralyn brings students together with FA cue and asks students to bring their writing to the carpet.

Ashley reinforces expectations around chairs and give positively prompts.
The class moves into a writer reflection.

Students are asked to choose one sentence from their own writing and identify:

What is the subject?
What is the verb?
Do the subject and verb agree?

Initially students are asked to raise their hand when they have completed this. Taralyn adjusts the instruction and asks students to first raise their hand when they have selected a sentence.

Taralyn and Ashley prompt and support students who do not yet have their hands raised.

Students are then asked to identify the subject and verb in their chosen sentence and decide whether they agree.

Students turn and share with a partner, with the prompt to explain how they know the subject and verb agree.

During student conversations, there appears to be some uncertainty around the underlying grammar.

Two students sharing with me were unable to identify what the subject of their sentence was. There was some understanding that a verb represented the doing, but identifying the verb became more difficult when tense or more complex verb structures were involved.

Taralyn shares an example from Javen to discuss with the class 
Mr Brown started to explain


Students could identify Mr Brown as the subject, but there was some confusion around identifying the verb because of the structure started to explain.

The grammatical explanation is more complex than some students are able to explain and some students became less confident in the discussion and appear unsure how to connect the terminology back to their own writing.

Taralyn uses a temperature check using thumbs up / sideways / down to gather student feedback on their level of understanding.

There are also references to previous lesson on run-on sentences and simple / complex sentence structures.
 
The lesson concludes with clear instructions for transition.

I wonder what your next step might be so that more students can access the grammar concept and transfer to their writing independently?

column18:
It was valuable to have an extra pair of eyes in the classroom. I appreciate learning which students were not yet transferring the grammar learning into their writing. During our next writing session, I will meet with these students first to clarify their understanding and help them apply the learning.

My intention was to address a common error in students writing: when writing longer sentences, they sometimes shift between verb tenses or use verb forms that do not agree. However, I recognize that it is still the beginning of the year and that students need a strong foundation before working with more complex structures. This was an important reminder.

As an immediate next step, I revisited past-tense verbs and infinitives during our morning meetings yesterday and today. We practiced structures such as started to plan and decided to run, supported by example sentences and verb lists on the screen.

I also created a reference poster that includes subjectverb agreement, infinitives, and different sentence structures for students to use at their tables. Another next step is to revisit a color-coded lesson on simple, compound, and complex sentences, beginning with clear, familiar structures before gradually introducing more complex examples. This will hopefully help students understand the grammar and transfer it more independently to their own writing.

We do talk about formative and summative assessment in Design because it is built into how we work. Students normally submit their portfolio work for a specific criterion as a formative first. I give them feedback, they make changes based on that feedback and then they submit the improved version as their summative, which is the one that is graded. Students returned from a special class and gathered on the carpet at the front of the room. Tammy shared an illustration from a book and led students through a series of questions about specific details they observed. As she turned the page, Tammy pointed out that one of the characters was looking through binoculars. A student commented that the character could see what was happening from far away. Before reaching the end of the story, Tammy asked students to predict what might happen. When one student suggested that the characters might get lost, Tammy asked whether that might be something that would happen at the end of the story and noted that this would make it a sad story. She then asked students to recall which character appeared at the beginning and consider whether that character might return at the end.

Tammy transitioned from the read-aloud to the writing task by explaining that the goal for writing was to draw pictures showing "first" and "next," and she connected this goal to the story students had just examined. She showed another book that modeled a first/next, or first/then, format. Tammy shared several possibilities for what students could draw and told them they could use the book for ideas if they were unsure what to draw. She also provided ideas for students who wanted to create a picture about themselves. Tammy showed a student's journal as an additional example and reminded students about their previous learning related to "true coloring" and "creative coloring." On the board, she modeled two options for organizing the work: drawing a line to divide one page in half or using two separate pages.

Tammy asked students to give a quiet thumbs-up if they understood the task. A couple of students responded with a thumb, after which Tammy checked for understanding with individual students. She reminded the class that students drawing themselves would use true coloring, while a student drawing something such as a unicorn could use creative coloring. Tammy displayed a 12-minute timer on the board. Students collected their journals, moved to the tables, and began drawing. During work time, Jasmine checked in with different students. Tammy circulated among students and asked them to explain their "first" and "next" ideas.

Thank you for coming and spending time with us  it was great to have you observe, and thank you for leaving us with such a thoughtful wondering.

Students have the opportunity to interact with the board throughout the day, not at one fixed time. We do have a morning routine where every student visits the board as they start their day, but beyond that we don't check in at the same time with everyone  sometimes it happens toward the end of the day, and other times it becomes part of the exit ticket.

When we first introduced the board, the students didn't yet know all the feelings on it. As we talked about it and inquired into it more together, we started to see them using a wider range of feelings, each with a reason behind it. We've also noticed friends choosing the same feeling as one another, which we've already used as a chance to talk about how we can feel the same thing while still being different and unique.

Monitoring this is still in its early stages  right now it's mostly the students identifying how they feel, and us following up and starting to look for patterns rather than drawing conclusions yet. We're also building on this through other classroom experiences, like inviting students to make different feelings with their faces and name them, which has now led into them inquiring into what actually makes them feel that way.

Through our planned experiences, we're hoping to see them answer with more depth over time and be able to reflect on real-life situations where they felt that way or used a strategy to manage it. I also listen in on conversations during play and observe how they handle conflict when it comes up, which helps me see whether they're actually applying what they're learning rather than just being exposed to it. Over time, this is what we're hoping will let them start noticing their own patterns and use that awareness to manage their emotions and reactions before they escalate.

Thank you again for the question  it's given us a good starting point for thinking about next steps in ho

Thank you for dropping in and for your thoughtful wondering and feedback. I also agree that there is potential to design more learning experiences like this. I found that the typing option in Seesaw gave students another way to demonstrate and communicate their understanding, and it also helped us better support different learning needs.
At the same time, I think its important to keep the personal and collaborative part of learning at the heart of these activities. Before getting on the iPads, students could first work with a partner or in a small group to read and discuss the questions, make sure they understand what is being asked, and talk about how they might respond. Then they could use the iPad to record or communicate their own understanding.
I think this balance is important when using technology as another tool to support students in expressing their learning, while still keeping the learning purpose, peer interaction, and teacherstudent connection at the centre.

Grade 5  Chinese B
Students are arriving at different times due to the transition from swimming. Three students from 4D arrive first and quietly begin the writing task that is already prepared for them.

As other students arrive, Lotus meets them outside the classroom and gives clear instructions for managing swimming bags and preparing for the lesson.

Collect your writing packet.
Get a pencil and sit ready to begin.

There is a brief conversation with Joshua as he arrives and Joshua leaves the classroom.
Once students are settled, Lotus explains that the task should not be rushed.

Do not do this super fast  take it slow to complete.

A timer is set for seven minutes.

There is no extended warm-up or further explanation at this point, however students appear to know the routine and understand what is expected. They settle quickly and begin working independently.

The task focuses on Chinese character formation. Students are practising the characters with increasing complexity, including tracing and forming the strokes accurately.

Lotus circulates, observes and prompts where needed. She gives specific praise around character formation and handwriting.

A time check is provided before the timer finishes.

When you hear the bell, put your writing packet in the box, head back to your seat and I will explain the next steps.

Joshua returns to the classroom during this time and independently joins the task without needing further direction.

When the bell rings, students transition quietly and efficiently.

Lotus asks students to move to the carpet.

She introduces the next part of the lesson:

Today we will be working on another story.

Students are invited to review the previous learning and recall the story of **Change / the Moon Lady**, connected to the Lantern Festival.

The new task is to create a small book, with students acting as illustrators for the story.

Lotus has prepared **two versions of the text** to support different language levels.

She explains that students may receive the more accessible version but can also attempt the more challenging version if they wish.

If you get the easier version and you would like the harder version, dont get upset  you can do both.

Students using the advanced version are expected to work more independently.

Lotus gives a clear strategy for approaching the text:

Dont translate the whole sentence. Circle the key words, translate and write below the character, then draw the scene.

She models this using examples from the text.

For example:
Long, long time ago


Lotus also highlights unfamiliar vocabulary and reinforces that students do not need to understand every word immediately.

If you dont know what it means, circle it and I can help you later.

There is some discussion around words that can have different meanings, including vocabulary connected to fire and hot / spicy.

Students working with the advanced version collect their booklets and transition quietly to begin.

The remaining students stay on the carpet.

Lotus reorganises seating, distributes papers and ensures students have the correct version of the text.

I will wait for 10 seconds and we will start.

The group begins reading together using a **read-and-repeat** structure.

Lotus models the Chinese and students repeat, supporting pronunciation, fluency and confidence before they move into the task independently.

The differentiation within the reading task provided access to the same learning for students at different stages of Chinese language development.

Preparing two versions of the story, while still giving students the option to challenge themselves, allowed students to engage with the same content without the different language levels becoming limiting. The strategy of identifying and translating "key words rather than every word" also supported students to focus on meaning and build greater independence as language learners.

column14:

I wonder if there may be an opportunity to make the purpose of the initial character-writing task more explicit for students before they begin, even though they clearly know the routine.

For example, a very brief prompt such as Today, pay particular attention to
 could focus students on one aspect of character formation or connect the practice to the reading and writing they will use later in the lesson.

I also wonder whether, during the read-and-repeat section, there may be opportunities to pause occasionally for students to predict meaning, identify a familiar character or make a connection to the illustration they will eventually create. Students are asked to come closer to the screen and organise themselves into teams for a Kahoot review game.

column7:
- Korean L&L class (grade 9-10 combined)
- Start of observation: 8:35
- Five students (all female)
- Students are preparing for a formative assessment (leading up to a summative assessment) using AssessPrep
- Students were asked to analyse a Korean poem and have to use academic writing (including essay structure as explained in class) to analyse the poem from a literary perspective
- As per the unit outline on Managebac, in this unit, students have to: "explore how poets utilize poetic devices and stylistic choices to convey ideas, emotions, and themes. Through the critical analysis of Korean poetry, students will examine how language, culture, and context shape meaning and influence interpretation, developing an appreciation of poetry as a powerful form of artistic expression and communication"
- On the classroom wall, there is evidence of a previous formative assessment in which the students collaboratively analysed a Korean poem, looking for 'tone', 'repetition', 'connotative meaning', 'symbolism', etc.)
- There is a nice atmosphere in the class. The students are clearly engaged and discussing the assignment back and forth with the teacher.
column9: To what extent are students utilizing authentic research, inquiry, and information literacy strategies?
column10:
Students are developing authentic literary analysis skills through close analysis of Korean poetry. 

Students are expected to identify and interpret poetic techniques such as tone, repetition, symbolism, and connotative meaning, and then communicate their analysis through structured academic writing. 

The previous collaborative analysis provides a useful scaffold toward independent application.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13:
Discussion and collaborative analysis appear to be established parts of the learning process. Evidence from the previous formative task shows students collaboratively analysing poetry, while the observed lesson included active dialogue between students and the teacher. 

This supports students in developing and testing their interpretations before applying them independently.
column14: How might students use their previous collaborative analysis and this formative AssessPrep task to identify one specific aspect of literary analysis or academic writing they want to improve before the summative assessment?
column16: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column18:
My intention with this formative assessment is to gradually move students from scaffolded analysis towards greater independence and agency. The learning process has progressed from **teacher-scaffolded close analysis ? peer collaboration ? individual analysis ? formative analytical writing ? independent summative writing**.

After collectively analysing poems in class, students independently researched a poet we had studied and analysed an additional poem that we had not explored together. They received feedback on this individual analysis before moving into the formative analytical essay. For the formative, students were then given the choice to write about either a poem closely studied with the teacher or their independently analysed poem.

The purpose of this formative is not for students to identify as many poetic devices as possible, but to practise **selecting the most relevant evidence for the guiding question, explaining how the poets choices create meaning and communicate intention, and organising their ideas logically in academic writing**.

Following the formative, students will use their feedback to identify **one specific area they want to improve** before the summativefor example, selecting stronger evidence, developing their analysis beyond identifying techniques, linking their analysis more explicitly to the guiding question, or organising their argument more logically. Over the next three lessons, they will practise with this individual focus in mind.

By the summative assessment, the scaffolding will be removed: students will independently select from the poems studied in the unit and write a formal analytical essay within 80 minutes without access to their previous annotations. My aim is for students to recognise their own strengths and areas for development and take greater ownership of their preparation as they move towards fully independent literary analysis.

column9: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column10: Students were intentionally given time to reflect on previous work and use feedback to improve their writing. Students revisited their formative work to identify areas for improvement, while the teacher provided individual feedback. Students could also explain the cycle of writing, receiving feedback, and acting on that feedback.
column13: Students were expected to actively communicate and justify their thinking rather than simply identify the correct answer. The thumbs-up/down routine gave all students an accessible way to initially respond, while follow-up questions such as Can you explain this a bit more? pushed students to articulate and defend their reasoning.
column14: Curious how students might use their formative feedback to set one specific writing goal for their next essay and monitor their progress toward that goal?
column16: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column18:
Great question, and a valid one at that. Individualized goal setting for student writing would be a great way to have students practically think about their current positioning as writers and identify a pathway they can deliberately and consistently focus on, rather than giving a stock response such as, I want to improve my writing. That kind of goal is vague and not particularly helpful, especially when many of them are still learning what improvement looks like in the context of our course.

For some students, improvement might mean syntax, word choice, spelling, or grammar. For others, it might mean applying what we have studied, using rhetorical devices effectively, or demonstrating a clearer understanding of the purpose behind a hook, providing context, or developing a thesis with a clear what/why structure. It could also mean recognizing vague terminology in their writing and working toward greater specificity. Good point, and something I will use as we continue to scaffold for different learning needs and levels of understanding of the English language. Thanks!

column7:
Bruce returned a formative assessment to students at the beginning of the lesson and reminded them about the summative assessment taking place the following week.

There were 14 students in the class. Students were seated at the front of the room and were working either individually or in pairs.

Students reviewed questions they had answered incorrectly on the formative assessment. They were asked to revisit their responses, identify the correct answer or add additional content to improve their original response. Students used their laptops and other resources to support this process.

The questions being reviewed were connected to the current ESS unit and included environmental systems, positive feedback loops and tipping points, and historical influences on the environmental movement. Student work included examples such as the Amazon rainforest, Rachel Carsons Silent Spring and the 1992 Rio Earth Summit.

Bruce circulated and met with individual students to answer questions about their formative assessment and responses. While Bruce was working with individual students, the rest of the class continued reviewing and revising their own work.

Students were using the Kognity ESS resource alongside their formative assessment. One student was reviewing the section on models and systems while working through their responses.
column9: To what extent is student work authentic and reflective of that done by experts outside of school?
column10: I appreciated the way students were asked to return to their formative assessment and actively improve their original responses rather than simply being given the correct answers. This reflects the kind of work experts do, where an initial response is rarely the end point and ideas are revisited as new information and evidence are considered. Students were using subject-specific resources to check their understanding, identify gaps and strengthen their responses, which made the process of revision an important part of the learning rather than simply correcting mistakes.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13: I liked how the formative review gave students the opportunity to focus directly on their own areas of need. Rather than everyone revisiting the same content, students returned to the questions they had struggled with and worked to improve their individual responses. You were then able to move between students and provide targeted support based on the questions and misconceptions each student had. This meant students were using the same learning time in different ways, based on what they individually needed to work on before the summative assessment.
column14: Bruce, thanks for having me for the end of your class today. I wonder if there are opportunities within ESS for students to take some of this learning beyond the classroom and apply it for a more authentic audience. The issues students are exploring, including environmental systems, sustainability and environmental justice, lend themselves well to work that could have a purpose beyond an assessment. How might students use their growing understanding of these issues to create something that informs, influences or supports an audience beyond their ESS class?
column16: In what ways are students creating products or performances for authentic audiences?
column18:
I have been pleased with the level of engagement and self-management students have shown as they prepare for their first summative assessment in ESS. Students have generally engaged well with class discussions and the subject content, and I have been encouraged by how proactive many have been in asking questions, seeking clarification and checking their understanding. Some students still require redirection to remain focused, but overall the class is developing positive learning habits.

One area I would like to continue developing is the ability of the students to use mark schemes effectively to critically assess and improve on their work. This will require further modelling and practice as they become more familiar with the expectations of ESS assessments.

In response to the Taking Action question, I see considerable opportunity as we move further into the course for students to apply their learning beyond the classroom. ESS lends itself particularly well to connections with CAS initiatives within the school and potentially the wider community. We are also exploring opportunities for ESS fieldwork outside the school, which should allow students to apply their understanding and develop practical skills in authentic contexts.
