column7:
There were 10 students in the class, working in three groups. Students were conducting an experiment connected to random energy distribution between two objects.

Students worked in pairs within their groups. For each trial, students flipped a coin to determine whether each of six numbered energy packets was placed into Object A or Object B. Once all six packets had been distributed, students recorded the resulting macrostate. Students repeated the process 20 times to collect their group data.

Students recorded results as they completed each trial. The shared Excel spreadsheet was then used to bring together data from across the groups. The spreadsheet calculated the percentage and total number of times each macrostate was observed and displayed the combined results as a graph.

Alexis brought students back together after the data had been collected and asked them to consider which macrostate was most likely based on the class results. Students used the combined data to respond to the question.

Alexis then connected the results of the experiment to the next question about how gas particles spread out, asking students to consider what distribution of gas particles would be most likely.
column9: In what ways are digital technologies used to facilitate cross-cultural exchanges and global collaborations in the classroom?
column10: I liked how the shared Excel document allowed students to contribute their group results to a larger class data set and then immediately see what emerged from the combined results. Students could see that their own small sample was only one part of a much bigger picture, and that bringing data together gave them stronger evidence to work from. This was a good use of digital technology to support collaboration and showed students how shared data can be used to build understanding collectively.
column12: In what ways does the learning environment support risk-taking?
column13: It was great how the learning environment gave students space to test an idea and see what happened, rather than working towards a predetermined correct result. The coin-flipping activity made uncertainty and variation an expected part of the learning, with students collecting their own data, comparing it with the larger class set and then making sense of the patterns that emerged. This created a low-stakes opportunity for students to take risks with their thinking, make predictions and adjust their understanding based on the evidence in front of them. It also allowed Jay and Jerry's late entry of data become a connection for the class and a good way to see how the addition of their data when everyone thought it was completed made changes in real time to the bar graph, but in a supportive, low stakes way.
column14: Thank you for inviting me into your class this morning to observe the experiment. I wonder how this kind of practical, inquiry-based learning could be further personalized to respond to the different needs, interests and levels of confidence within the class. Students were working collaboratively towards a shared outcome, but there may be opportunities within this structure for students to make more individual choices about how they engage with the concept, analyse the data or demonstrate their understanding. How might you build greater choice into learning experiences like this so that students can draw on their own strengths and interests, while still working towards the same learning goals?
column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18: I enjoyed this lesson for several reasons, first because it helped students understand that entropy isn't that things "like to spread out" or "like disorder" but it is simply probabilities. It's math come to life, it also was absolutely amazing how well the activity worked, students could see in real time why being evenly distributed isn't anything magical, its just the most likely situation. However, reflecting on the activity I wish that I had students reflect individually first, instead of immediately bringing it together as a class. I think this would have helped students draw on their own strengths instead of immediately being part of a group. Perhaps some students still needed some time to sit with the data and understand it on their own time. I also wish that I had prepared discussion questions as well that students could reflect on individually or with their table partner first before sharing as a class, this may have helped students draw on their own ideas before moving on. I have a range of abilities in this class and I think providing choice for how much time they want or need to spend on certain concepts and ideas would be beneficial for all as a group.

column7:
3 students were present in the DP2 Mandarin B class, seated together at a table with Bei.

Students were reviewing conditional relationships in Mandarin, which Bei identified as a challenging area of the DP Paper 2. Students worked from a review sheet containing different sentence structures and examples and made notes and annotations directly onto the paper.

The majority of the conversation took place in Mandarin. Bei moved between Mandarin and English at points to clarify meaning or explain a particular structure, and students also used English occasionally when working through an explanation.

Bei reviewed the conditional structures with the students, asking questions and working through examples together. Students responded verbally, added notes to their review sheets and asked Bei questions as they worked.

The small group remained seated together throughout the observed portion of the lesson, with the discussion moving between Bei and the three students.

The whiteboard contained prompts for analysing a conversation, including identifying the text type, the relationship between the speakers, when and where the interaction took place, and the main content of the recording. Vocabulary connected to the context was also recorded on the board, including language related to shopping, trying on clothes, payment and returning or exchanging goods.

The class was quiet throughout the observation, with all three students participating in the review and discussion.
column9: To what extent are students utilizing authentic research, inquiry, and information literacy strategies?
column10: I appreciated how the learning was grounded in the kind of authentic language students will encounter and need to interpret outside the classroom. Students were not simply working with vocabulary or grammar in isolation; they were considering the context of a conversation, the relationship between the speakers, where and when it was taking place, and what was actually being communicated. The discussion around a real-world context such as shopping also required students to use contextual clues and their existing language knowledge to make meaning, which felt much closer to how we actually use and understand language in everyday life.
column12: In what ways are students creating products or performances for authentic audiences?
column13: I liked how the learning was connected not only to what they need for a paper 2, but also to situations where students would genuinely need to use Mandarin beyond the classroom. The focus on conversations around shopping, payment, trying on clothes and returning or exchanging goods gave students opportunities to think about how they would communicate with a real Mandarin-speaking audience. Rather than language being practised only for an assessment, students were working with the vocabulary, structures and conventions they would need to successfully navigate these interactions themselves.
column14: Thanks for having me in your class this morning Bei. I wonder how the small size of this class could allow you to personalize the learning even further for each of the three students. The close discussion already gives you opportunities to respond to individual questions and areas of difficulty, but there may also be space for students to have more choice in the contexts, topics or types of language they use as they prepare for the DP assessments. How might you use what you know about each students individual strengths, needs and interests to give them greater ownership over some of the contexts through which they practise and develop their Mandarin?
column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18:
I would say that the small class size gives me quite a lot of opportunities to personalize the learning. I usually start with a 1530 minute mini-lesson to introduce the key language and ideas related to the topic. During the mini-lesson, I check students understanding through activities such as reading and recognizing sentences, identifying key points, and discussing examples.
For writing practice in particular, I can give students more individualized and detailed feedback based on the topics they are interested in. After each writing task, I also guide each student to identify a specific goal for their next piece of writing and discuss strategies for how they can achieve it. This helps students understand their own strengths and areas for improvement and gradually take more ownership of their learning.

column7:
You opened by asking students how they were feeling, using emojis and French vocabulary displayed on the screen. Students responded verbally in French, you then were asking follow-up questions and encouraging them to explain their answers. You corrected pronunciation when needed and gave students the vocabulary or structures needed to extend their responses.

Students were able to use English when they did not know a particular French word, that you then provided the French vocabulary for and had students incorporate it into their response.

The opening conversation connected to students own experiences. One student explained that she was tired because she had been swimming that morning, while another talked about sleeping late. This gave students an opportunity to use the target language in relation to their own lives rather than responding only to predetermined examples.

You reviewed the date in French. The date and related language were recorded on the whiteboard, alongside English annotations to clarify meaning and sentence structure. A student notebook showed students recording these examples and translations.

Visual supports were used throughout, including emojis for feelings and images for weather vocabulary. You introduced/reviewed expressions including heureuse, fatiguée, anxieuse, triste, frustrée and confiante, as well as weather expressions such as il pleut, il y a du vent, il fait chaud and il fait froid.

Students were given opportunities to answer orally throughout the observed portion of the lesson rather than simply listening to vocabulary instruction.

For the next activity, you changed students table partners. You initially gave the instructions in French and then repeated/clarified them in English when students indicated that they did not fully understand.

The classroom atmosphere was relaxed and informal. Students appeared comfortable responding even when they did not immediately have the French vocabulary they needed, and Leila supported them in moving from their initial idea in English towards expressing it in French.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: Leila, I really liked the way you created space for students to bring their own experiences into their French learning. The opening conversation about how students were feeling allowed them to talk about what was actually happening in their lives, rather than simply practising predetermined responses. I also appreciated the flexibility you gave students to use English when they did not yet have the French vocabulary they needed, before supporting them to express that same idea in French. This felt particularly responsive to the different levels of confidence and language development within the class. Students were able to start from where they were, while you continued to stretch their vocabulary and encourage increasingly independent use of French.
column12: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column13: I really liked the agency students had in shaping the conversations and deciding what they wanted to communicate in French. Rather than simply reproducing set phrases, students were making decisions about how to respond based on their own feelings and experiences, and then working out how to communicate those ideas with the language they currently have. I also liked that students could take a risk by starting with English when they did not know a word, knowing that you would help them find the French rather than allowing the missing vocabulary to stop the conversation. This gave students ownership over what they wanted to say while still moving them towards greater confidence and independence in French.
column14: Leila, I wonder how you might build on the confidence students are developing in using strategies when they do not immediately have the French they need. I saw students draw on English, visual cues, prior vocabulary and your support to find a way to communicate their ideas. There could be an opportunity to make those strategies more explicit so students begin to recognise that what they are learning is not only French vocabulary, but also how to navigate situations where they do not yet have all the language or knowledge they need. How might you help students identify the strategies they are using successfully in French and reflect on where else, either in another subject or beyond school, those same strategies could help them work through uncertainty or communicate effectively?
column16: How do we help students generalize a mindset or strategy from one subject or setting to another?
column18: I try to make these strategies explicit when there is a reading or listening support. I find that this is better for the students when they are practicing a receptive skill rather than a productive skill (speaking or writing). We look for roots, word families, etc. Sometimes, this has to happen on an individual basis for this age.

column7:
At the time of observation, Amelie was seated on the carpet with the PK4 Tigers. She used a familiar song to signal the transition from play to group learning, and students began gathering quietly on the carpet. Once settled, Amelie invited students to recall their previous learning about being caring and helpful. Students shared examples from their own lives of ways they could demonstrate caring and helpful behavior. 

Throughout the discussion, Amelie reinforced participation expectations by calling on students who raised their hands and gently redirecting those who called out. She then introduced the idea of an opposite, using familiar examples such as hot and cold and big and small before connecting this concept to caring and unkind behavior. 

Amelie used a series of photographs to help students identify different examples of unkind behavior. These included pushing, taking something from another person, drawing on another person's back, and excluding someone during lunch. When students initially interpreted one image as sharing, Amelie encouraged them to look more closely at the children's facial expressions. Students reconsidered their initial thinking and identified the interaction as unkind. 

Amelie then introduced the idea that when unkind behaviors happen repeatedly, they may be considered bullying. Using additional images, she introduced different ways bullying might occur, including physical behavior, exclusion, taking or damaging belongings, and verbal behavior. Students were then invited to apply their understanding by categorizing photographs according to the type of behavior represented.
column9: Do students have access to strategies for self-care and emotional well-being?
column10: You provided multiple entry points into a complex social-emotional concept through familiar examples, discussion, photographs, facial expressions, and categorization. This was particularly responsive to the cognitive and linguistic needs of PK4 learners, as students did not have to rely on verbal explanation alone to understand ideas such as opposite, kind, and unkind.
column12: In what ways does authentic learning promote a sense of connection to the broader world?
column13: You connected the learning to situations young children can recognize from their own social worlds. Students first contributed examples of caring and helpful behavior from their lives and then considered realistic situations involving pushing, belongings, words, and exclusion. This aligns strongly with the emphasis on connecting learning to meaningful real-world contexts. Because the scenarios were recognizable, students were able to move beyond identifying vocabulary and begin making sense of behaviors they may encounter in their own relationships.
column14: As students become increasingly able to identify and categorize unkind behaviors, how might they also begin to practice what they could do when they encounter one? For example, could students choose from or role-play simple PK4 responses such as using words to say stop, moving away, inviting an excluded peer to join, or seeking help from a trusted adult.
column16: To what extent do students apply what they learn to real-world contexts?
column18:
Thank you! I intentionally adjusted the language in this lesson based on my reflection from last year. Previously, I introduced terms such as physical bullying, verbal bullying, exclusion, and damaging belongings. This year, I used simpler, more developmentally appropriate language to help PK4 students understand these concepts. The photographs and repeated examples were also intentional supports for the two students in the class who are still developing their language skills, allowing them to access the learning without relying solely on verbal explanations.

I also appreciate the wondering about taking action. The observed section focused on building the foundational skill of recognizing and categorizing unkind and bullying behaviors. The response strategies come later in the lesson sequence. Students will learn and practise what they can do when these situations occur, including saying Stop clearly and telling a trusted adult. Visuals, discussion, and role-play will help them rehearse these responses and apply their learning to real-life situations.

column7:
At the time of observation, Kitty prepared the KA and KB students for learning by ensuring they were seated quietly on the carpet. She began by greeting students individually and asking them questions in Chinese, such as, What is your name? and How old are you? Kitty appeared to adjust the level of language and questioning based on each students Chinese language proficiency. When students needed additional support, she used translanguaging to scaffold their understanding and enable them to respond successfully. 

Kitty then transitioned students into a series of songs focused on reinforcing number vocabulary and counting. Before beginning, she showed students a visual representation of how numbers are represented using fingers in Chinese and reviewed the numbers orally with them. She then played a song and accompanying video. During the first song, students were also transitioning from the carpet back to their seats, which meant that not all students were fully attending to the song and visual representation. As students settled, Kitty sang along and some students joined in when they recognized familiar sections. 

A second number-themed song followed, and students were noticeably more able to participate. Kitty periodically paused or interacted with the song by asking number-related questions and reinforcing related Chinese vocabulary. 

Following the songs, Kitty explained that students would complete their paper dice, which displayed numbers they had been learning, and would be able to take them home once finished. Students who had already completed their dice used them by rolling and identifying the number in Chinese. The Educational Assistant documented students demonstrating their learning on an iPad so that this evidence could later be shared through Seesaw.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: You were particularly responsive to the different Chinese language proficiency levels within the group. By adjusting your questions for individual students and using translanguaging when additional scaffolding was needed, you created an accessible entry point that allowed students at different stages of language development to participate successfully. The combination of spoken Chinese, gesture, finger representations, music, video, and oral rehearsal further provided students with multiple ways to access and make sense of the number vocabulary.
column12: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column13: You shifted students from practicing numbers collectively to individually demonstrating their understanding through the paper dice. Students rolled their own dice, identified the resulting number in Chinese, and had their learning documented for Seesaw. This moved them beyond simply repeating vocabulary after an adult and gave them an opportunity to independently retrieve and communicate what they knew.
column14: How might students take an even more active role during the song and counting portion of the lesson? For example, could individual students lead the finger representations, choose a number for classmates to represent, or ask a number question of the group? This could shift more of the talk and thinking from you to the students, while still maintaining the repetition and language scaffolds that are important at this age.

Moving forward, I could invite individual students to lead the finger representations, choose a number for the class to show, or ask a number-related question to their peers. I could also give students more opportunities to take the lead in familiar songs, while continuing to provide the visual and language scaffolds they need. This would help shift more of the talk and decision-making to students and further support their agency.Thank you?

At the time of observation, Brittany had just completed a self-regulation activity focused on the strategy of squeezing lemons. She then introduced the picture book The Lion Inside and invited students to examine the cover and share what information they could glean from the illustration. Students offered a wide range of observations and predictions. 

As Brittany prepared to begin reading, she noticed that several students were becoming dysregulated at their tables. She responded by inviting the class to move to the carpet and took a moment to re-establish expectations for full body listening before continuing. Brittany then read The Lion Inside, using the mouses journey to explore the idea that finding your voice is not about being the loudest or strongest, but about having the confidence and courage to speak up when something matters. Throughout the story, she paused to ask questions that encouraged students to make connections and think about the characters choices. She also connected the mouses actions to the Learner Profile attribute of being a risk-taker. 

At the conclusion of the story, Brittany displayed the statement, Stop. I dont like that! and explicitly modelled how it could be communicated using an assertive voice. Students then practised the phrase along a continuum from a voice that was too soft, to assertive, to one that was too strong. This provided students with a concrete communication strategy they could use when standing up for themselves or others and connected directly to the schools current focus on Upstander Month.
column9: Do students have access to strategies for self-care and emotional well-being?
column10: You were highly responsive to students regulation needs throughout the lesson. Beginning with the squeezing lemons strategy and later recognizing when students needed a change of setting before the read-aloud demonstrated that regulation was treated as an integral part of readiness for learning rather than something separate from it. By explicitly teaching and revisiting these strategies, you were helping students build a repertoire they can increasingly draw upon to manage their own emotional states.

column13: You made the focus of Upstander Month concrete and actionable for students by moving beyond simply discussing courage in The Lion Inside. Modelling and practising Stop. I dont like that! gave students specific language and an opportunity to experience the difference between being passive, assertive, and overly forceful. This helped translate the idea of being an upstander into a practical skill students can use to advocate for themselves and others in authentic social situations.

column18:
I really appreciate this wondering because increasing student agency was an intentional next step in the lesson. After the portion of the lesson that was observed, students moved from practicing the modeled phrase Stop. I dont like that to applying the assertive-voice strategy more independently. During a movement-based partner activity, students responded to short peer scenarios. Rather than being given a script, students decided for themselves what they might say and practiced communicating their response using a calm, clear, and strong voice.

Students then applied the skill independently through Seesaw. They were presented with a new scenario, typed what they would say, and recorded themselves using their own words and an assertive voice. I see this progression as, I hear it, I practice it, I choose what to say, I use it.

I also see the Guidance lesson as the Tier 1 learning foundation rather than the endpoint of the learning. What I particularly value is what happens after the lesson, when students encounter authentic peer situations and have an opportunity to use the strategy in context. During individual check-ins, conflict interventions, or restorative conversations, I can return to the shared language from GuidanceWhat do you need? How could you say that with a calm, clear, and strong voice?and support students in choosing and using the strategy themselves. Over time, the goal is for students to need less adult prompting and increasingly draw on these tools independently.

I do wonder if perhaps a blue sky type visualizing would work - Once you have created the three sketches come up with a Blue sky design where everything is OK, maybe there is zero gravity, circular features, plasma doors or windows

This was my lesson on impulse and momentum.  The kids enjoy this lesson because they can directly observe its effects.  We started the lesson with some mathematical derivations, some examples, then we did some demonstrations in rolling chairs.  The kids were engaged in this and this is where I asked them to think of other situations where this is applicable (which is where we got the examples in class). 
Depending on the class, I will tailor this lesson to the kids interests and from discussions with these students, I was aware that many of them are fans of racing and cars so for this lesson, I used that to get their buy-in.  The start of the lesson was examples of the physics of car crashes and the ramification of the momentum and energy involved and then finally the subsequent calculations.  Its a great way for me to meet the kids where they are at.  

Closure of the lesson is typically the weakest part of my lesson, it's something I have been trying to work on for quite some time.  This lesson is a good example as to why I struggle with it . column18:
The aim of this lesson was to introduce students to the origins of Chinese and Western poetry, and to the close relationship between poetry and the arts of music and dance.
During the lesson, I showed two scenes: one was a reconstruction of a Han dynasty court banquet, where poems were chanted to musical accompaniment; the other depicted an ancient Greek rhapsode performing the Homeric epics.
I then posed three questions to the class:
What connections did you notice between ancient Chinese poetry, music, and dance? How would you describe their relationship to one another?
What connections did you notice between ancient Greek poetry and music? How would you describe their relationship?
What similarities and differences do you see between ancient Chinese and ancient Greek poetry? Please be specific.
Students then broke into small groups to discuss these questions, and each group shared their conclusions with the whole class. Drawing on their discussions and presentations, I closed the lesson with a summary and feedback of my own. My hope was that by moving through this cycle of thinking, exchanging, sharing, and receiving feedback, students would come to a deeper understanding  and that cycle is essentially the framework behind how I designed the lesson.

- Grade 7 Science class. 16 students in this class. Start of observation at 10:30
- EAL and LIT push-in support is available in this class.
- Students are working on sample data about thermal energy transfer.

- The teacher is asking students what are some challenges they had as they were conducting the experiments with their peers. For example: it was difficult to get the exact amounts, measuring the temperature was slow.

column9: How might we ensure students have opportunities to reflect on their planning, thinking, work, and/or progress?
column10: Students were explicitly encouraged to reflect on their experimental process and identify improvements. Students considered challenges they experienced during the experiment, such as accurately measuring quantities and temperature, and then identified what they could do differently next time. This makes reflection an active part of the scientific process.
column12: To what extent are students utilizing authentic research, inquiry, and information literacy strategies?
column13: Students were using experimental data to identify and communicate scientific patterns and trends. Creating graphs from the thermal-energy data required students to organize and interpret evidence rather than simply describe the experiment, directly supporting the skills assessed through Criterion C.
column14: How can you use the students' reflections on their experimental challenges to help them to independently propose one specific change to the investigation?
column16: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column18:
The lesson was part of a formative investigation. The investigation was very scaffolded and had identified variables students could manipulate. Students reflect on their challenges and consider them in their next formative/summative. 

We identified the challenge ? cause ? category ? specific change; so they see what "specific" actually looks like (e.g., "use Loggerpro to reduce reaction-time error in the timing" rather than "be more accurate"). We investigate it together an then they investigate it on their own.

Were just practicing, while also affirming the quality of thinking he observed. column14: Really loved getting into your class. column18:
Thanks for the observation, Andrew. The calm you noticed is partly due to a recent seating change. I mixed 9th and 10th graders with boys and girls to curb spoken Chinese, which worked almost too well; I actually miss some of their chatty energy and am still figuring out how to bring that back in a more structured way. 

The "just practicing" framing and handout with extension fables were deliberate scaffolds for the students who shut down when they cant find the right answers, and the predictability you saw helps reduce cognitive overload for students still building their confidence in English. I want them to feel successful but also challenged.

As for sharing this with colleagues, Im honestly a bit hesitant to claim expertise. Much of what works here is specific to language acquisition contexts, but I'd be happy to chat with anyone about what might actually transfer, like making the invisible visible through clear materials and explicit permission to be wrong. Maybe its the scaffolding?

column18:
Thank you for the thoughtful observation and feedback yesterday  it really means a lot, especially since improving my literacy centers has been my individual goal this year, so it was great to hear that the aspects I've been focused on are landing well.

To answer your question: groupings are flexible across every subject area except reading centers. For reading, I group students based on their phonics and decoding data to place them into instructional bands (I use five color-coded groups: Blue, Yellow, Orange, Green, Purple). This lets me target word work and guided reading at each group's actual instructional level.

These groups aren't fixed forever  I do shift students as I see their skills develop and new strengths emerge. That said, I've deliberately kept them fairly consistent from week to week for now, because with a rotating cycle of centers, moving students too frequently would make it hard to guarantee that every child is getting a balanced spread of literacy activities (phonics, fluency, word work, guided reading, etc.) over the course of a cycle. So the trade-off I've made is: less week-to-week fluidity in reading groups, in exchange for more precise, level-matched instruction and a more reliable balance of activity types for each student.

Thanks again for the encouraging feedback!

column7: I observed a Learning Inclusion teacher working in the learning resource room with a Grade 6 student in a pull-out one-on-one session. The student and teacher were sitting side-by-side. The teacher used the tabletop whiteboards to discuss dividing fractions. The student watched and contributed as the teacher worked through 4 different ways of solving a fraction question. The student answered questions when prompted, and the teacher used scaffolded questions or references to prior learning, such as equivalent fractions. The teacher retaught how the Math teacher showed the student the question. Then asked the student how she felt about each strategy. The room had one other Learning Inclusion teacher working with another student. This did not seem to bother them. The teacher had the student show me ways they had developed for the student to ask for help without using words, rather using a hand-gesture prompt that other teachers recognize. The student and teacher were laughing at a few points as they went through the problem-solving process. Prior to this observation, I knew that the teacher had created a student profile for all teachers to understand the student's learning needs and strategies that support her learning. The teacher has also had a stand-up with the teachers to discuss this student. The classroom environment was organized with tools, such as whiteboard markers, pens, pencils, etc readily accessible to the students. The teachers have also created two study boxes for a quiet or testing workspace that the students can access.
column9: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column10: You have intentionally developed a non-verbal hand gesture the student can use to ask for help, and you have collaborated with her teachers so this strategy is understood across learning environments. This strengthens the students independence and agency by giving her an accessible way to communicate what she needs rather than relying on adults to anticipate it. The student profile and stand-up meetings with teachers further support consistency across her team. This strongly reflects AISGs One Student. One Team. One Plan. approach.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13: You provided multiple entry points into dividing fractions by modeling four strategies, connecting to prior learning such as equivalent fractions, and using scaffolded questioning. Importantly, you then asked the student how she felt about each strategy. This moved beyond simply reteaching the mathematics and invited the student to identify which approaches worked for her as a learner. The accessible materials and availability of quieter workspaces further demonstrate attention to reducing barriers within the learning environment. This aligns with UDLs emphasis on proactively designing access and reducing barriers.
column14: I wonder how self-advocacy and strategy-selection skills you are developing with this student might increasingly transfer into her Tier 1 Math learning environment. column16: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?

My goal with students, particularly this student, is to build confidence and show them how to ask for support and what that means. In all of our sessions, I intentionally make it light and fun and they feed off of that and it has been working well. Laughter also reduces stress and allows the student to learn more effectively. The hand gesture is a strategy that we are working on to help the student communicate their needs with their teachers. The next step is to collaborate with their Math teacher to 1) encourage/remind them to use the signal before the student gets frustrated or overwhelmed, 2) help the teacher continue to provide multiple ways of showing Math thinking in class and to allow all students to select their preferred method of showing their thinking (i.e. exit ticket), and 3) ask the student when in Strategies class how often they are using the signal and go from there. Ideally, this student could also be a model for others who would benefit from the same strategies and they could show others how to ask for support.

I was also happy to involve students in connecting the learning to situations from their own lives. Allowing enough time for students to think, share, and reflect was a wondering from my previous observation, so this is something I have been intentionally working on. Thank you for noticing the difference and recognizing the progress in this area.

I also appreciate the wondering about the vocabulary-rich content. Although I used Mandarin at times to support individual students, I would like to make the key concepts more accessible to all learners through consistent visuals, gestures, photographs, role-play, and child-friendly definitions. I can also introduce fewer new words at one time, provide sentence stems, allow partner discussion before whole-group sharing, and revisit the same vocabulary across several lessons. One students asks about having mulitple characters and if they need a second graphic organsier.  SW says she will show a way to address that.  She continues to add to her graphic organiser and then shows the group her plan.  Then she introduces a second way to plan, using posit-it notes, suggesting they can take a post-it for each character, one for setting and so on.  She points out there are different sizes of post-it notes. She then shows they might want to take paper and cut shapes for different parts of the story, coming back to the idea that there are different ways to plan.
SW then asks the children to turn to the person next to them to tell them how they will plan today, listing the choices they have and adding they might just want to use the paper without cutting.  
She asks the students to show her their choices using a visual signal (hand on head if
, finger on nose if
.  Ect).  Then she sends the students to start planning a table at a time.  She writes on the board the parts they need to include in their plan: character, setting, problem and solution. 
Students choose the materials they need and go to tables to work.
column9: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column10: During this session students were being empowered to make decisons about thier learning. You were very clear throughout the minilesson that students have options for how they might want to plan.  You modelled one but also provided several others.  Students were given a framework of what to think about but could then choose how they orgasnied thier thinking around these sections.  With phrases such as "this might not work for you" "you might prefer" you reenforced the idea that not everyone works the same way.  As students went to plan, a variety of formats were used.  They were encroauged to try out and see what works.  This "permission" is freeing and suports learners who need to approach the task differently.
column12: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column13: Although all the students were working on the same task (realistic fiction picture book), you modelled a planning process that took inspiration form publushed authors and from your own experience.  This modelling supports studnets to think about thier own experiences and use that to help them create stories.  You mentioned "inspiration" several times when thinking about ideas, which sends a message of using what we see, know, have read about as a basis for our stories is ok, in fact  it is something writers do! Modelling your process and vocalizing your thinking helps give students a template for how they might approach a task and shows you as a learner alongside them.
column14: The focus of this minilesson was to give students different formats for organising their ideas when planning, and it did that sucessfully.  However, in order for planning to be a useful exercise, it helps to know  why writers do this and how they refer to it as they write.  I am wondering if you have explored with them already why writers might plan before writing?

column10:
There was a strong sense that students ideas and connections were valued within the discussion.

Lots of students were keen to contribute, ask questions and make connections to the text. I particularly noticed how you paraphrased what students shared and then connected their thinking back to the vocabulary on the board or ideas within the text.

column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13:
There were a number of supports in place to help students access the Chinese text and make meaning as they read.

The combination of Pinyin, vocabulary on the whiteboard and additional notes alongside the text gave students different reference points as they worked through the language as well as some visuals included in the text.

This supported students having different ways to access and make sense of the learning while still participating in the same shared text and discussion.
column14:

column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18: Thank you for visiting the Grade 5 Chinese A class. The turn and talk activity was aimed for a comprehension check and a reinforcement of the understanding the mentor text. To strengthen students' participation, I will continue to work with students on pairing discussion partners, and setting clear roles (such as summarize or build on what the partner says). Also, I have been utilizing Class Dojo as a visual reminder for acknowledging students' on task participation. Sometimes I record students' participation after every prompt or question is being discussed; other times I record them when the whole activity is completed. Students respond well to this system that encourages more risk-taking and positive contribution.

column7: I was observing Amy's English B DP1 class. There were 6 students in the class. They were working on a reading practice and DP practice paper. There were two students sitting at desks across from each other reading independently. 4 students were sitting in the flexible seating area reading out loud together, taking turns. They called the teacher over for clarification on some vocabulary. I spoke to one of the student working independently. He told me he found the reading interesting and we discussed the strategies he uses when he comes up to words he does not know. First he reads it a few times to see if he can get the meaning from the sentence. Then he writes it in his note book and looks it up in the dictionary later. One of the students went off topic and started talking about work from other classes, the teacher was in proximity to help her get back to work. The teacher gave reminders on how to answer questions for DP examination purposes as they started answering the comprehension questions.
column9: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column10: Students demonstrated independence during the reading practice. One student clearly articulated the strategies he uses when encountering unfamiliar vocabulary: rereading the word and sentence several times to infer meaning from context, recording the word in his notebook, and looking it up later. This provides evidence of a student monitoring his own understanding and independently selecting strategies to support comprehension. From a Tier 1 perspective, developing these self-regulation and metacognitive strategies supports students in accessing challenging texts without immediately relying on teacher assistance. This aligns with the TLF emphasis on students taking increasing ownership of their learning and developing confidence and independence.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: Students engaged with the reading task through both independent and collaborative structures. Four students chose to read aloud together, took turns, and recognized when they needed additional support, calling the teacher over to clarify the meaning of a word. Two other students worked independently. The teacher remained available without taking over the learning, responding to questions and using proximity to support a student in returning to the task. From a Tier 1 perspective, these different participation structures provided students with multiple ways to engage while maintaining access to teacher support. The collaborative group also demonstrated communication and self-regulation as they worked toward a shared learning goal.
column14: Students demonstrated considerable independence during the DP reading practice, while the teacher provided vocabulary clarification, proximity support, and reminders about DP examination expectations. I wonder how quick formative checks for understanding might make each students comprehension and application of DP strategies more visible while preserving this independence. This could provide additional evidence for deciding who is ready to continue independently, who might benefit from further modelling or scaffolding, and who is ready for extension.
column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18: Hi Sam, thanks for coming in to see my DP students. Rather than having students complete all of the comprehension questions at once, the questions were chunked by question type. After each section, we checked and discussed responses before students moved on. This allowed me to see how well students understood both the reading and the different DP question types, while giving students the opportunity to clarify misunderstandings and then apply that feedback to the next set of questions. The task itself was also scaffolded for where the students currently are in DP1. In the DP examination, students normally work with three texts, whereas this practice focused on just one. Reducing the reading load gave students more time to process the text, practice their reading strategies, and focus specifically on how to approach the different types of comprehension questions they will encounter on the exam. As students become more confident with these strategies, the amount of scaffolding can gradually be reduced and the reading demands increased toward full DP examination expectations.

column7:
There were 17 students present, initially seated around the piano. A guest performer was seated at the piano and performed Loving You, singing while accompanying herself. Students watched and listened during the performance, while Cy stood slightly to the side of the group.

Following the performance, Cy gave instructions for the next part of the class. He explained that students would begin by working together as a whole ensemble and that smaller groups would later work with the guest performer.

Students then worked on Let Me Listen with Cy conducting. Each student had a copy of the score, They started from the top of the piece with instructions that they would begin rehearsing from approximately measure 56 later in their smaller groups. Students sang their individual parts while moving between looking at their scores and looking towards Cy as he conducted.

Cy gave specific reminders about vowel and mouth placement as well as volume. Students repeated sections following this feedback while Cy continued to conduct. Different vocal parts were performed simultaneously as the group worked through the piece.

The guest performer remained present during the whole-ensemble rehearsal, with smaller groups scheduled to work with her afterwards.
column9: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column10: I really liked the way collaboration was built into the rehearsal. Students needed to know their own vocal part, but they also had to listen to the other parts and adjust how they were singing as the ensemble came together. I noticed students moving between their scores, watching Cy and listening to each other as they rehearsed and repeated sections. The opportunity to work with the guest musician also extended this collaboration, giving students another person to learn with and from. This was a good example of students needing each other for the learning to work; no individual voice could sit separately from what the rest of the ensemble was doing.
column12: To what extent is student work authentic and reflective of that done by experts outside of school?
column13: I really liked the authenticity of the learning in this class. Students were not learning about how a choir rehearses; they were actually working as a choir. They were reading from a published score, responding to a conductor, listening across different vocal parts, receiving specific feedback and then immediately applying that feedback as they rehearsed again. Having a guest musician working alongside the students added another layer to this, giving them the opportunity to observe and then work directly with someone beyond their regular classroom teacher. The process I observed closely reflected the way musicians work together to develop and refine a performance.
column14:
Thanks for having me in your class today. It was also espcially lucky for me to see the students working with the guest vocalist. 

I wonder about how personalization can work within a learning experience like choir, where there is necessarily a strong collective goal and students need to work together towards a shared performance. I could see students managing their own vocal parts and responding to feedback as the ensemble rehearsed, but I wonder where there might also be space for individual needs, interests or goals to shape the learning. The planned small-group work with the guest musician may provide one opportunity for this, particularly if students are able to receive more targeted feedback or focus on an aspect of their own performance.

How might you create opportunities within the collective work of the choir for students to identify and work towards individual goals, needs or interests, while still maintaining the shared goals of the ensemble?
column16: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column18: Thank you for coming to observe our class today. Thank you also for your personalization Wonder as it is especially appropriate given today's rehearsal plan. Prior to this class period, students engaged with an individual assignment (FOR due Thursday last week) where they record themselves singing at their current progress  level in our repertoire. I will view those videos and open conversations with those students both in-person and in formative feedback on the formative assessment. Students will then continue to develop their strategies to improve their vocal music skills. Eventually, they will have between three to five video and audio performance recordings and a variety of reflections and feedback which summarizes and journals their progress as an individual singer. We also do work in small groups led by students at nearly every rehearsal. I drop in to each rehearsal to listen and support their learning through encouragement and feedback.

Children are sat on the carpet playing a game from morning meeting What are you doing.  WH and IC are standing watching the game.  On the screen are the instructions for the game.

WH sat on stool by screen on laptop.  IC monitoring students.

.. They talk a little more then A returns to desk.
Children begin sitting at desks.  Two children are sat with heads down on the table. 2 minutes left on timers and most are back. 
On screen is IM slide showing Cumulative propert and snorkl QR code.
WH gives out papers and IC goes outside to bring in last couple of students.  WH does a call and respond to bring class to focus,

WH moves the slide to show Lets plan a game night.

A clear time limit was given for transition, with a description of where and how the students would be at the end of that time.  A personal reminder was given to one student that now would be a good time to go to the restroom.  Other students left the room, some gathered together, others sat on thier own.  The time limt was genreous and in the end not needed as studnets were almost all back well before the end.  They had been given the trust and agency to use this time to meet their needs (water, restroom, talking, moving, sitting) so that they could be ready to learn.  They were also given responsbilitiy to ensure that they then had the equipement needed.  Some children took pencils from a zipbag they had in their chair poskces, others from a communcal pot.  IC was monitring students but onyl intervened at the end when it was clear the group was ready to start and two studetns were still outisde. In intentionally planning this transition time, and etablishing this routine you are showing the students you aknowledge they have different needs and trust them to meet them in a repsonsible way, thus supporting them to develop self regulation skills and readiness for learning.

From that being abstract, it made sense and they could see people sat around a mahjong table. column7: I was observing Ashley the EAL specialist co-teaching with a grade 5 HR teacher. Students were all working on iPads, researching different biomes independently. The research questions were on the screen for everyone to access in English. The HR teacher told me the students had started with a map provocation. Ashley was moving between students to support and answer clarifying questions. With one student, she sat next to her providing support with vocabulary, with another she made the student's thinking visible by writing out what the student was saying. For other students on the EAL roster, they independently picked strategies to help them complete this task - one student used headphones to have Epic read the book aloud, another used Google Translate, and two students seemed to be translanguaging. I spoke to two students, and they could tell me what they were doing - researching different types of biomes. They were unsure why they were doing it or what they would do with their research.
column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10: Students had access to a range of language supports while participating in the same biome inquiry as their peers. Several multilingual learners independently selected strategies that supported their individual language needs: one student used headphones so Epic could read the text aloud, another used Google Translate, and two students appeared to be translanguaging as they processed information. These visible Tier 1 accommodations provided multiple pathways into the same learning without separating students from the core task. Particularly encouraging was the independence with which students selected these tools, suggesting that they were able to draw on strategies that supported their own access and understanding.
column12: In what ways are students empowered to make decisions about their learning?
column13: Ashley moved between students, responding to questions and providing clarification while students remained responsible for their own research. In one interaction, she captured a students spoken ideas in writing, making the students thinking and language visible rather than taking over the thinking for them. This provided a useful Tier 1 scaffold between oral language, ideas, and written language. Together with students independently selecting digital and linguistic supports, the learning environment allowed students to receive support while continuing to develop independence and ownership.
column14: Students could explain that they were researching different biomes, while some were less clear about why they were doing the research or what they would do with it next. I wonder how making the purpose of the inquiry more visible, alongside key language and vocabulary supports, might help multilingual learners connect what they are doing with why they are doing it and where the learning is going.
column16: How might we design lessons to highlight diverse contributions to fields that may not often be highlighted within the mainstream curricula?

column7:
Grade 5D  Music 

Students are in the middle of their Music lesson and are discussing the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival performance, which includes songs in both Mandarin and Cantonese.

Students move into a reflection activity using their iPads. Three reflection prompts are displayed together as one phrase. Students respond independently using either voice-to-text or writing.

Tchafikah calls Isabella, Renee, Simon and Liam to support with the next activity. The students help organise the claps, rhythms, movements and timing for a whole-class game.

Impress me with your dancing  earn a point back.

FA: "5D ready to go in 3, 2, 1.

Part 1.

Part 2.

The lyrics are displayed and students perform accompanying actions. Students appear familiar with the movements and choreography and participate together.

Tchafikah stops the rehearsal and explains that the choreography for this class needs to move in the opposite direction from another class.

I forgot
 other classes have to do this backwards and I have to retrain my brain.

column9: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column10:

column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13:
There was a high level of energy and enjoyment as students moved between rhythm, movement and performance.

Students were clearly familiar with many of the routines and responded quickly to countdowns and cues. During the production rehearsal, students appeared confident with the lyrics, actions and choreography and were able to reset when the direction of the movements needed to change.
column14:
Thank you Tchafikah  it was great to see the energy and enjoyment students brought to Music and how comfortable many of them already appeared with the performance material.

Although a high energy class with smooth transitions, overall the volume was very high at times, which can be disconcerting for some students.  I wonder how building in quieter moments for instructions, reflection and rehearsal might help all students hear cues, process what they need to do and then bring that same energy back into the learning.

column12: To what extent do students take ownership of their learning process?
column13:

column14:
Thanks for having me in your class!!

column7:
- Grade 6 I&S class. Start of observation at 10:10
- 21 students in class (approx.). EAL support (Ms. Nora) is available
- At the start of the observation, the teacher is assigning students a certain 'potato identity' (e.g. round potato, sweet potato, etc.)
- After assigning each student a potato identity, the teacher shows the students a scenario ('At Potato Academy, there is the belief that round potatoes are naturally better stduents than the other potatoes'). The students are then asked to determine if this scenario as either 'stereotype', 'discrimination', or 'oppression'.
- After this, there is another scenario. This one about Sweet Potatoes not being very creative. 
- The students were, to an extent, able to explain the difference between the concepts in their own words. However, there seemed to be a bit of confusion about the difference between stereotypes and discrimination. 
- The teacher, afterwards, discusses the answers with all students, clarifying the difference between both concepts (i.e. stereotypes link to assumptions and discrimination links to taking an action).
column9: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column10:
The potato identities provided a creative and accessible way for students to explore complex concepts.

Using fictional potato groups gave students a lower-risk context for discussing stereotypes, discrimination, and oppression before potentially connecting these ideas to more sensitive real-world examples.
column12: To what extent does collaborative learning enhance student learning and promote social well-being?
column13: The whole-class discussion helped surface misconceptions and develop a shared understanding of key concepts. When students showed some confusion between stereotypes and discrimination, the teacher used their responses to clarify the important distinction between an assumption and an action.
column14:
Thanks for having me in your class, Cameron. 

As someone who previously taught this unit, I am very happy to see that it developed from our initial unit we designed a couple of years ago. I think this activity is low-risk and allows the students to practice these rather difficult and challenging concepts in an engaging and rather funny matter. 

I am curious how you can then link this learning to real-world examples. In other words, how might students transfer their understanding from the fictional Potato Academy scenarios to carefully selected real-world examples of stereotypes, discrimination, and oppression?

column7:
- grade 8 Design class (start of observation at 14:10)
- 23 students in class
- Students are submitting their design ideas (criterion B) and are now working on criterion C ('Creating the Solution')
- The teacher is checking with individual students on the status of their submission and the progress of their criterion C work.

column9: To what extent do students have the opportunity to design, create, make, or otherwise add value that is unique to them?
column10:
Students are moving from planning into creating their own 3D design solutions.

Using Shapr3D allows students to turn their individual design ideas into more developed digital models, giving them space to make and refine something unique.
column12: To what extent are the  learning experiences personalized to meet student's individual needs and interests?
column13:
Students appear to have some flexibility in how they document and communicate their design thinking.

Some students used the provided PPT template, while at least one student worked from a paper design. This suggests that students can access and represent their thinking in different formats while progressing toward the same design outcome.
column14: How might students be given more explicit choice in how they document Criterion C progress? I.e. with regards to the Action Plan required for criterion C, what are some possibilities students can utilise?
column18:
Thank you very much, Ralph, for taking the time to observe the class and for your detailed and positive feedback. I especially appreciate that you highlighted how students are moving from planning towards creating their individual solutions in Shapr3D, as well as the flexibility they have to communicate their design process.

Regarding your question, each criterion has a template that students can use as a starting point to document their work. The templates keep a consistent visual identity and use the Design Cycle colours to help students identify where they are in the process, while still allowing them to add pages and personalise how they present their progress.

For Criterion C1, students use a logical-plan table to document each component of their design, including its name, dimensions, material, and quantity. However, they may also use photos, screenshots, diagrams, or video links to communicate their process. The template is intended to ensure that all required evidence is included, rather than restrict students creativity.
